adept.definition: highly skilled and proficient at something
sentences: Although she had never sailed before, the young diplomat proved adept at navigating the delicate negotiations between the two rival delegations.
Years of practice made the old carpenter so adept with his tools that he could craft a flawless drawer in an afternoon.
adept.mnemonic: Adept ≠ adepte (disciple) : l'adept est surtout doué, pas fidèle.

advocate.definition: to publicly support or recommend a cause or policy
sentences: The senator has long advocated stricter environmental regulations, arguing that voluntary measures by industry have repeatedly failed to protect the nation's rivers.
Many economists advocate lowering trade barriers, convinced that open markets ultimately benefit consumers even if some domestic producers suffer in the short term.
advocate.mnemonic: Un avocat plaide, mais to advocate = prôner une cause, pas exercer la profession.

affluent.definition: having a great deal of money; wealthy
sentences: The affluent suburb, with its sprawling lawns and gated mansions, stood in sharp contrast to the struggling neighborhoods just across the highway.
Because the region had become increasingly affluent, restaurants and boutiques catering to wealthy residents multiplied rapidly along the once-quiet main street.
affluent.mnemonic: Affluent = « qui afflue » : l'argent afflue chez lui. Pas la rivière !

sentences: The photographer's most arresting image showed a lone fisherman silhouetted against a blood-red sky, and visitors paused before it for several minutes.
Critics praised the novel's arresting opening line, which was so startling that readers felt compelled to continue past the first page.
arresting.mnemonic: Une image « arrête » le regard : elle vous saisit.

candid.definition: honest and straightforward, even when the truth is uncomfortable
sentences: In a candid interview, the retiring coach admitted that the team's poor season resulted from his own strategic mistakes rather than from bad luck.
Her candid assessment of the manuscript, though painful for the author to hear, was exactly the honest feedback needed to improve the book.
candid.mnemonic: Candid ≠ candide : en anglais, franc ; en français, naïf.

catholic.definition: broad and wide-ranging, especially in interests or tastes
sentences: The librarian's catholic taste in reading ranged from medieval poetry and quantum physics to detective fiction and obscure cookbooks.
Unlike colleagues who studied only one narrow period, the historian had catholic interests that embraced almost every era and region of the world.
catholic.mnemonic: Catholique vient du grec « universel » : catholic = très large.

censure.definition: to criticize or condemn formally and severely
sentences: The committee voted to censure the mayor for misusing public funds, though it stopped short of demanding that he resign from office.
Parliament moved to censure the minister after he misled lawmakers, publicly condemning his conduct as a serious breach of the trust of voters.
censure.mnemonic: Censure anglaise = blâme officiel, pas interdiction d'un contenu.

chauvinism.definition: prejudiced belief in the superiority of one's own sex or group
sentences: The executive's open chauvinism, which led him to ignore every suggestion made by his female colleagues, eventually prompted a formal complaint to human resources.
Feminist writers of the 1970s exposed the male chauvinism embedded in everyday language, advertising, and hiring practices, which had long been dismissed as harmless tradition.
chauvinism.mnemonic: Chauvinisme patriotique en français ; au GRE, souvent « male chauvinism ».

complacent.definition: smugly self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers or the need to improve
sentences: After three consecutive championships, the team grew complacent, skipping practices and assuming that victory would come automatically, and a humiliating defeat soon followed.
Health officials warned that the public must not become complacent about the virus, since relaxed precautions could quickly allow infections to surge again.
complacent.mnemonic: Complacent ≠ complaisant : trop content de soi, donc endormi.

condone.definition: to overlook or tolerate wrongdoing, treating it as acceptable
sentences: The principal refused to condone cheating, insisting that any student caught copying answers would face suspension regardless of past academic performance.
By failing to punish the offenders, the board seemed to condone the harassment, and critics accused its members of quietly tolerating abuse.
condone.mnemonic: Condone ≠ condamner : c'est exactement le contraire !

contention.definition: a claim or argument asserted in a debate
sentences: The biologist's central contention, that the species evolved far earlier than previously believed, was challenged by several skeptical colleagues at the conference.
Her contention that the policy would reduce unemployment was undermined by the data, which showed that joblessness had actually risen since its introduction.
contention.mnemonic: Contention ≠ contention médicale : ici, thèse défendue ou querelle.

destitute.definition: lacking the basic necessities of life; extremely poor
sentences: After the factory closed and the family lost their home, they were left destitute, dependent on charity for food and shelter.
The novelist depicted the destitute orphans of the industrial city, children so poor that they scavenged scraps of bread from the gutters.
destitute.mnemonic: Destitué = démis ; destitute = dépourvu de tout, sans un sou.

disinterested.definition: impartial; free from personal bias or self-interest
sentences: A judge must remain disinterested in the outcome of a trial, ruling solely on the evidence rather than on any personal gain.
Seeking a disinterested opinion, the company hired an outside auditor with no financial stake in the results to review the disputed accounts.
disinterested.mnemonic: Disinterested = impartial ; ne pas confondre avec uninterested (indifférent).

enervate.definition: to weaken or drain of energy and vitality
sentences: The oppressive tropical heat seemed to enervate the expedition members, who dragged themselves forward with barely enough strength to lift their packs.
Critics argued that years of constant fighting would enervate the nation, draining its resources and leaving its citizens too exhausted to rebuild.
enervate.mnemonic: Enervate ≠ énerver : il ne rend pas nerveux, il affaiblit.

exigent.definition: urgent and demanding immediate attention or action
sentences: The hospital's exigent need for blood donors, caused by a sudden highway accident, led administrators to broadcast an emergency appeal across the region.
Faced with exigent circumstances, the captain abandoned his careful plans and ordered the crew to patch the hull at once before the ship sank.
exigent.mnemonic: Exigent ≠ exigeant : ce sont les circonstances qui sont pressantes.

expeditious.definition: quick and efficient, done with speed and skill
sentences: The clerk's expeditious handling of the paperwork meant that applicants received their permits within a day instead of waiting several weeks.
Praising the engineers for their expeditious repair of the bridge, the governor noted that traffic resumed far sooner than anyone had predicted.
expeditious.mnemonic: Expeditious ≠ expéditif : vite ET bien fait, sens positif.

fastidious.definition: very attentive to detail and hard to please
sentences: The fastidious editor combed through every paragraph, correcting even the smallest errors in punctuation before allowing the book to go to press.
Known for his fastidious habits, the chef insisted that every knife be polished and every ingredient measured precisely before service began.

fitness.definition: suitability or qualification for a particular purpose or role
sentences: The committee questioned the nominee's fitness for the judgeship, citing her lack of experience and several controversial rulings earlier in her career.
Darwin argued that an organism's evolutionary fitness depends on how well its traits suit its environment, not on its strength alone.
fitness.mnemonic: Fitness = adéquation (« fit for the job »), pas seulement le sport.

formidable.definition: inspiring fear or awe because of size, power, or difficulty
sentences: The challenger faced a formidable opponent, a champion who had never lost a match and whose sheer power intimidated even veteran players.
Scaling the icy north face proved a formidable task, so daunting that most of the climbers privately doubted they would succeed.
formidable.mnemonic: Formidable en anglais fait peur : il ne veut pas dire « génial ».

sentences: A fortuitous meeting with a publisher on the train led the unknown author to a lucrative contract she had never expected.
The discovery of penicillin is often called fortuitous, since the mold that spoiled Fleming's experiment happened by luck to produce a life-saving drug.
fortuitous.mnemonic: Fortuitous contient « fortune » : un hasard heureux.

futile.definition: pointless; incapable of producing any useful result
sentences: Rescuers realized that further digging was futile, since the collapsed mine had been sealed for days and no one could have survived.
Arguing with the committee proved futile; despite hours of eloquent protest, the members refused to reconsider their decision.
futile.mnemonic: Futile ≠ futile (frivole) : en anglais, inutile, voué à l'échec.

gauche.definition: socially awkward, lacking tact or polish
sentences: The teenager's gauche attempt at small talk, in which he loudly asked the ambassador how much his watch cost, left the guests cringing.
Although brilliant in the laboratory, the young scientist was gauche at formal dinners and often committed embarrassing blunders in front of influential donors.
gauche.mnemonic: Gauche = côté gauche, maladroit : « avoir deux mains gauches ».

hardy.definition: robust and able to endure difficult conditions
sentences: Only the hardy mountain goats could survive the brutal winters on the exposed ridge, where temperatures dropped far below freezing.
The gardener chose hardy perennials that would withstand frost and drought, since she rarely had time to protect the flowers.

incense.definition: to make extremely angry; to enrage
sentences: The company's decision to lay off hundreds of workers while paying executives huge bonuses incensed the community and sparked angry protests outside headquarters.
Nothing could incense the old professor more than students who plagiarized, and he would turn red with fury whenever he discovered copied passages.
incense.mnemonic: Incense verbe = mettre en fureur, pas l'encens (qui est un nom : incense).

inconsequential.definition: of little or no importance or significance
sentences: The mayor dismissed the complaints as inconsequential, insisting that the minor delays would have no effect on the project's overall success.
What seemed an inconsequential remark at the dinner party later proved crucial, for it revealed the secret that the detective had been seeking.
inconsequential.mnemonic: Inconsequential ≠ inconséquent : sans conséquence, donc sans importance.

sentences: The inept waiter spilled soup on two customers and then forgot the third table's order entirely, prompting the manager to apologize profusely.
Critics blamed the crisis on the government's inept handling of the economy, pointing to a series of blunders that showed its lack of competence.

ingenuous.definition: innocent and trusting; lacking worldly cunning
sentences: The ingenuous young tourist trusted every stranger who offered help, never suspecting that some of them intended to cheat him.
Her ingenuous questions about politics, asked with complete sincerity and no hidden agenda, charmed the senator and disarmed his usual defensiveness.
ingenuous.mnemonic: Ingenuous ≠ ingenious (ingénieux) : ingénu, naïf et sincère.

integral.definition: essential and necessary to make something complete
sentences: Music is an integral part of the festival, so organizers refused to cut the orchestra even when the budget shrank dramatically.
The treaty's final clause, once viewed as a minor detail, proved integral to the agreement, because without it neither side would have signed.
integral.mnemonic: Integral = partie intégrante : on ne peut pas l'enlever.

martinet.definition: a person who enforces strict discipline and rigid obedience to rules
martinet.definitionFr: personne qui impose une discipline de fer
sentences: The new sergeant was a notorious martinet, inspecting every bunk with white gloves and punishing recruits for the slightest wrinkle in a blanket.
Employees dreaded working for the office martinet, who timed their lunch breaks to the second and reprimanded anyone who arrived a minute late.
martinet.mnemonic: Le martinet (fouet) = image du chef qui fouette la discipline.

mercurial.definition: unpredictable and prone to sudden changes of mood
sentences: The director's mercurial temperament made rehearsals unpredictable, for he could shift from joyful praise to furious shouting within a single minute.
Investors grew wary of the mercurial founder, whose enthusiasm for new projects changed so quickly that no strategy ever lasted through a single quarter.
mercurial.mnemonic: Mercure, le métal liquide et vif : humeur qui change sans cesse.

sentences: The detective examined the minute traces of blood on the floor, each smaller than a grain of sand, through a powerful magnifying glass.
Even a minute error in the calculation could cause the spacecraft to miss its target by thousands of miles, so engineers checked every figure.
minute.mnemonic: Minute adjectif se prononce maï-nioute : minuscule, pas la durée.

miscreant.definition: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law; a wrongdoer
sentences: The village constable chased the miscreant who had been vandalizing shop windows at night, and soon brought the young troublemaker before the magistrate.
Once a respected banker, he was now branded a miscreant by the press after investigators uncovered his scheme to defraud thousands of elderly clients.
miscreant.mnemonic: Miscreant ≠ mécréant (incroyant) : un voyou, pas un athée.

miser.definition: a person who hoards money and spends as little as possible
sentences: The old miser refused to heat his house in winter, counting every coin in his cellar while his neighbors wondered at his poverty-like habits.
Dickens's Scrooge is the classic miser, a man so devoted to hoarding wealth that he begrudges his clerk a single lump of coal.
miser.mnemonic: Miser rime avec misère : il vit pauvre alors qu'il est riche.

motif.definition: a recurring theme, subject, or distinctive idea in a work of art
sentences: The recurring motif of water in the novel, appearing in storms, rivers, and tears, symbolizes the characters' longing for renewal.
Throughout the symphony, a haunting four-note motif returns in different keys, tying the separate movements together into one unified work.
motif.mnemonic: Motif ≠ raison : en anglais, thème récurrent d'une œuvre.

mundane.definition: ordinary, dull, and concerned with everyday matters
sentences: After the thrill of the expedition, the explorer found the mundane routines of office life, with its meetings and memos, almost unbearable.
The poet had a gift for finding beauty in mundane objects, transforming a chipped teacup or a worn doorstep into subjects of wonder.
mundane.mnemonic: Mundane ≠ mondain : du monde quotidien, pas de la haute société.

sentences: The magician's final trick continued to mystify the audience, who could find no explanation for how the elephant had vanished from the stage.
Scientists remain mystified by the strange signal from deep space, which follows a pattern that none of their existing theories can account for.
mystify.mnemonic: Mystify ≠ mystifier : ici on désoriente, on ne dupe pas.

noisome.definition: having an extremely offensive or foul smell; disgusting
sentences: The noisome stench rising from the abandoned sewer forced the workers to cover their faces and retreat before they could finish the inspection.
Residents complained about the noisome fumes drifting from the chemical plant, a repulsive odor so strong that it made schoolchildren feel sick.
noisome.mnemonic: Noisome n'a rien à voir avec noisy : ça sent mauvais, ça ne fait pas de bruit.

notorious.definition: famous or well known for something bad
sentences: The notorious bandit, wanted in three states for robbing stagecoaches, was finally captured after a decade of eluding the sheriff.
The city became notorious for its corrupt police force, a bad reputation that discouraged tourists and investors from coming to the region.
notorious.mnemonic: Notorious ≠ notoire : toujours en mal, jamais en bien.

novel.definition: new, original, and unlike anything previously known
sentences: The young engineer proposed a novel approach to desalination, one that differed so radically from existing methods that experts were initially skeptical.
Because the technique was entirely novel, no textbook described it, and surgeons had to learn the procedure directly from its inventor.
novel.mnemonic: Novel adjectif = nouveau (nova), pas un roman.

officious.definition: intrusively eager to offer unwanted help or advice
sentences: The officious clerk kept hovering over customers, offering unwanted advice and rearranging their purchases until they politely begged him to leave them alone.
Her officious neighbor constantly interfered in the family's affairs, offering opinions on their parenting and garden that nobody had requested.
officious.mnemonic: Officious ≠ officieux : trop zélé, il se mêle de tout.

onerous.definition: burdensome; requiring great effort or involving heavy obligations
sentences: The new regulations imposed such onerous paperwork on small businesses that many owners hired extra staff just to keep up with the demands.
Caring for three aging relatives was an onerous duty, one that left her exhausted and with almost no time for her own life.
onerous.mnemonic: Onerous ≠ onéreux (coûteux) : c'est la charge qui pèse, pas le prix.

patent.definition: obvious and plain to see; clearly evident
sentences: It was patent to everyone in the room that the witness was lying, for his story contradicted itself within a few sentences.
The senator's patent disregard for the facts, obvious even to his supporters, damaged his credibility more than any rival's attack could have.
patent.mnemonic: Patent = « patent » = ouvert à tous les yeux : évident.

pedestrian.definition: dull and unimaginative; ordinary and lacking inspiration
sentences: Reviewers dismissed the film as pedestrian, noting that its predictable plot and flat dialogue offered nothing that audiences had not already seen many times.
Although technically correct, the student's essay was pedestrian, lacking the spark of original thought that would have distinguished it from the other submissions.
pedestrian.mnemonic: Le piéton marche à pied, terre à terre : style plat, sans éclat.

petulant.definition: childishly sulky and irritable when not getting one's way
sentences: When the referee overturned his goal, the star striker threw a petulant tantrum, kicking the ball into the stands and sulking on the bench.
The petulant child folded her arms and refused to eat, complaining loudly that nobody had asked her what she wanted for dinner.
petulant.mnemonic: Petulant ≠ pétulant (plein d'entrain) : ici, il boude comme un enfant.

plastic.definition: easily shaped or molded; capable of being changed
sentences: The sculptor preferred wet clay because its plastic quality allowed her to reshape the figure repeatedly until she achieved the form she wanted.
Neuroscientists describe the young brain as remarkably plastic, able to rewire itself in response to new experiences far more easily than an adult's.
plastic.mnemonic: Plastic ici = modelable (du grec plassein, former), pas la matière.

prevaricate.definition: to speak evasively in order to avoid telling the truth
prevaricate.definitionFr: éluder la vérité, noyer le poisson
sentences: Rather than admit that the funds were missing, the treasurer chose to prevaricate, answering each pointed question with vague and rambling remarks.
Pressed by reporters about the scandal, the spokesman continued to prevaricate, offering evasive replies that avoided any direct statement of the facts.
prevaricate.mnemonic: Prevaricate ≠ prévariquer : on tourne autour du pot, on n'est pas corrompu.

prominent.definition: important, well known, or standing out in a position of note
prominent.definitionFr: en vue, important, de premier plan
sentences: As a prominent surgeon and former head of the medical association, she was frequently consulted by journalists on questions of national health policy.
The company's founder played a prominent role in the town's affairs, funding the library and serving on nearly every important civic committee.
prominent.mnemonic: Prominent ≠ proéminent (physique) : ici, de premier plan.

propriety.definition: conformity to accepted standards of proper behavior and manners
sentences: Victorian society placed enormous value on propriety, expecting young women to follow strict rules about how they dressed, spoke, and conducted themselves.
Offended by the senator's crude jokes, the audience felt he had violated all sense of propriety expected of a public official at such a ceremony.
propriety.mnemonic: Propriety ≠ propriété : les convenances, ce qui est « proper ».

prowess.definition: exceptional skill or ability in a particular activity
sentences: The young pianist's technical prowess astonished the judges, who agreed that no competitor had ever played such difficult passages with such ease.
Admired for his military prowess, the general won battle after battle, and his skill in strategy became legendary throughout the empire.
prowess.mnemonic: Prowess : la prouesse, mais au sens de compétence habituelle.

rapport.definition: a harmonious relationship marked by mutual understanding and sympathy
sentences: The therapist worked hard to build rapport with her patients, knowing that trust and mutual understanding were essential before any real progress could begin.
A natural rapport developed between the two negotiators, who quickly found common ground and began to joke easily despite representing opposing sides.
rapport.mnemonic: Rapport ≠ rapport écrit : ici, une bonne entente, une complicité.

rebut.definition: to disprove or argue against a claim with evidence
sentences: In her closing statement, the defense attorney sought to rebut each of the prosecutor's claims by presenting documents that proved her client's innocence.
The scientist published a detailed paper to rebut critics who had questioned her data, offering new experiments that directly disproved their objections.
rebut.mnemonic: Rebut ≠ rebut (déchet) : ici on réfute un argument.

refrain.definition: to hold oneself back from doing something
sentences: Visitors to the museum are asked to refrain from using flash photography, since the bright light can damage the fragile paintings.
Although he was tempted to retort angrily, the diplomat chose to refrain from replying, knowing that silence would better protect the delicate talks.
refrain.mnemonic: Refrain verbe = se retenir (« refrain from »), pas le refrain d'une chanson.

restive.definition: restless and unable to stay still or be controlled
restive.definitionFr: agité, incapable de tenir en place
sentences: As the lecture dragged into its third hour, the restive audience began shifting in their seats and glancing impatiently at their watches.
The restive horse pawed the ground and tossed its head, refusing to stand still while the rider tried to mount it.
restive.mnemonic: Restive ≠ rester : au contraire, il ne peut pas rester en place.

sanction.definition: to give official permission or approval for something
sentences: The university refused to sanction the protest, insisting that students needed official permission before holding any demonstration on the campus grounds.
Only the governor had the authority to sanction the new highway, and she approved the plan after months of study and public hearings.
sanction.mnemonic: Sanction verbe = approuver (sens rare) ; attention, pas punir ici.

sanguine.definition: optimistic and confident, especially in a difficult situation
sentences: Despite three consecutive failed experiments, the sanguine researcher remained confident that a breakthrough was only weeks away and encouraged her discouraged team.
Analysts were sanguine about the economy's prospects, predicting that growth would recover soon even though recent figures had been disappointing.
sanguine.mnemonic: Sanguine ≠ sanguin (colérique) : le sang chaud rend optimiste, pas furieux.

solicitous.definition: showing attentive care and concern for someone's well-being
sentences: The solicitous nurse checked on the elderly patient every hour, adjusting his pillows and asking whether he needed water or another blanket.
Her solicitous host hovered around the guests, constantly refilling glasses and inquiring whether everyone was comfortable and enjoying the meal.
solicitous.mnemonic: Solicitous ≠ soucieux (inquiet) : attentionné, aux petits soins.

solvent.definition: having enough money to pay all one's debts
solvent.definitionFr: solvable, capable de payer ses dettes
sentences: Despite the recession, the family business remained solvent, with enough cash in reserve to pay all its suppliers and employees on time.
Auditors confirmed that the bank was still solvent, meaning its assets exceeded its debts, and they urged depositors not to panic.
solvent.mnemonic: Solvent adjectif ≠ solvant chimique : il peut payer ses dettes.

suppress.definition: to forcibly put an end to or hold back something
sentences: The regime used troops to suppress the uprising, arresting its leaders and crushing every attempt at open resistance across the northern provinces.
Officials tried to suppress the report, hoping that hiding its damaging findings would prevent a public scandal before the election.
suppress.mnemonic: Suppress ≠ supprimer (effacer) : on étouffe, on écrase.

susceptible.definition: likely to be affected by something; vulnerable
sentences: Elderly patients are especially susceptible to pneumonia, so doctors recommend that they receive vaccinations before the cold season begins.
Because he was so susceptible to flattery, the king was easily manipulated by advisors who praised every one of his decisions.
susceptible.mnemonic: Susceptible ≠ susceptible (vexable) : exposé à un danger ou une influence.

testament.definition: clear proof or evidence of something's existence or value
sentences: The cathedral's soaring spires stand as a testament to the skill and devotion of the medieval craftsmen who built it.
Her recovery after the accident was a testament to her courage, offering clear evidence of the extraordinary determination she possessed.
testament.mnemonic: Testament = « testimony » : preuve, pas seulement le testament d'héritage.

titular.definition: holding a title or office in name only, without real power
titular.definitionFr: de nom seulement, sans pouvoir réel
sentences: The queen was merely the titular head of state, since real power lay with the elected parliament and its prime minister.
Although he was the company's titular chairman, he rarely attended meetings, leaving every important decision to the executives who actually ran the firm.
titular.mnemonic: Titular ≠ titulaire : il porte le titre mais n'a pas le pouvoir.

treatise.definition: a formal, systematic written work on a particular subject
sentences: Adam Smith's lengthy treatise on economics, published in 1776, systematically examined how wealth is created and distributed across a nation.
The philosopher spent a decade writing a treatise on ethics, a dense scholarly work that scholars still study in universities today.
treatise.mnemonic: Treatise ≠ treaty : l'un est un livre, l'autre un accord.

truculent.definition: eager to fight; aggressively defiant and hostile
sentences: The truculent customer slammed his fist on the counter and shouted threats at the staff, apparently eager to start a fight.
Truculent and defiant, the prisoner glared at his guards and answered every question with an insult, refusing to cooperate in any way.
truculent.mnemonic: Truculent ≠ truculent (haut en couleur) : en anglais, il cherche la bagarre.

urbane.definition: polite, refined, and confident in social situations
urbane.definitionFr: courtois, policé, à l'aise en société
sentences: The urbane ambassador charmed the guests with witty conversation and impeccable manners, putting even the most nervous visitors at ease.
With his urbane charm and polished manners, the diplomat handled the awkward dinner gracefully, smoothing over every tense moment.
urbane.mnemonic: Urbane ≠ urbain (de la ville) : poli et raffiné, comme un citadin.

vex.definition: to annoy or irritate someone, especially with petty troubles
sentences: The constant delays at the airport began to vex even the most patient travelers, who muttered complaints and glared at the departure board.
Her brother knew exactly how to vex her, teasing her about her accent until she finally slammed the door in irritation.
vex.mnemonic: Vex ≠ vexer : en anglais, simplement agacer, pas blesser l'amour-propre.

discreet.definition: careful to avoid attention or giving away secrets; prudent in speech and action
sentences: The diplomat was known for her discreet handling of sensitive negotiations, never revealing a single detail to the curious reporters waiting outside.
Because the couple wanted a quiet wedding, they made discreet inquiries about private venues rather than announcing their plans to everyone they knew.
discreet.mnemonic: discreet = discret (avec 'ee'); discrete (distinct) se termine par 'te' séparé.

discrete.definition: separate and distinct; made of individual, unconnected parts
sentences: The researchers divided the long study into three discrete phases, each with its own goals, participants, and methods, so results could be compared separately.
Unlike a continuous flow of water, the data arrived as discrete packets, each one clearly separated from the next by a brief gap.
discrete.mnemonic: discrete : les deux 'e' sont séparés par le 't' — des éléments séparés.

demur.definition: to raise objections or show reluctance to accept something
sentences: When the committee proposed cutting the library's hours, only one member dared to demur, arguing that students would be seriously harmed by the change.
The manager asked her to work through the holiday weekend, and although she wanted to demur, she nodded and agreed to avoid conflict.
demur.mnemonic: demur (verbe, objecter) ≠ demure (adjectif, réservé) : le 'e' final = sagesse.

demure.definition: modest, quiet, and reserved in manner, often shyly so
sentences: With her demure smile and softly spoken replies, the young heiress seemed far too shy to ever challenge her formidable father.
Victorian novels often portrayed the ideal woman as demure, lowering her eyes in company and speaking only when addressed by someone else.

allay.definition: to reduce or calm fears, doubts, or suspicions
sentences: The company released detailed safety data in an effort to allay the public's fears about the new vaccine and restore confidence in its research.
To allay her nervous child's worries before the surgery, the mother explained patiently what would happen and promised to stay by his side.
allay.mnemonic: allay ≈ 'à l'aise' : on met à l'aise les craintes.

assuage.definition: to make an unpleasant feeling such as pain, hunger, or guilt less intense
sentences: A warm bowl of soup was enough to assuage the hunger of the exhausted hikers, who had not eaten since dawn.
Nothing the minister said could assuage the guilt she felt over the failed project, which had cost dozens of employees their jobs.
assuage.mnemonic: assuage ≈ 'suave' : rendre la douleur suave, plus douce.

mollify.definition: to calm someone who is angry or upset
sentences: The airline offered free tickets to mollify the furious passengers, who had spent six hours stranded in the terminal without any explanation.
It took several apologies and a handwritten note to mollify the irate client, who had threatened to cancel the entire contract.
mollify.mnemonic: mollify ≈ 'mou' (mollis) : rendre mou quelqu'un de raide de colère.

placate.definition: to calm someone's anger by giving in or making concessions
sentences: The mayor agreed to reduce the new parking fees in order to placate the angry shopkeepers who had gathered outside city hall.
Parents often try to placate a crying toddler with a snack, hoping the small treat will end the tantrum quickly.
placate.mnemonic: placate ≈ 'plaire' (placere) : on cède pour plaire et calmer.

mitigate.definition: to make something harmful or severe less serious or damaging
sentences: Engineers built higher walls along the river to mitigate the risk of flooding, although they admitted that no barrier could eliminate the danger entirely.
Her apology did little to mitigate the damage caused by her careless remarks, which had already spread across social media.

temper.definition: to moderate or soften something by adding a balancing quality
sentences: The critic tried to temper her harsh review with a few words of praise for the lead actor's moving performance.
A wise leader will temper bold ambition with caution, so that enthusiasm does not lead the organization into reckless and costly decisions.

abate.definition: to become less intense, strong, or widespread
sentences: After several hours of heavy rain, the storm finally began to abate, and residents cautiously stepped outside to inspect the damage.
The protesters' anger did not abate even after the president promised reforms, and thousands returned to the streets the following morning.

subside.definition: to become less intense, active, or violent; to sink to a lower level
sentences: Once the floodwaters began to subside, volunteers rushed to the village to clear the mud and rebuild the damaged homes.
He waited quietly for his anger to subside before replying to the insulting email, knowing that a calm answer would serve him better.

equanimity.definition: calmness and even temper, especially in difficult situations
sentences: The veteran pilot faced the sudden engine failure with remarkable equanimity, calmly guiding the aircraft toward a safe landing as passengers panicked.
Monks in the mountain monastery are trained to accept both praise and criticism with equanimity, neither elated by success nor crushed by failure.

unflappable.definition: remaining calm and composed even in a crisis
sentences: The unflappable nurse continued checking charts and giving orders while the emergency room filled with injured patients and frightened relatives.
Even when the microphone failed in the middle of her speech, the unflappable candidate simply smiled, raised her voice, and carried on.
unflappable.mnemonic: un-flap-able : impossible de faire 'flapper' (s'agiter comme un oiseau).

forbearance.definition: patient self-control and tolerance, especially in the face of provocation
sentences: The teacher showed great forbearance with the disruptive student, calmly repeating her instructions instead of responding to his rude interruptions with anger.
The bank's forbearance allowed the struggling family extra months to repay the loan, sparing them from immediate foreclosure on their home.

quiescent.definition: temporarily inactive or dormant, but capable of becoming active
sentences: Scientists monitored the quiescent volcano closely, since it had been silent for decades but could erupt again with little warning.
The disease can remain quiescent in the body for years, producing no symptoms until a weakened immune system allows it to flare up.
quiescent.mnemonic: quiescent ≈ 'quies' = repos (quiet) : calme en attendant de se réveiller.

blithe.definition: cheerfully carefree, often showing a thoughtless lack of concern
sentences: With blithe disregard for the warnings of his advisers, the young prince spent lavishly while the kingdom slid toward bankruptcy.
She walked into the meeting with a blithe smile, apparently unaware that her careless mistake had angered every one of her colleagues.
blithe.mnemonic: Blithe : léger comme un oiseau, sans un souci (parfois trop insouciant).

aloof.definition: emotionally distant and reserved; not friendly or involved with others
sentences: Although the new director seemed aloof at first, she turned out to be merely shy, and soon warmed to her colleagues.
The old professor remained aloof from campus politics, preferring to spend his evenings alone with his books rather than attending faculty gatherings.
aloof.mnemonic: aloof : à 'loof' (au vent) — on reste à l'écart, au large.

lenient.definition: merciful or tolerant; not strict in punishing or enforcing rules
sentences: The judge was unusually lenient with the first-time offender, sentencing him to community service instead of the prison term prosecutors had demanded.
Students loved the lenient teacher, who accepted late homework without penalty, but critics said her relaxed rules failed to prepare them for college.

curtail.definition: to reduce or cut short, especially by imposing a limit
sentences: The university was forced to curtail its research budget after the government slashed funding, leaving several promising projects unfinished.
Authoritarian regimes often curtail press freedom, closing newspapers and jailing journalists who dare to criticize those in power.

curb.definition: to restrain or keep something harmful within limits
sentences: The central bank raised interest rates in an attempt to curb inflation, which had been climbing steadily for more than a year.
She tried to curb her appetite for sweets by keeping only fruit in the house, but the cravings proved stubborn.
curb.mnemonic: curb : le trottoir (kerb) borne la route, il contient.

bridle.definition: to hold back or restrain; (also) to show anger or resentment
sentences: The new manager had to bridle his impatience and listen to every proposal before announcing any decision to the anxious team.
Governments sometimes try to bridle the power of large corporations through strict regulations, though lobbyists often resist such limits fiercely.

stinting.definition: ungenerous; sparing to the point of meanness
sentences: Unlike his stinting uncle, who counted every coin, the old banker was famously generous, funding scholarships and hospital wings without hesitation.
The charity criticized the government's stinting contribution to disaster relief, calling it embarrassingly small compared with the scale of the crisis.

hamper.definition: to hinder or obstruct the movement or progress of
sentences: Heavy snow continued to hamper rescue efforts, delaying the arrival of trucks carrying food and blankets to the stranded villagers.
Outdated software can hamper productivity, because employees waste hours struggling with slow programs instead of focusing on their real work.
hamper.mnemonic: Un hamper est un panier d'osier encombrant : il gêne celui qui le porte.

hinder.definition: to create difficulties that delay or obstruct progress
sentences: Poor roads and a lack of electricity hinder economic development in many rural regions, discouraging investors from building factories there.
Nothing could hinder the determined athlete from completing the marathon, not even the blisters that covered both of her feet.

impede.definition: to obstruct or slow the progress of something
sentences: Fallen trees impeded the firefighters' progress along the narrow mountain road, forcing them to stop and clear the way by hand.
Critics argue that excessive paperwork impedes innovation, since scientists spend more time filling out forms than conducting experiments.

mire.definition: to cause to become stuck in mud or in a difficult situation
sentences: The tractor became mired in the soft mud after the rain, and it took four men and a rope to pull it free.
Endless legal disputes threatened to mire the merger in controversy, delaying a deal that both companies had hoped to complete within weeks.
mire.mnemonic: La mire (bourbier) : on s'y enlise ; to mire = embourber.

stultify.definition: to impair or dull the mind or enthusiasm, especially through boring routine
sentences: Critics claim that rigid memorization can stultify young minds, leaving students unable to think creatively or question what they are told.
Years of repetitive paperwork began to stultify the once-ambitious clerk, who slowly lost every trace of curiosity and enthusiasm for his job.

unwieldy.definition: hard to handle or manage because of size, weight, or complexity
sentences: The unwieldy sofa would not fit around the narrow staircase, so the movers finally lifted it through the second-floor window.
Critics called the tax code an unwieldy mass of exceptions and amendments that even trained accountants struggled to interpret correctly.
unwieldy.mnemonic: UN-WIELD-y : qu'on ne peut pas manier (wield = manier).

cumbersome.definition: large or heavy and therefore awkward and slow to use
sentences: The early computers were so cumbersome that they filled entire rooms, requiring teams of technicians to operate and maintain them.
Applicants complained that the cumbersome approval process, with its many forms and slow committees, discouraged small businesses from seeking permits.

unencumbered.definition: free from burdens, obstacles, or debts
sentences: Unencumbered by heavy luggage, the travelers moved quickly through the crowded station and boarded the train just before it departed.
Having inherited the house unencumbered by any mortgage, the young couple could invest their savings in a new business instead.

preclude.definition: to make impossible or prevent from happening in advance
sentences: A strict confidentiality agreement precludes employees from discussing the project with anyone outside the company, even their own family members.
His poor eyesight did not preclude him from becoming a respected photographer, since he learned to rely on careful planning and touch.
preclude.mnemonic: pre-clude : 'clore' avant, fermer la porte d'avance.

forestall.definition: to prevent something by acting in advance
sentences: The government raised the bank's reserves to forestall a financial panic before frightened customers could begin withdrawing their savings.
She tried to forestall any criticism by admitting her mistakes at the very start of the presentation, leaving her rivals little to attack.

preempt.definition: to prevent or forestall something by acting first
sentences: The senator released her own tax plan early to preempt her opponent's attack, depriving him of the chance to define the debate.
Engineers moved quickly to preempt the problem by replacing the worn parts, thereby avoiding a costly shutdown of the entire factory.

obviate.definition: to make unnecessary by anticipating and removing a need or difficulty
sentences: The new online system will obviate the need for customers to visit the office, saving everyone hours spent waiting in line.
Careful planning at the start of the experiment obviated any need for repeating the tests, which saved the lab both time and money.
obviate.mnemonic: obviate ≈ 'obvier' (ob-via) : écarter l'obstacle de la route.

deter.definition: to discourage someone from acting by instilling doubt or fear of consequences
sentences: Heavy fines and visible cameras are meant to deter drivers from speeding, although some motorists still ignore the warnings.
Neither the freezing rain nor the long distance could deter the loyal fans, who traveled all night to see their team play.
deter.mnemonic: deter ≈ 'dé-terrer' : faire reculer par la peur (terror).

debar.definition: to officially exclude or prohibit someone from entering or doing something
sentences: The tournament rules debar any athlete who has failed a drug test from competing, regardless of how talented the player may be.
Lawyers who commit serious fraud may be debarred from practicing, losing the right to represent clients in any court of the country.
debar.mnemonic: de-bar : mettre une barre devant, interdire l'accès.

quash.definition: to suppress forcibly or to officially cancel a decision or verdict
sentences: Soldiers moved swiftly to quash the rebellion, arresting its leaders and imposing a strict curfew across the capital city.
The appeals court agreed to quash the conviction after new evidence showed that the key witness had lied under oath.

admonish.definition: to warn or reprimand someone gently but firmly
sentences: The coach gently admonished the team for arriving late, reminding the players that punctuality was a basic form of respect.
Her grandmother would admonish her to wear a coat in winter, warning that she would catch a cold if she ignored the advice.

rebuke.definition: to criticize or reprimand someone sharply
sentences: The editor sharply rebuked the young reporter for publishing an unchecked rumor, warning that such carelessness would not be tolerated again.
In a rare public statement, the council rebuked the mayor for ignoring its advice and spending money without approval.

upbraid.definition: to scold someone severely for a fault or error
sentences: The captain upbraided the sailors for neglecting their duties, shouting that their laziness had nearly caused the ship to run aground.
She upbraided her roommate for leaving dirty dishes in the sink for the third time that week, and the argument lasted until midnight.
The principal chastised the students harshly for vandalizing the gymnasium, and ordered them to pay for the repairs from their own savings.
Critics chastised the government for its slow response to the crisis, accusing officials of ignoring the suffering of thousands of families.

castigate.definition: to criticize or reprimand someone very severely, often publicly
sentences: The newspaper editorial castigated the senator for abandoning his campaign promises, calling his behavior a betrayal of the voters who trusted him.
Reviewers castigated the director's latest film, describing it as a tedious and pretentious work that wasted the talents of its cast.

lambaste.definition: to criticize someone or something harshly and angrily
sentences: Critics lambasted the film as a shallow and badly written spectacle, and several reviewers said it was the worst release of the year.
The coach lambasted his players after the humiliating defeat, shouting that their lack of effort had embarrassed the entire club.
lambaste.mnemonic: lambaste : 'lam' = frapper (lam it) + baste : rouer de coups verbaux.

sentences: The critic's scathing review described the novel as dull, derivative, and so poorly written that it should never have been published.
Her scathing remarks about the proposal left the committee silent, and the embarrassed author quietly left the room before the meeting ended.
scathing.mnemonic: scathing ≈ 'scathe' = blesser : un propos qui brûle comme du vitriol.

disparage.definition: to speak of someone or something as having little value or importance
sentences: Rival companies often disparage each other's products in advertisements, hoping to persuade customers that their own brand is far superior.
It is unkind to disparage a colleague's efforts in public, especially when she has worked for months on a difficult project.

belittle.definition: to make someone or something seem unimportant or less valuable
sentences: A good mentor never tries to belittle her students, but instead corrects their errors patiently and encourages them to keep improving.
He tended to belittle his sister's achievements, calling her award a lucky accident, which only made her more determined to prove him wrong.

malign.definition: to speak harmful untruths about someone; to slander
sentences: The tabloid maligned the innocent scientist for months, printing false rumors that destroyed his reputation before the truth finally emerged.
Jealous rivals sought to malign the young artist by spreading stories about her supposed plagiarism, none of which turned out to be true.

slander.definition: a false spoken statement that damages a person's reputation
sentences: The actor sued the magazine for slander, claiming that its false report about his supposed crimes had ruined his career overnight.
Spreading slander about a rival may bring temporary advantage, but it usually destroys the trust of everyone who hears the lie.
slander.mnemonic: slander ≈ 'scandale' : même racine, propos qui salit.

impugn.definition: to challenge or call into question the honesty or validity of
sentences: The defense attorney tried to impugn the witness's credibility by pointing out that he had lied under oath on previous occasions.
No one wished to impugn the scientist's motives, but several colleagues questioned the validity of her data and her methods.

tarnish.definition: to damage or spoil the good quality or reputation of
sentences: The bribery scandal threatened to tarnish the senator's spotless reputation, which he had spent thirty years carefully building.
Silver will tarnish if left in damp air, gradually losing its shine and turning a dull gray unless polished regularly.
tarnish.mnemonic: tarnish ≈ 'ternir' : même sens, perdre son éclat.

scoff.definition: to speak about something with mocking contempt
sentences: Skeptics scoffed at the inventor's claims, insisting that no machine could possibly do what he promised, until the demonstration silenced them.
When the new employee suggested working from home, her boss scoffed and said that such an idea would never work in a serious company.
scoff.mnemonic: Scoff ≈ « s'esclaffer » : on rit avec mépris.

mock.definition: to tease or make fun of someone, often by imitating them
sentences: The older children would mock the new student's accent, repeating his words in a silly voice until the teacher stepped in.
It is unfair to mock someone for making a mistake, since everyone fails sometimes while learning a difficult skill.

lampoon.definition: to publicly ridicule someone or something using satire or parody
sentences: The comedy show regularly lampoons politicians, exaggerating their habits and speeches until the audience is roaring with laughter.
Cartoonists have long lampooned the monarchy, drawing the king as a pompous figure who cares more about banquets than about his subjects.
lampoon.mnemonic: lampoon ≈ 'lampion' ? non : 'lampooner' = chansons satiriques ; imaginez une pochade.

sentences: At the retirement dinner, speaker after speaker extolled the professor's generosity, patience, and brilliance as a teacher over four decades.
Travel brochures extol the beauty of the island, describing its white beaches and clear water in glowing terms.

tout.definition: to promote or praise something aggressively, usually to attract customers
sentences: Advertisers tout the new phone as the most revolutionary device ever made, although reviewers found only modest improvements over earlier models.
The candidate touted his economic record at every rally, hoping that voters would overlook the scandals that had marked his term.
tout.mnemonic: tout ≠ 'tout' français : en anglais, vanter bruyamment, comme un camelot.

lionize.definition: to treat someone as a celebrity or hero worthy of great admiration
sentences: After the championship victory, fans began to lionize the young goalkeeper, naming streets and sandwiches in his honor within a single week.
Society tends to lionize wealthy entrepreneurs, though critics warn that such worship may blind the public to unethical business practices.
lionize.mnemonic: lionize : traiter quelqu'un comme un lion, roi de la jungle.

sentences: The charming stranger hoodwinked the elderly couple into handing over their savings, promising a fantastic investment that did not actually exist.
Voters felt hoodwinked when the candidate abandoned every promise he had made during the campaign within weeks of taking office.
hoodwink.mnemonic: hood-wink : mettre une cagoule (hood) sur les yeux (wink).

dissemble.definition: to conceal one's true feelings or intentions behind a false appearance
sentences: Though furious at the verdict, the senator learned to dissemble, smiling warmly for the cameras while privately plotting his revenge.
The witness began to dissemble under questioning, pretending to remember nothing, although the evidence clearly showed that he had been present.

malinger.definition: to pretend to be ill in order to avoid work or duty
malinger.definitionFr: simuler la maladie pour éviter le travail
sentences: The army doctor suspected that the soldier was trying to malinger, since his supposed back pain disappeared whenever the sergeant was not watching.
Employers worry that some workers will malinger on Mondays, calling in sick for imaginary illnesses just to enjoy a longer weekend.

obfuscate.definition: to deliberately make something unclear or confusing
sentences: The company's lawyers tried to obfuscate the facts with confusing jargon, hoping that regulators would give up before understanding the truth.
Rather than answer the simple question, the spokesman chose to obfuscate, burying the key information beneath long and meaningless sentences.

whitewash.definition: to cover up wrongdoing or make something bad appear acceptable
sentences: Critics accused the committee of trying to whitewash the scandal, issuing a report that ignored every serious charge against the minister.
The official biography seemed to whitewash the dictator's crimes, describing him as a stern but beloved father figure to his people.
whitewash.mnemonic: whitewash : badigeonner de blanc pour cacher la saleté.

conceal.definition: to keep something hidden or secret
sentences: The thief tried to conceal the stolen jewels inside a hollow book, but the airport scanner quickly revealed the hiding place.
She could not conceal her disappointment when the results were announced, and her tight smile fooled no one in the room.

covert.definition: hidden or secret; not openly acknowledged or displayed
sentences: The agency ran a covert operation for months, deliberately hiding its activities from both the public and most members of Congress.
Because the investor's covert purchases of shares were concealed through shell companies, regulators did not learn who was acquiring control of the firm until it was too late.
covert.mnemonic: COVERT ≈ « couvert » : caché sous une couverture, secret.

underhanded.definition: secretive and dishonest; achieved through deceit rather than fair means
sentences: The candidate won the primary through underhanded tactics, spreading false rumors about his rival while publicly pretending to run a clean and respectful campaign.
Many customers felt that the company's underhanded practice of hiding fees in the fine print was a betrayal of the trust it claimed to value.
underhanded.mnemonic: Under-handed : sous la main, en cachette, pas à la loyale.

artful.definition: clever and skillful, especially at deceiving or manipulating others
sentences: With artful questions that seemed innocent, the lawyer led the witness step by step into contradicting her own earlier testimony without ever raising his voice.
The artful negotiator concealed his true bottom line behind a show of reluctance, and so persuaded the other side to concede far more than it intended.
artful.mnemonic: Artful : plein d'art… pour tromper, rusé et manipulateur.

guile.definition: sly, cunning skill used to deceive or get one's way
sentences: Lacking the strength to defeat the larger army in open battle, the general relied on guile, luring his enemy into a narrow valley and ambushing it.
Although she appeared sweet and harmless, the young broker used considerable guile to persuade elderly clients to invest in schemes that mostly benefited herself.
guile.mnemonic: Guile ressemble à « gilet » : on cache ses ruses sous un gilet.

chicanery.definition: deception by trickery, especially in legal or political dealings
sentences: Voters grew weary of the political chicanery that allowed incumbents to redraw district boundaries so that they could never lose an election.
The auditor uncovered years of financial chicanery, including invented invoices and doctored ledgers, all designed to hide the company's steady losses from its shareholders.
chicanery.mnemonic: Chicanery : la « chicane » des avocats, qui tordent la loi.

cajole.definition: persuade someone to do something by flattery or gentle, insistent coaxing
sentences: The toddler tried to cajole her father into buying candy, alternating sweet compliments with pleading looks until he finally relented at the checkout counter.
Rather than threatening the reluctant donors, the director chose to cajole them with praise for their past generosity, and several soon increased their pledges.
cajole.mnemonic: Cajoler : on caresse dans le sens du poil pour obtenir ce qu'on veut.

glib.definition: fluent and smooth in speech but insincere or superficial
sentences: The salesman's glib patter impressed the crowd at first, but listeners soon noticed that he never answered a single question about the product's actual performance.
Critics dismissed the senator's glib reassurances about the economy as slick slogans that ignored the real hardships facing families in the struggling region.
glib.mnemonic: GLIB ≈ glisse : ça glisse tout seul, mais sans profondeur.

disingenuous.definition: not candid; pretending to know less or to be more innocent than one is
sentences: It was disingenuous of the CEO to claim surprise at the scandal when internal emails showed that he had personally approved the questionable accounting.
The official's disingenuous question, asking why anyone would object to the plan, was meant to conceal that he had already designed it to exclude his critics.
disingenuous.mnemonic: DIS-ingenuous : le contraire d'ingénu, il fait semblant d'être naïf.

spurious.definition: false or invalid because based on faulty logic or lacking authenticity
sentences: The scientist rejected the spurious correlation between ice cream sales and drowning, pointing out that both simply rise during hot summer weather.
Experts quickly exposed the spurious claim that the painting was a lost masterpiece, since the canvas had been manufactured decades after the artist's death.
spurious.mnemonic: Spurious ≈ « spurieux » (rare en français) : qui n'est pas authentique.

sentences: Police arrested the man for selling bogus designer handbags, which looked convincing from a distance but fell apart after only a few days of use.
The reporter discovered that the survey cited in the campaign advertisement was bogus, because no such organization existed and no voters had ever been polled.
bogus.mnemonic: Bogus ≈ « bogue » : ça ne marche pas, c'est du faux.

mendacity.definition: the habit or tendency of telling lies; untruthfulness
sentences: Colleagues eventually stopped trusting the manager because his mendacity was so habitual that he lied even about trivial matters, such as where he had eaten lunch.
The biographer was shocked by the mendacity of her subject, whose memoirs invented heroic deeds and entirely erased the failures that his friends clearly remembered.
mendacity.mnemonic: Mendacity : « mentir » + audace. Un menteur audacieux.

baffle.definition: to confuse or perplex someone completely so that no explanation can be found
sentences: The sudden disappearance of the ancient manuscript continues to baffle historians, who can find no trace of a thief or any record of its removal.
Detectives were baffled by the locked-room murder, since every door and window had been sealed from the inside and no weapon was found anywhere.
baffle.mnemonic: Baffle ≈ « baffe » : une claque d'étonnement, on reste sans réponse.

bewilder.definition: to confuse someone deeply, leaving them lost or unable to think clearly
sentences: The maze of unfamiliar streets and conflicting signs began to bewilder the tourists, who soon had no idea in which direction the station lay.
Visitors to the stock exchange were bewildered by the shouting traders, flashing screens, and frantic hand signals, none of which made any sense to them.
bewilder.mnemonic: Be-WILD-er : perdu en pleine nature sauvage (wild), complètement désorienté.

befuddle.definition: to confuse and muddle someone's mind, as if by alcohol or complexity
sentences: The professor's rambling explanation only served to befuddle the students further, and by the end of the lecture even the best of them were lost.
Exhausted and befuddled after thirty hours without sleep, the pilot misread the instruments twice before the co-pilot gently took over the controls.
befuddle.mnemonic: Befuddle : l'esprit embrumé, comme après un verre de trop.

flummox.definition: to confuse someone so completely that they cannot respond
sentences: The unexpected question seemed to flummox the usually confident candidate, who stood silent at the podium for several seconds before offering a feeble reply.
Even seasoned chess players were flummoxed by the young prodigy's strange opening, which broke every principle they had been taught and yet somehow worked.
flummox.mnemonic: Flummox sonne comme un choc : on reste coi, sans réaction.

confound.definition: to surprise and confuse by defying expectations or thwarting plans
sentences: The underdog team continued to confound the experts, who had predicted a crushing defeat but now watched it advance round after round.
The unexpected results confounded the researchers, whose carefully constructed theory had predicted exactly the opposite outcome from the one their instruments recorded.
confound.mnemonic: Con-FOUND : tout est mélangé, on ne retrouve plus rien ; aussi déjouer.

nonplussed.definition: so surprised and confused that one does not know how to react
sentences: When the guest of honor announced that she was leaving the company immediately, the board members sat nonplussed, unable to think of anything to say.
The comedian was nonplussed when the audience met his best joke with complete silence, and he simply stared at his notes for a moment.
nonplussed.mnemonic: Du latin « non plus » : on ne peut aller plus loin, on ne sait plus quoi faire.

discomfit.definition: to make someone feel uneasy, embarrassed, or frustrated
sentences: The reporter's blunt questions about his finances seemed to discomfit the mayor, who tugged at his collar and glanced anxiously at his aides.
Nothing could discomfit the veteran diplomat, who answered even the most hostile accusations with the same calm smile and unhurried voice.
discomfit.mnemonic: DIS-comfit : l'opposé du confort, on est mal à l'aise.

disquiet.definition: to make someone anxious or uneasy, often in a lingering way
sentences: News of the factory's sudden closure began to disquiet local residents, who feared that other employers might soon follow and leave the town without work.
The doctor was disquieted by the patient's strangely normal test results, since they did not explain the persistent symptoms that kept her awake at night.
disquiet.mnemonic: DIS-quiet : plus de calme, une inquiétude sourde.

recondite.definition: little known and difficult to understand; understood only by specialists
recondite.definitionFr: savant, hors de portée du profane
sentences: The professor's lecture on recondite medieval theology left most undergraduates baffled, since only a handful of scholars in the world understood its terminology.
Fond of recondite references, the novelist filled her pages with obscure allusions that delighted specialists but frustrated ordinary readers who lacked the necessary background.
recondite.mnemonic: Du latin reconditus = mis à l'écart, caché ; savoir réservé aux spécialistes.

arcane.definition: known or understood only by a few; mysterious and secret
sentences: The club's arcane rituals, known only to its oldest members, were never written down and were passed from one generation to the next by word of mouth.
Few taxpayers can navigate the arcane rules of the tax code without help, since the language is so specialized that even accountants disagree about its meaning.
arcane.mnemonic: Les « arcanes » : les secrets que seuls les initiés connaissent.

inscrutable.definition: impossible to understand or interpret; revealing nothing of thoughts or feelings
sentences: The poker champion's inscrutable face gave opponents no clue about the quality of his cards, and he won hand after hand through sheer bluffing.
The ruler's motives remained inscrutable even to his closest advisors, who could only guess at the reasons behind his sudden and puzzling decisions.
inscrutable.mnemonic: IN-scrutable : impossible à scruter, visage indéchiffrable.

elusive.definition: difficult to find, catch, or pin down; evading capture or definition
sentences: The elusive snow leopard is so skilled at hiding among the rocks that researchers may spend years in the mountains without seeing a single one.
Happiness remains an elusive goal for many people, because every time they achieve what they wanted, their satisfaction slips away and a new desire appears.
elusive.mnemonic: Elusive ≈ « éluder » : qui se dérobe, insaisissable.

convoluted.definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow, with many twists and turns
sentences: The film's convoluted plot, full of double agents and flashbacks within flashbacks, left many viewers unable to explain what had actually happened at the end.
Applicants complained that the convoluted procedure for requesting a permit, which required eleven forms and four separate offices, was designed to discourage anyone from applying.
convoluted.mnemonic: Les convolutions du cerveau : plein de replis, donc alambiqué.

circuitous.definition: longer than the most direct way; indirect and roundabout
sentences: Because the main bridge was closed, we took a circuitous route through the hills that added almost two hours to what is normally a short drive.
The lawyer's circuitous argument wandered through several unrelated topics before reaching its point, and the judge repeatedly urged him to speak more directly.
circuitous.mnemonic: CIRCUITous : on fait tout un circuit, un détour.

sentences: The attorney presented such a cogent argument, supported by clear evidence and flawless logic, that even the skeptical jurors were persuaded to change their minds.
Her essay was praised for its cogent analysis, in which every claim was backed by data and every objection was answered in a calm, rational manner.
cogent.mnemonic: Du latin cogere = forcer : un argument qui force l'esprit à acquiescer.

pithy.definition: brief and forcefully expressive, packing much meaning into few words
sentences: The editor admired the columnist's pithy style, in which a single well-chosen sentence could sum up a complex political crisis better than a whole page.
Benjamin Franklin's pithy sayings, such as "early to bed and early to rise," remain popular because they express practical wisdom in just a few memorable words.
pithy.mnemonic: Pith = moelle : on garde l'essentiel, court et percutant.

terse.definition: using few words, often in a way that seems abrupt or unfriendly
sentences: Her terse reply to the long, emotional letter consisted of just two words, which left the sender wondering whether she had offended his old friend.
The general issued a terse statement confirming the retreat, offering no explanation and refusing to answer any of the questions shouted by the waiting journalists.
terse.mnemonic: Du latin tersus = net, lisse : style sec et dépouillé.

brevity.definition: the quality of using few words; shortness of expression or duration
sentences: The speaker was applauded for her brevity, since she summarized the entire plan in three minutes while previous presenters had taken more than an hour.
Shakespeare observed that brevity is the soul of wit, suggesting that a joke or argument loses its force when it is stretched out too long.

straightforward.definition: direct, honest, and easy to understand, without complications or deception
sentences: The instructions were refreshingly straightforward, listing each step in order so that even a complete beginner could assemble the bookshelf in less than an hour.
I appreciate her straightforward manner: she tells you exactly what she thinks, never hides behind polite hints, and never pretends to agree when she does not.
straightforward.mnemonic: Straight + forward : tout droit devant, sans détour.

unvarnished.definition: plain and direct, with no attempt to soften or embellish the facts
sentences: The inspector gave the committee an unvarnished account of the dam's condition, making no effort to soften the alarming fact that it could fail within a year.
Readers admired the memoir for its unvarnished honesty, since the author described her own mistakes and cruelty without any attempt to excuse or glamorize them.
unvarnished.mnemonic: Un-varnished : pas de vernis sur la vérité.

blunt.definition: speaking in a very direct way that may offend, without tact or politeness
sentences: Her blunt assessment of the manuscript, which she called dull and badly organized, hurt the young author but also forced him to rewrite the entire book.
The coach was known for his blunt speech; he never softened bad news, and players who wanted flattery quickly learned to look for it elsewhere.
blunt.mnemonic: Blunt = émoussé : une lame qui ne coupe pas finement, un franc-parler brutal.

curt.definition: rudely brief; abrupt and almost impolite in manner or speech
sentences: The receptionist gave a curt nod and returned to her computer, without bothering to greet the nervous visitors or ask how she could help them.
Offended by his boss's curt dismissal of the proposal, which lasted barely ten seconds, the analyst resolved to present his ideas to someone else.
curt.mnemonic: CURT ≈ « court » : phrase écourtée, un peu sèche.

bombastic.definition: high-sounding and pompous but lacking real meaning or substance
sentences: The candidate's bombastic speech was full of thundering promises and grand phrases, but when journalists examined it, they found almost no concrete proposals at all.
Impatient with the professor's bombastic prose, which used a dozen long words where one short word would do, students began to skim his articles.
bombastic.mnemonic: Bombastic : une « bombe » de mots, du bruit mais rien dedans.

florid.definition: overly elaborate and ornate in style; also flushed or reddish in complexion
sentences: The Victorian novelist's florid prose, overloaded with elaborate metaphors and decorative adjectives, now strikes modern readers as more exhausting than beautiful.
The hotel lobby was decorated in a florid style, with gilded mirrors, heavy curtains, and ornate carvings on every available surface of the ceiling and walls.
florid.mnemonic: Florid : « floral », trop de fleurs partout.

ponderous.definition: slow, heavy, and laborious, especially in movement or writing; dull and clumsy
sentences: The ponderous elephant moved across the clearing with slow, heavy steps, while the smaller animals around it scattered quickly out of its way.
Reviewers found the historian's ponderous prose almost unreadable, since every idea was buried under long, clumsy sentences and tedious, laborious qualifications.

overwrought.definition: too elaborate or excessive; or extremely nervous and agitated
overwrought.definitionFr: surchargé ; ou à bout de nerfs
sentences: Critics found the poem overwrought, complaining that its swollen metaphors and exaggerated emotion smothered whatever simple feeling the poet had originally wished to express.
After three sleepless nights spent caring for her sick child, the mother was so overwrought that she burst into tears at the smallest inconvenience.
overwrought.mnemonic: Over-wrought : trop travaillé (surchargé), ou les nerfs à vif.

stilted.definition: stiff, unnatural, and overly formal in manner or writing
sentences: The actors delivered their lines in a stilted manner, as though reading from cards, and so the dialogue never sounded like real conversation between friends.
His stilted speech at the wedding, full of formal phrases he had clearly memorized, made the guests uncomfortable instead of conveying the warmth he intended.
stilted.mnemonic: Stilted : monté sur des échasses (stilts), guindé et peu naturel.

histrionic.definition: overly dramatic or theatrical in behavior, intended to attract attention
sentences: The teenager's histrionic sighs and dramatic collapse onto the sofa were obviously meant to win sympathy for what was, in fact, a very minor disappointment.
Observers found the senator's histrionic outrage unconvincing, since his trembling voice and theatrical gestures appeared suddenly whenever a camera was pointed in his direction.

garrulous.definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
sentences: Our garrulous neighbor could turn a simple hello into an hour-long monologue about his garden, his health, and the shortcomings of the local government.
Unlike her garrulous brother, who filled every silence with chatter, the young diplomat spoke rarely and only when she had something truly important to say.
garrulous.mnemonic: Garrulous ≈ « gargouille » : ça coule sans arrêt, bavard intarissable.

discursive.definition: wandering from topic to topic rather than staying focused on the main point
discursive.definitionFr: qui part dans tous les sens
sentences: The professor's discursive lectures drifted from economics to folk music to his childhood, and students often left unsure what the main point had been.
Though the essay was charming, its discursive structure, which wandered through anecdotes and digressions, made it difficult for readers to follow any central argument.
discursive.mnemonic: Du latin currere = courir : il court dans tous les sens.

headstrong.definition: stubbornly determined to do what one wants, ignoring advice or authority
headstrong.definitionFr: qui n'en fait qu'à sa tête
sentences: The headstrong young prince ignored every warning from his advisors and marched his army into the mountains, where it was soon trapped by the winter snow.
Her parents described her as headstrong, a child who refused to wear a coat in the cold simply because someone had told her to.
headstrong.mnemonic: Head-strong : tête dure, n'en fait qu'à sa tête.

intractable.definition: hard to control, manage, or solve; stubborn and unyielding
intractable.definitionFr: impossible à résoudre ou à gérer
sentences: Decades of negotiations failed to resolve the intractable border dispute, because neither side was willing to give up even the smallest portion of its claim.
The horse proved intractable, refusing every command and kicking at anyone who approached, until the trainer finally admitted that it could not be ridden.
intractable.mnemonic: IN-tractable : impossible à tirer, à mener (trait = tirer).

hidebound.definition: rigidly conventional and narrow-minded, resistant to new ideas
sentences: The hidebound committee rejected the innovative design simply because it differed from the traditional style that the organization had used for more than a century.
Reformers accused the university of being hidebound, clinging to old teaching methods while the world outside its walls changed dramatically every year.
hidebound.mnemonic: Hide-bound : la peau (hide) trop serrée, figé dans ses habitudes.

balk.definition: to hesitate or refuse to proceed, as if unwilling to accept something
sentences: The horse began to balk at the edge of the stream, planting its hooves and refusing to move despite the rider's gentle urging.
Many shareholders balked at the proposed merger, fearing that the high price would leave the company in debt and without money for new research.
balk.mnemonic: Balk : le cheval se braque devant l'obstacle et refuse d'avancer.

brook.definition: to tolerate or allow, usually used in negative statements
sentences: The strict headmaster would brook no disobedience, and any student who broke the rules was sent to his office without further discussion.
The dictator could not brook criticism of any kind, and journalists who dared to question his policies soon found themselves in prison.
brook.mnemonic: Brook = ruisseau, mais en verbe : « brook no delay » = ne tolérer aucun retard.

tractable.definition: easily managed, controlled, or persuaded; docile
sentences: After years of training, the once wild horse had become so tractable that even a small child could lead it calmly around the paddock.
Unlike her stubborn predecessor, the new manager found the staff tractable and willing to accept changes in procedure as long as they were clearly explained.
tractable.mnemonic: TRACTable ≈ tracteur : facile à tirer, docile.

amenable.definition: open and willing to accept a suggestion or to be persuaded
sentences: The landlord was amenable to a lower rent once the tenants explained that they would sign a three-year lease and take care of all repairs.
Although she had strongly opposed the plan at first, the director proved amenable to compromise after hearing the staff describe how it would improve their work.
amenable.mnemonic: Amenable ≈ « amener » : on peut l'amener à accepter.

subservient.definition: excessively obedient and eager to serve others; submissive or secondary in importance
sentences: The subservient assistant agreed with every opinion his employer expressed, never offering a different view even when he knew that the boss was clearly mistaken.
In the feudal system, peasants were expected to remain subservient to the lords who owned the land, obeying every order without complaint or question.

sycophant.definition: a person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage
sentences: The king surrounded himself with sycophants who praised every foolish decision, and so he never learned that his policies were ruining the kingdom.
A good leader needs honest advisors rather than a sycophant who simply repeats what the leader wants to hear and laughs at every one of her jokes.
sycophant.mnemonic: En français, « sycophante » = délateur ; en anglais, le lèche-bottes.

fawning.definition: flattering excessively in order to win favor; servilely attentive
sentences: The newspaper's fawning profile of the billionaire praised his every decision and never mentioned the lawsuits filed against his company by former employees.
Embarrassed by the fawning attention of the hotel staff, who bowed at every step and complimented his tie, the visitor longed for a normal conversation.
fawning.mnemonic: Fawn : comme un chien qui fait la fête pour obtenir une faveur.

lackadaisical.definition: lacking enthusiasm, energy, or care; casually indifferent
sentences: The team's lackadaisical effort in the first half, marked by missed passes and slow movements, made it clear that the players had little interest in winning.
Her lackadaisical attitude toward deadlines frustrated her colleagues, who had to complete her share of the project at the last minute every single month.

sluggish.definition: slow-moving and lacking energy, activity, or alertness
sentences: After the enormous lunch, the sluggish employees dragged themselves through the afternoon meeting, struggling to stay awake while the manager discussed quarterly figures.
Economists warned that the sluggish economy, with weak hiring and low consumer spending, might take several more years to recover from the long recession.
sluggish.mnemonic: SLUG = limace : lent comme une limace.

plodding.definition: proceeding slowly and laboriously in a dull, heavy, unimaginative way
