sentences: Although the author's plodding narrative moved with painful slowness through hundreds of pages, patient readers were finally rewarded by a powerful and surprising conclusion.
The plodding investigation, carried out by a tired team with little imagination, took years to uncover facts that a clever detective might have found in weeks.
plodding.mnemonic: Plod = marcher d'un pas lourd, pas à pas, laborieusement.

alacrity.definition: cheerful readiness and eagerness to act or respond promptly
sentences: When the director offered her the chance to lead the new project, she accepted with alacrity, clearly delighted and ready to begin the following morning.
The volunteers responded with alacrity to the call for help, arriving within minutes of the flood warning and working happily through the night to fill sandbags.
alacrity.mnemonic: Alacrity : « alacre » en français, vif et empressé.

impetus.definition: a driving force or stimulus that causes a process to begin or accelerate
sentences: The discovery of gold in the region gave a powerful impetus to the settlement of the territory, drawing thousands of newcomers within a few years.
Public outrage over the scandal provided the impetus for sweeping reforms that legislators had spent a decade avoiding because of pressure from lobbyists.
impetus.mnemonic: Impetus : « impétueux », ce qui lance avec force.

spur.definition: to encourage or stimulate someone or something to greater speed or activity
sentences: The government introduced generous tax credits to spur investment in renewable energy, hoping that private companies would build new wind farms and solar plants.
Her teacher's praise spurred the shy student to enter the national science competition, in which she eventually won a prize for her original experiment.
spur.mnemonic: Spur = éperon : on pique le cheval pour qu'il avance.

goad.definition: to provoke or urge someone to action by annoying or taunting them
sentences: The older boys tried to goad him into a fight by mocking his clothes, but he calmly turned away and walked home.
Critics accused the minister of attempting to goad the opposition into walking out of parliament so that the bill could pass without any serious debate.
goad.mnemonic: Goad = aiguillon : on pique le bœuf pour le faire réagir.

invigorate.definition: to give strength, energy, or new life to someone or something
sentences: A cold shower and a brisk walk in the morning air always invigorate me, leaving me alert and ready for a long day of difficult work.
The arrival of several talented young researchers helped to invigorate the stagnant department, which soon began producing creative studies that attracted attention across the field.
invigorate.mnemonic: Invigorate : « vigueur » dedans, redonner de la vigueur.

buoy.definition: to keep afloat; to lift the spirits or confidence of someone
sentences: The unexpected news that the rescue team had located survivors served to buoy the spirits of the exhausted families who had waited for days.
Strong sales of the new phone buoyed the company's profits during an otherwise difficult year, preventing the layoffs that many employees had feared.
buoy.mnemonic: Buoy = bouée : elle garde le moral à flot.

sedulous.definition: diligent and persistent, working with steady care and attention
sentences: Through sedulous study, the immigrant mastered the language in two years, spending every evening on grammar exercises and every weekend reading difficult newspaper articles.
The sedulous archivist spent decades cataloguing thousands of fragile letters, carefully repairing each page so that future historians could consult the collection with ease.
sedulous.mnemonic: Sedulous ≈ « assidu » : toujours à la tâche.

unremitting.definition: never stopping or easing; continuing without pause or relief
sentences: The villagers suffered through weeks of unremitting rain, which flooded the fields, destroyed the harvest, and gave them no single dry day in which to recover.
Her unremitting efforts to find a cure, continuing day and night for fifteen years, finally earned the admiration of even the most skeptical colleagues.
unremitting.mnemonic: UN-remitting : qui ne se relâche jamais.

steadfast.definition: firmly loyal and unwavering in purpose or belief
sentences: Despite years of criticism and lost elections, the senator remained steadfast in her commitment to the cause and never abandoned her original principles.
His steadfast devotion to his sick friend, whom he visited every single day for nearly a decade, was admired by everyone who knew them both.

stalwart.definition: loyal, reliable, and strong, especially in difficult circumstances
sentences: Even when the party lost badly, its stalwart supporters continued to attend rallies and knock on doors, refusing to give up on the cause they loved.
The stalwart old sergeant stayed at his post through the entire bombardment, calmly encouraging the frightened recruits around him until reinforcements finally arrived.
stalwart.mnemonic: Stalwart : un poste (stal) solide, fidèle au poste.

painstaking.definition: done with great care, thoroughness, and attention to detail
sentences: After years of painstaking research in the archives, the historian finally verified every date and name in her biography of the obscure poet.
The restorer's painstaking work on the fresco, done one square centimeter at a time, took nearly three years to complete.
painstaking.mnemonic: Peine + taking : il faut se donner de la peine pour le faire.

punctilious.definition: showing great attention to correct behavior, etiquette, and small details
sentences: The punctilious butler never forgot a single rule of protocol, correcting the guests whenever they placed a fork or addressed a duchess improperly.
Known for being punctilious about deadlines and formatting, the editor returned the manuscript because the margins were a quarter inch too narrow.
punctilious.mnemonic: Vient de « point » : il s'attache au moindre point de détail.

exacting.definition: demanding great effort, precision, or high standards
sentences: Her exacting supervisor rejected the report three times, insisting that every figure be checked against the original data before submission.
Surgery is an exacting profession that leaves no room for carelessness, since even a tiny error can have fatal consequences.
exacting.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « exact » seulement, mais qui exige l'exactitude.

stringent.definition: strict, severe, and rigorously enforced (of rules or requirements)
sentences: The government imposed stringent safety regulations on the factory after the explosion, and inspectors now visit every month without warning.
Because admission standards at the conservatory are so stringent, only a handful of the hundreds of applicants are accepted each year.
stringent.mnemonic: Même racine que « stringer » / « astreindre » : on serre la vis.

cursory.definition: hasty and superficial, done without attention to detail
sentences: The inspector gave the wiring only a cursory glance, so he missed the frayed cable that later started the fire.
A cursory reading of the contract suggested it was fair, but a careful review revealed several clauses that favored the seller.
cursory.mnemonic: Du latin « currere », courir : on court sur le texte.

perfunctory.definition: done as a routine duty, with little interest or genuine effort
sentences: The clerk gave a perfunctory nod without looking up from his screen, clearly uninterested in the customer's complaint.
Her perfunctory apology, delivered in a flat voice and without eye contact, convinced no one that she regretted her remarks.
perfunctory.mnemonic: Per-functory ≈ « par fonction » : fait pour la forme, machinalement.

haphazard.definition: lacking order, planning, or method; random
sentences: The books were arranged in such a haphazard way, with novels beside cookbooks and atlases, that finding anything took hours.
Critics blamed the haphazard planning of the city's roads for the daily gridlock, noting that no one had coordinated the projects.
haphazard.mnemonic: Hap = hasard : ça se fait au hasard.

shoddy.definition: poorly made or done; of low quality
sentences: The tenants complained about the shoddy construction of the building, noting that the walls cracked and the pipes leaked within a year.
Shoddy workmanship ruined the reputation of the company, as customers discovered that its furniture collapsed after only a few months.
shoddy.mnemonic: Shoddy : du chiffon recyclé, de mauvaise qualité.

desultory.definition: lacking a plan or purpose; jumping from one thing to another
sentences: The conversation at the dinner party was desultory, drifting from politics to gardening to football without any thread connecting the topics.
After losing his job, he made only desultory efforts to find another, sending a résumé now and then but never following up.
desultory.mnemonic: Latin « desultor » : cavalier qui saute d'un cheval à l'autre.

sentences: Fresh fruit was plentiful at the market that summer, so vendors sold peaches at half the usual price and still made a profit.
In regions where rain is plentiful, farmers rarely worry about drought, whereas those in arid zones must ration every drop of water.

replete.definition: filled to the brim; abundantly supplied (with)
sentences: The old library was replete with rare manuscripts, its shelves so crowded that some volumes were stacked on the floor.
Her memoir, replete with vivid anecdotes and unexpected humor, kept readers engaged from the first page to the very last.
replete.mnemonic: Ressemble à « replet » en français : bien rempli, plein.

rife.definition: widespread and common, especially of something undesirable
sentences: Rumors were rife in the office after the sudden resignation, and employees whispered about layoffs and scandal in every corridor.
The early industrial city was rife with disease, since crowded housing and polluted water allowed infections to spread unchecked.
rife.mnemonic: Rife : ça pullule, les rumeurs sont rife.

surfeit.definition: an excessive amount of something, often causing disgust
sentences: After the holiday feast, the guests suffered a surfeit of rich food and could hardly look at another dessert.
A surfeit of cheap imports flooded the market, driving prices down so far that local producers could no longer cover their costs.
surfeit.mnemonic: Sur + fait : on en a trop fait, trop mangé.

inordinate.definition: unreasonably or excessively great; out of proportion
sentences: The committee spent an inordinate amount of time debating the color of the logo while ignoring the project's serious budget problems.
He took an inordinate pride in his small garden, mentioning it in every conversation and boasting to anyone who would listen.
inordinate.mnemonic: In + ordinaire : hors de l'ordre, hors mesure.

slew.definition: a large number or quantity of something
sentences: The new policy provoked a slew of complaints from residents, who flooded the mayor's office with calls and emails within hours.
She returned from the conference with a slew of ideas, filling three notebooks with proposals for improving the department.
slew.mnemonic: A slew of : tout un tas de.

swathe.definition: a broad strip or large area of something
sentences: The wildfire cut a wide swathe through the forest, leaving a broad strip of blackened trees that stretched for miles.
A large swathe of the electorate remained undecided until the final week, leaving pollsters unable to predict the outcome.
swathe.mnemonic: Swathe : une large bande (de tissu, de terrain).

burgeon.definition: to grow or increase rapidly; to flourish
sentences: Once a sleepy fishing village, the town began to burgeon after the railroad arrived, and its population tripled within a decade.
Her interest in astronomy burgeoned during adolescence, so that by eighteen she was reading graduate-level textbooks and building telescopes.
burgeon.mnemonic: Ressemble à « bourgeon » : ça pousse vite.

sentences: The detectives had scant evidence against the suspect, only a single blurry photograph and a vague description from one witness.
Paying scant attention to the lecture, he scribbled in his notebook and was unable to answer the professor's simple question.
scant.mnemonic: Scant : à peine suffisant, un peu juste (cousin de scarce).

scarce.definition: insufficient in supply; rare and hard to find
sentences: During the drought, clean water became scarce, and families had to walk several miles each morning to fill their buckets.
Jobs for historians are scarce, so many graduates with doctorates compete for a handful of university positions every year.
scarce.mnemonic: Scarce ≈ « scarcité » : rare, difficile à trouver.

sparse.definition: thinly scattered or spread out; not dense
sentences: The desert vegetation was sparse, with only a few shrubs scattered across miles of bare, cracked earth.
Because the population of the mountain region is sparse, the nearest hospital can be a two-hour drive from many villages.

paltry.definition: so small or worthless as to be insulting or trivial
sentences: The workers were outraged by the paltry raise of two dollars a month, which did not even cover the rising price of bus fares.
He sold the antique desk for a paltry sum, never realizing that collectors would have paid thousands of dollars for it.
paltry.mnemonic: Paltry : une somme si petite qu'elle en est vexante.

dearth.definition: a scarcity or lack of something
sentences: A dearth of qualified teachers in rural districts forced several schools to combine classes and cancel advanced courses altogether.
The critic lamented the dearth of original ideas in recent films, most of which were sequels or remakes of older movies.
dearth.mnemonic: Dearth ressemble à « death » : le manque, c'est presque la mort.

paucity.definition: smallness of number or quantity; scarcity
sentences: The paucity of reliable data made it impossible for the researchers to draw any firm conclusions about the drug's effectiveness.
Despite the paucity of her income, she managed to save a little each month by cooking at home and walking to work.
paucity.mnemonic: Même racine que « peu » / « pauvre » (latin paucus).

shortfall.definition: a deficit; the amount by which something falls short of what is needed
sentences: The university faced a budget shortfall of two million dollars after enrollment dropped, and administrators were forced to freeze all hiring.
To cover the shortfall in grain production caused by the floods, the country had to import thousands of tons of wheat.
shortfall.mnemonic: Short + fall : tomber court, le manque à gagner.

sentences: After the bankruptcy of his firm, the once wealthy merchant lived in penury, unable to afford even a decent meal.
Many of the great composers died in penury, their genius recognized only long after they had passed away without any money.
penury.mnemonic: Proche de « pénurie » en français : c'est le manque d'argent extrême.

thrifty.definition: careful and wise in the use of money and resources
sentences: Raised by thrifty parents who saved every spare coin, she learned early to compare prices and never waste food.
The thrifty shopkeeper reused packaging and repaired old equipment rather than buying new, and over the years his savings grew considerably.
thrifty.mnemonic: Thrifty ≈ « thrive » : on prospère en économisant.

sparing.definition: restrained and economical in using or giving something
sentences: The coach was sparing in his praise, so when he finally told the young runner she had done well, she was thrilled.
Because water was scarce on the expedition, the guide urged everyone to be sparing in washing and to drink only what they needed.

spare.definition: plain and simple, without unnecessary detail; also, extra or left over
sentences: The poet's spare style, stripped of ornament and adjectives, achieves its power through a few carefully chosen words.
Since he had no spare time during the week, the busy surgeon reserved his weekends for gardening and reading with his children.
spare.mnemonic: Spare = épargné : dépouillé du superflu, ou en trop (la roue de secours).

squander.definition: to waste something, such as money or opportunities, foolishly
sentences: The heir managed to squander his entire inheritance within five years, spending it on racehorses, parties, and a series of failed ventures.
By refusing to prepare for the exam, she would squander the opportunity that her teachers had worked so hard to give her.
squander.mnemonic: Squander : jeter l'argent par les fenêtres.

spendthrift.definition: a person who spends money recklessly and wastefully
sentences: Her brother was a notorious spendthrift who bought expensive gadgets every week and was always borrowing money before the end of the month.
Unlike the careful saver in the family, the spendthrift emptied his bank account on a luxury watch he rarely wore.
spendthrift.mnemonic: Spend + thrift (économie) : celui qui dépense l'épargne.

profligate.definition: recklessly extravagant, or shamelessly immoral in behavior
sentences: The king's profligate lifestyle, with its endless banquets and gambling, drained the royal treasury and left the kingdom deeply in debt.
Moralists condemned the profligate nobleman, who squandered his fortune and was notorious for scandalous behavior throughout the capital.
The billionaire threw a lavish wedding, with imported flowers, a famous orchestra, and a banquet that lasted until dawn.
Reviewers gave lavish praise to the debut novel, calling it the most remarkable first book that they had read in years.
lavish.mnemonic: Lavish ≈ « lavage » : l'eau coule à flots, on prodigue.

acquisitive.definition: eager to acquire money, possessions, or property
sentences: The acquisitive young executive was never satisfied, constantly buying more companies and properties in his hunt for greater wealth.
Critics described the museum's director as acquisitive, since he was always seeking to add new paintings to a collection already too large to display.
acquisitive.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « acquis » mais qui veut acquérir toujours plus.

embezzle.definition: to steal money entrusted to one's care, especially from an employer
sentences: The treasurer was arrested for trying to embezzle thousands of dollars from the charity, which he had been secretly transferring to his own account.
Auditors discovered that the accountant had been embezzling small sums for years, hiding the missing money through false entries in the company's ledgers.
embezzle.mnemonic: Embezzle : détourner l'argent qu'on vous a confié, comme un comptable infidèle.

parlay.definition: to turn an initial advantage or sum into something much greater
parlay.definitionFr: transformer un atout en gain plus grand
sentences: She managed to parlay a small inheritance into a large fortune by investing wisely in real estate throughout the 1990s.
The actor hoped to parlay his success in a minor television role into a career in films, and he soon won a leading part.
parlay.mnemonic: Parlay ≈ « parier » : on remise ses gains pour gagner plus.

sentences: The mayor's decision to close the library provoked the ire of local residents, who gathered outside city hall to shout their protest.
Her ire was evident in her trembling voice and clenched fists when she learned that her colleague had taken credit for her work.
ire.mnemonic: Ire = « ire » du latin ira, comme « irascible ».

animus.definition: strong hostility or ill will, often deep-seated
sentences: The two rival families had felt such animus toward one another for generations that nobody could remember how the quarrel had begun.
The judge had to recuse himself because his obvious animus against the defendant would have made a fair trial impossible.

enmity.definition: deep-rooted and lasting hatred or hostility between people
sentences: The enmity between the neighboring countries lasted for centuries, surviving treaties, royal marriages, and several changes of government.
Their friendship turned to bitter enmity after the business partner betrayed him, and the two men never spoke again.

umbrage.definition: offense or resentment at a perceived slight
sentences: The senator took umbrage at the suggestion that he had been bribed, and he demanded an immediate apology from the reporter.
She took umbrage at her colleague's offhand remark about her age, and she left the meeting early without saying a word.
umbrage.mnemonic: Du latin umbra, l'ombre : on se sent « ombragé », vexé. Cf. ombrageux.

strife.definition: bitter conflict or discord between people or groups
sentences: Years of civil strife left the country divided and impoverished, with rival factions fighting over the capital and the best farmland.
The family business was torn by strife after the founder's death, as his children quarreled openly over who should lead the firm.
strife.mnemonic: Strife : la discorde ouverte (rime avec knife, le couteau est sorti).

inimical.definition: hostile, or harmful and unfavorable in effect
sentences: Dictatorships are inimical to free speech, since leaders who fear criticism usually silence writers, journalists, and anyone who disagrees with them.
The harsh, dry climate proved inimical to the settlers' crops, and within two seasons most of the colony's farms had failed.
inimical.mnemonic: Même racine que « inimitié » et « ennemi ».

spiteful.definition: motivated by a desire to hurt or annoy someone out of malice
sentences: In a spiteful act of revenge, she deleted her former partner's files, knowing that the loss would cause him serious trouble.
The spiteful neighbor deliberately played loud music late at night, hoping to annoy the family who had complained about his dog.
spiteful.mnemonic: Spite = dépit : il agit par dépit, pour nuire.

treacherous.definition: betraying trust; also, hazardous and deceptively dangerous
sentences: The treacherous minister secretly sold state secrets to the enemy while publicly swearing loyalty to the king he was serving.
Icy patches made the mountain road treacherous, and several drivers who had trusted its apparently dry surface skidded off the edge.
treacherous.mnemonic: Treachery ≈ « tricherie » : trahison, ou terrain traître.

sentences: It began to irk her that her roommate never washed the dishes, and eventually she posted a stern note on the refrigerator.
Nothing seemed to irk the teacher more than students who arrived late and then loudly interrupted the lesson to ask what they had missed.
irk.mnemonic: Irk ≈ « irriter » : même idée, en plus court.

rankle.definition: to cause lingering resentment or bitterness
rankle.definitionFr: rester en travers de la gorge
sentences: The unfair criticism continued to rankle long after the meeting ended, and she found herself repeating the insult in her mind all week.
It still rankles the veteran player that the club chose a younger rival for the captaincy, despite his years of loyal service.
rankle.mnemonic: Rankle ≈ « rancune » : ça reste en travers, la rancœur.

nettlesome.definition: causing irritation or annoyance; troublesome and difficult
sentences: The nettlesome problem of funding for the bridge divided the council for months, and each proposed solution created fresh complaints.
He found the constant interruptions from his younger cousin nettlesome, as they kept him from finishing his essay before the deadline.
nettlesome.mnemonic: Nettle = ortie : une situation qui pique comme une ortie.

harrow.definition: to cause acute mental distress; to torment
sentences: The documentary about the refugees' long journey was so harrowing that many viewers left the theater in tears and unable to speak.
Memories of the accident continued to harrow him for years, and he often woke at night with his heart pounding.
harrow.mnemonic: Une herse (harrow) déchire la terre : on déchire l'âme.

sentences: It would be churlish to refuse the invitation after our hosts went to such trouble, so we accepted with a smile.
The churlish shopkeeper grunted at customers and slammed the cash drawer, and soon most regulars were going elsewhere.

boorish.definition: rude, insensitive, and lacking in manners or refinement
sentences: His boorish behavior at the formal dinner, which included belching loudly and insulting the hostess, left the other guests appalled.
The boorish tourist shouted at the waiter and ignored local customs, which embarrassed his companions and offended everyone in the restaurant.
boorish.mnemonic: Boor = rustre : mal élevé, sans manières.

crass.definition: crude and insensitive; lacking refinement or sensitivity
sentences: Mourners were shocked by his crass remark about the inheritance, made only minutes after the funeral had ended.
The advertisement was so crass in its exploitation of the tragedy that public outrage forced the company to withdraw it.
crass.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « crasse » (saleté) mais grossier dans les manières.

brash.definition: self-assertive in a rude, tactless, and overconfident way
sentences: The brash young lawyer interrupted senior partners and boasted about his victories, and his lack of tact made enemies quickly.
Her brash prediction that she would defeat the champion in the first round amused the crowd, but it also made her a target.
In a brazen robbery, the thieves walked into the gallery at noon and carried out the painting while the guards watched.
He told a brazen lie, looking the judge straight in the eye and showing no sign of embarrassment about the evidence against him.
brazen.mnemonic: Brazen = de bronze (brass) : un front d'airain, sans honte.

unseemly.definition: not proper or appropriate for the occasion; improper
sentences: Laughing loudly at the funeral struck the mourners as unseemly, and several relatives frowned at him until he fell silent.
The senator regarded it as unseemly for officials to haggle over their salaries while the city's schools were short of money.
unseemly.mnemonic: UN-seemly ≈ qui ne sied pas : inconvenant.

impolitic.definition: unwise and tactless; poorly judged for the circumstances
sentences: It was impolitic of the candidate to criticize the region's main industry while campaigning in a town that depended on it for jobs.
The ambassador's impolitic joke about the host country's cuisine nearly caused a diplomatic incident and forced the minister to apologize.
impolitic.mnemonic: Im + politic : le contraire de politique, sans tact diplomatique.

flippant.definition: showing a lack of proper respect or seriousness
sentences: The judge was angered by the defendant's flippant answers, which treated the serious charges as though they were a joke.
Her flippant reply to the question about the budget crisis suggested that she did not understand how grave the situation was.
flippant.mnemonic: Faux ami : rien à voir avec « flipper » ; c'est la désinvolture.

facetious.definition: treating serious matters with inappropriate humor; jokingly
sentences: The professor's facetious comment during the solemn ceremony drew a few nervous laughs but earned a stern look from the dean.
Please don't be facetious; this is a serious question, and I need a real answer rather than another joke.
facetious.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « facétieux » au sens aimable, mais plaisanterie déplacée.

diffident.definition: modest or shy because of a lack of self-confidence
sentences: The diffident young scientist spoke so quietly during her presentation that the audience could hardly hear her important results.
Though brilliant, he was diffident about his talents and rarely offered his opinions unless the group specifically asked for them.
diffident.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « différent » mais « dé-fiant » : sans confiance en soi.

coy.definition: pretending to be shy or reluctant, often to tease
sentences: When reporters asked whether she would run for office, the senator gave a coy smile and refused to give a direct answer.
The company remained coy about its new product, hinting at a launch date without revealing a single technical detail.
coy.mnemonic: Coy ≈ « coi » : faussement timide, qui se tait en minaudant.

reticent.definition: reluctant to speak about one's thoughts or feelings; reserved
sentences: The witness was reticent about the details of the incident, answering questions in single words and avoiding the lawyer's gaze.
Normally talkative, he became reticent when asked about his childhood, changing the subject whenever the conversation turned to his family.
reticent.mnemonic: Faux ami : pas « réticent » (hésitant à agir) mais réservé à parler.

wary.definition: cautious about possible dangers or problems
sentences: After being cheated once, the traveler grew wary of strangers who offered help and checked every price before agreeing to pay.
Investors remain wary of the new technology, since several similar ventures collapsed within a year of attracting millions in funding.

chary.definition: cautious and reluctant to give or risk something
sentences: Having lost money before, the banker was chary of lending to new businesses and demanded extensive guarantees from every applicant.
The famous author was chary of granting interviews, fearing that reporters would distort his words and invade his private life.
chary.mnemonic: Chary ≈ « chère » (précieux) : on ménage ce qu'on donne.

sentences: The skittish horse bolted at the slightest noise, so the rider had to speak softly and keep a firm grip on the reins.
Skittish investors sold their shares at the first rumor of trouble, causing the market to fall even though the company was sound.
skittish.mnemonic: Skittish : il part en sursaut comme un cheval ombrageux.

sentences: The craven soldier threw down his weapon and fled at the first sound of gunfire, leaving his comrades to face the enemy alone.
Critics denounced the craven politician who, afraid of public anger, abandoned his principles and voted against the bill he had promised to support.
craven.mnemonic: Craven : un lâche qui crève de peur.

foolhardy.definition: recklessly bold; taking risks without sensible thought
sentences: It was foolhardy to attempt to cross the frozen lake in spring, and the hikers narrowly escaped when the ice cracked beneath them.
The foolhardy investor put all his savings into a single unproven start-up, ignoring warnings from every financial adviser he consulted.

rash.definition: acting or done without careful thought about possible consequences
sentences: The investor made a rash decision to sell all his shares in a panic, ignoring the advice of every financial analyst he consulted.
Her rash remark during the negotiation offended the delegates, and she spent the following week trying to repair the damage she had caused.
rash.mnemonic: Rash = éruption : on agit sur un coup de tête, sans réfléchir.

hasty.definition: done with excessive speed, often producing careless results
sentences: Because the committee reached a hasty verdict after only ten minutes, several members later admitted that they had overlooked crucial evidence in the case.
The editor regretted her hasty revisions, since the rushed changes introduced more errors into the manuscript than they had removed from it.
hasty.mnemonic: Hasty ressemble à haste/hâte : fait trop vite.

bleak.definition: bare and desolate; offering no hope or cheerful prospect
sentences: The bleak, windswept moor stretched endlessly before the travelers, without a single tree or building to break the gray monotony of the horizon.
With factories closing and unemployment rising, economists painted a bleak picture of the region's future, seeing little reason for any optimism at all.
bleak.mnemonic: Bleak ≈ « blême » : un paysage pâle, morne, sans espoir.

grim.definition: serious and gloomy; harsh and forbidding in manner or reality
sentences: The doctor delivered the grim news that the disease had spread, and the family sat in stunned silence for several long minutes.
Rescuers faced the grim task of searching the rubble for survivors, knowing that each passing hour made a happy outcome less likely.
grim.mnemonic: Grim ≈ « grimace » : un visage sinistre, une situation très grave.

sullen.definition: bad-tempered and silent, showing resentful ill humor
sentences: After losing the argument, the sullen teenager slumped in the back seat and refused to answer any of his parents' friendly questions.
The sullen clerk grunted at each customer without looking up, which quickly drove away patrons who had once enjoyed the cheerful old shop.
sullen.mnemonic: Sullen : sol-itaire et boudeur, il reste dans son coin.

dirge.definition: a slow, mournful song or piece of music played at a funeral
sentences: As the coffin was lowered into the ground, the band played a solemn dirge that brought many of the mourners to tears.
The critic compared the symphony's final movement to a dirge, noting that its slow, heavy rhythms evoked loss rather than any triumphant celebration.
dirge.mnemonic: Dirge : le chant funèbre (du latin « dirige », début d'un office des morts).

maudlin.definition: tearfully and foolishly sentimental, often because of drinking
sentences: After three glasses of wine, the usually reserved professor grew maudlin and began weeping over the memory of his childhood dog.
Critics dismissed the film as maudlin, complaining that its relentless appeals to the audience's emotions felt manipulative rather than genuinely touching.
maudlin.mnemonic: Maudlin vient de Madeleine (Marie-Madeleine en pleurs).

mawkish.definition: sentimental in a weak, sickly and embarrassing way
sentences: The greeting card's mawkish verse, full of syrupy promises of eternal devotion, made the recipient wince rather than smile.
Although the novelist could write moving scenes, her later books grew mawkish, drowning interesting characters in excessive and unconvincing sentimentality.
mawkish.mnemonic: Mawkish : une mièvrerie qui donne la nausée, trop larmoyant.

cloying.definition: disgusting or unpleasant because of excessive sweetness or sentimentality
sentences: The dessert was so cloying that after two bites I pushed the plate away, craving something sharp and bitter instead.
Many viewers found the sitcom's cloying sentimentality hard to bear, since every episode ended with the same sugary lesson about friendship.
cloying.mnemonic: Cloying ≈ « clou » : trop de sucre colle et écœure.

aghast.definition: filled with shock and horror by something seen or heard
sentences: The villagers stood aghast as the flood swept away their homes, unable to speak or move in the face of such devastation.
She was aghast at the size of the bill, since the repairs had cost ten times what the mechanic had originally promised.
aghast.mnemonic: A-ghast ≈ « ghost » : on a vu un fantôme, frappé d'horreur.

appall.definition: to shock and fill someone with horror or deep dismay
sentences: The graphic photographs of the disaster zone were meant to appall the public and finally push the government into taking decisive action.
Reports of the factory's dangerous conditions appalled investors, who immediately demanded that the company explain why it had ignored safety inspectors for years.

dismay.definition: a feeling of distress and worry caused by something unexpected and unwelcome
sentences: To the dismay of the organizers, heavy rain began falling an hour before the outdoor concert, leaving thousands of ticket holders huddled under umbrellas.
The board expressed dismay at the sudden resignation of the director, fearing that the unexpected departure would unsettle both employees and clients.
dismay.mnemonic: Dis-may ≈ « dis-moi » : consternation mêlée d'inquiétude (esmayer en ancien français).

jarring.definition: harshly clashing and unpleasant, causing a shock to the senses
sentences: The jarring blare of the car alarm shattered the peaceful morning and made everyone on the quiet street wince.
Critics found the sudden shift from a tender love story to graphic violence jarring, since the two tones seemed completely incompatible.
jarring.mnemonic: Jar = secouer : un son qui fait sursauter, discordant.

humdrum.definition: lacking excitement or variety; dull and repetitive
sentences: Tired of her humdrum office routine, with the same meetings and reports every single day, she quit to travel across Asia.
The memoir transforms an otherwise humdrum life of commuting and paperwork into a fascinating story through its author's sharp wit and keen observation.
humdrum.mnemonic: Hum-drum : le bourdonnement monotone d'un tambour toujours pareil.

sentences: Copying thousands of figures by hand into the ledger was a tedious chore that left the accountant yawning long before lunch.
The lecture grew so tedious, with endless digressions and repeated examples, that half of the students quietly began checking their phones.
tedious.mnemonic: Tedious : tédieux ressemble à ennuyeux, mais pas faux ami.

tiresome.definition: causing weariness or annoyance because of being dull or repetitive
sentences: His tiresome habit of interrupting every conversation with a long personal anecdote eventually made his colleagues avoid him at lunch.
The senator found the constant press questions about the old scandal tiresome, and she answered each one with visible and growing irritation.

vapid.definition: lacking liveliness, flavor or interesting ideas; dull and insipid
sentences: The talk show host filled the hour with vapid chatter about celebrities, offering viewers not a single thoughtful or memorable idea.
Critics called the film vapid, noting that its stunning visuals could not disguise a plot with no depth and dialogue with no wit.
vapid.mnemonic: Vapid ~ vapeur : de la vapeur, rien de consistant dedans.

trite.definition: made dull and unoriginal by overuse; commonplace
sentences: The speaker's advice to 'follow your dreams' sounded trite to the graduates, who had heard the same phrase at countless ceremonies.
Although the poem began with promise, its trite rhymes about love and roses made it indistinguishable from thousands of greeting-card verses.
trite.mnemonic: Trite ≈ « trituré » : usé à force d'être répété.

hackneyed.definition: lacking freshness because of having been used too often
sentences: The detective novel relied on hackneyed devices, such as the butler who did it, so no reader was surprised by the ending.
Her essay was weakened by hackneyed phrases like 'at the end of the day', which made the argument sound tired and unoriginal.
hackneyed.mnemonic: Hackney : chevaux de louage fatigués, comme des expressions usées.

trope.definition: a recurring theme, device or cliché in a genre or work of art
sentences: The lone hero who rejects society is a familiar trope in Westerns, appearing in countless films across several generations of moviemaking.
Scholars of rhetoric study the trope of the noble savage, tracing how writers repeatedly used the image to criticize their own civilization.
trope.mnemonic: Trope ≈ « trope » (figure de style) : un cliché récurrent.

lackluster.definition: lacking brilliance, energy or excitement; dull
sentences: The team delivered a lackluster performance in the final, playing without energy and failing to create a single real scoring chance.
Despite the lavish advertising campaign, the product's lackluster sales disappointed shareholders, who had expected the launch to be a spectacular triumph.

staid.definition: sedate, serious and unadventurous, often in an old-fashioned way
sentences: The staid old bank, with its dark wood paneling and formal dress code, resisted every trend toward casual or experimental business practices.
Her staid parents were shocked when she dyed her hair bright green, since the family had always valued quiet respectability above all else.
staid.mnemonic: Staid ≈ « stay » : qui reste en place, sérieux et vieux jeu.

riveting.definition: completely engrossing; holding one's attention firmly
sentences: The lecturer gave a riveting account of the expedition, and not one member of the audience glanced at a watch during the whole hour.
Critics praised the documentary as riveting, noting that its suspenseful structure kept viewers glued to their seats from the first scene to the last.
riveting.mnemonic: Rivet = rivet : l'attention est rivée, clouée.

gripping.definition: holding attention through excitement or suspense
sentences: The author's gripping thriller kept me awake until dawn, since I simply could not put the book down before learning who the killer was.
Audiences described the courtroom drama as gripping, praising the way every scene raised the tension until the shocking final verdict.
gripping.mnemonic: Grip = poigne : le récit vous tient serré.

enthrall.definition: to capture and hold the complete attention of, as if by magic
sentences: The storyteller managed to enthrall the children for hours, and they sat motionless as she described dragons, castles and hidden treasure.
Audiences were enthralled by the young pianist, whose dazzling technique and emotional depth held the entire concert hall in rapt silence.
enthrall.mnemonic: En-thrall : thrall = esclave ; on devient esclave du charme.

engross.definition: to absorb all of someone's attention or interest
sentences: The mystery novel began to engross her so completely that she missed her train stop and arrived at work an hour late.
He was so engrossed in solving the equation that he failed to notice the bell, and the classroom emptied around him.
engross.mnemonic: En-gross : on prend tout (gros) de votre attention.

mesmerize.definition: to hold someone's attention so completely that they seem entranced
sentences: The swirling patterns of the fireworks seemed to mesmerize the crowd, which stood in silent wonder long after the display had ended.
Her hypnotic voice mesmerized listeners, and many of them later admitted that they could not recall anything but its soft, steady rhythm.
mesmerize.mnemonic: Du nom de Mesmer, médecin qui hypnotisait ses patients.

transfix.definition: to render motionless with awe, terror or amazement
sentences: The sight of the enormous bear emerging from the trees seemed to transfix the hikers, who stood frozen and unable to flee.
The magician's final trick transfixed the audience, holding every eye on the stage until the curtain finally came down.
transfix.mnemonic: Trans + fix : fixé sur place, immobile.

sentences: The lawyer presented such compelling evidence of the defendant's innocence that the jury needed less than an hour to acquit him.
The memoir is compelling reading, for its author describes her escape from war with a honesty that few readers can ignore.
compelling.mnemonic: Compelling ≈ « compeller » : on ne peut pas résister, il vous pousse.

staggering.definition: astonishing because of enormous size or amount
sentences: The company reported staggering losses of several billion dollars, a sum so large that analysts struggled to explain how it had accumulated.
Archaeologists were amazed by the staggering scale of the buried city, which stretched across an area far larger than they had imagined.
staggering.mnemonic: Stagger = chanceler : tellement énorme qu'on titube.

dazzle.definition: to amaze or overwhelm with brilliant display, or blind with bright light
sentences: The dancer's flawless technique and dramatic costumes were meant to dazzle the judges, who had seen hundreds of ordinary performances that week.
Headlights from the oncoming truck dazzled the driver, who braked sharply and squinted until his vision gradually returned to normal.
dazzle.mnemonic: Dazzle ≈ « dazed » : ébloui, assommé de lumière.

enticing.definition: attractive and tempting, drawing people in
sentences: The aroma of fresh bread drifting from the bakery was so enticing that few passersby could resist stepping inside for a loaf.
The company offered enticing bonuses to attract talented engineers, hoping that the promise of generous rewards would persuade them to leave their rivals.

palatable.definition: pleasant to taste; or acceptable and satisfactory to the mind
sentences: The chef added a little sugar to make the bitter sauce more palatable, and even the fussiest guests cleaned their plates.
To make the unpopular budget palatable to voters, the minister emphasized its benefits for schools and softened its most controversial tax increases.
palatable.mnemonic: Palatable : palais (du goût) ; ce qui plaît au palais.

relish.definition: to enjoy greatly and take keen pleasure in
sentences: After months of hard work, she began to relish every quiet morning on her porch, sipping coffee and watching the sun rise.
The old professor did not relish the prospect of retirement, for he had always loved lecturing and debating with eager students.
relish.mnemonic: Relish = condiment : on savoure avec goût.

revel.definition: to take great delight in; to celebrate noisily
revel.definitionFr: se délecter de ; faire la fête
sentences: The villagers gathered in the square to revel in their team's victory, singing and dancing through the night until sunrise.
He seemed to revel in the controversy surrounding his book, giving interview after interview and clearly enjoying every moment of the debate.
revel.mnemonic: Revel ≈ « réveillon » : on fait la fête.

fleeting.definition: lasting for only a very short time
sentences: She caught only a fleeting glimpse of the rare bird before it vanished into the dense forest canopy above her.
Fame in the music industry is often fleeting, since a song that tops the charts one summer is usually forgotten by the next.

wane.definition: to decrease gradually in strength, size or influence
sentences: As the evening wore on, the crowd's enthusiasm began to wane, and by midnight only a handful of fans remained in the stadium.
Once the most powerful empire in the region, the kingdom saw its influence wane steadily as rivals grew richer and better armed.
wane.mnemonic: Wane (déclin de la lune) s'oppose à wax (croissant).

dwindle.definition: to become gradually smaller, fewer or weaker
sentences: As the drought continued, the village's supply of fresh water began to dwindle, and families were forced to ration every drop.
Public support for the policy dwindled over the following months, until only a small group of loyal activists still defended it.
dwindle.mnemonic: Dwindle : diminuer petit à petit, comme une bougie.

fledgling.definition: new and inexperienced, just starting to develop
sentences: The fledgling company struggled in its first year, lacking both the capital and the experience needed to compete with established rivals.
Mentors helped the fledgling democracy establish courts and elections, though many of its institutions remained fragile and untested in their early years.
fledgling.mnemonic: Fledgling = oisillon qui vient d'avoir ses plumes, encore maladroit.

tyro.definition: a beginner with no experience in a skill or field
sentences: Although the veteran chess master crushed the tyro in only a dozen moves, he kindly explained each of the beginner's mistakes afterward.
As a tyro in the laboratory, the first-year student needed constant supervision, since she had never before handled any of the delicate instruments.
tyro.mnemonic: Tyro ~ « tiro » : le tirailleur novice latin (tiro).

trailblazer.definition: a person who makes a new path, pioneering something that others later follow
sentences: As the first woman to lead a major research university, she was a trailblazer who opened doors for countless female scholars after her.
The engineer was a trailblazer in renewable energy, building working solar plants decades before other companies took the technology seriously.
trailblazer.mnemonic: Trail + blaze : tracer le sentier en marquant les arbres.

groundbreaking.definition: pioneering and innovative, introducing completely new methods or ideas
sentences: The scientist's groundbreaking discovery of the new particle transformed physics, forcing researchers to rewrite textbooks that had stood for fifty years.
Critics hailed the director's groundbreaking film for its original techniques, which no studio had ever attempted before and which many later imitated.
groundbreaking.mnemonic: Ground-breaking : on casse la terre, on ouvre un chantier inédit.

maverick.definition: an independent person who refuses to conform to the views of a group
sentences: The senator, a maverick who often voted against his own party, earned admiration from voters who valued independence over loyalty.
As a maverick in the fashion world, the designer ignored seasonal trends and produced bold collections that no other label would have dared to show.
maverick.mnemonic: Maverick : veau sans marque du Texan Maverick, qui échappe au troupeau.

herald.definition: to announce, or to be a sign that something is coming
sentences: Trumpets sounded to herald the arrival of the king, and the crowd along the road fell silent and bowed their heads.
Many economists believe that the new invention will herald a revolution in manufacturing, changing how goods are made throughout the world.

harbinger.definition: a person or thing that signals the approach of something
sentences: The first robin of the year is often called a harbinger of spring, since it appears just as the snow begins to melt.
Analysts viewed the sudden bank failure as a harbinger of wider financial trouble, and they warned that other institutions might soon collapse.
harbinger.mnemonic: À l'origine, celui qui part devant préparer le logement : signe avant-coureur.

portend.definition: to be a sign or warning that something, usually bad, will happen
sentences: Dark clouds gathering over the harbor seemed to portend a violent storm, and the fishermen hurried to secure their boats.
Many historians argue that the rising unrest in the capital portended the collapse of the regime, though few contemporaries recognized the danger.
portend.mnemonic: Portend ≈ « porter » : ça porte un présage, souvent mauvais.

foreseeable.definition: able to be predicted or expected in advance
sentences: The accident was entirely foreseeable, since engineers had warned for years that the aging bridge could not bear the weight of modern traffic.
Because the company expects steady demand for the foreseeable future, its managers have decided against any further reductions in staff.

impending.definition: about to happen, especially of something threatening
sentences: Residents of the coast were warned of the impending hurricane and urged to leave their homes before the first heavy winds arrived.
The student felt anxious about the impending exam, which loomed only two days away and covered material she had barely begun to review.
impending.mnemonic: Im-pending ≈ « pendant » : suspendu au-dessus de nous.

beget.definition: to cause or bring about, as a result; to father
sentences: Historians often say that violence begets violence, since each act of revenge provokes a new response and prolongs the cycle of conflict.
Poverty can beget poor health, which in turn begets further poverty, creating a cycle that is extremely difficult for families to escape.
beget.mnemonic: Beget : l'ancien « engendrer » (« et il engendra… »).

spawn.definition: to give rise to or produce in large numbers
sentences: The success of the original film went on to spawn a dozen sequels, each of which copied its formula with less and less originality.
Rapid industrialization tended to spawn crowded slums at the edges of cities, as thousands of workers arrived with nowhere affordable to live.
spawn.mnemonic: Spawn = frai : les poissons pondent en masse, ça en produit à la chaîne.

foster.definition: to encourage the development or growth of something
sentences: The teacher tried to foster a love of reading by letting students choose their own books and discuss them in small groups.
Government grants were intended to foster innovation in small businesses, giving young entrepreneurs the resources they needed to test bold ideas.
foster.mnemonic: Foster : famille d'accueil, on aide à grandir.

coalesce.definition: to come together and form a single whole
sentences: Over several months, scattered protests across the country began to coalesce into a single organized movement with a clear set of demands.
As the oil droplets coalesced on the surface of the water, they formed larger pools that eventually separated entirely from the liquid below.

suffuse.definition: to spread over or through, gradually filling with color, light or feeling
sentences: The setting sun seemed to suffuse the valley with a warm golden glow, and every hillside looked as if it were lit from within.
A sense of quiet joy suffused the room as the family gathered around the table, and all their earlier quarrels were forgotten.
suffuse.mnemonic: Suf-fuse ≈ « fuser » : ça se répand doucement partout.

imbue.definition: to fill thoroughly with a quality, feeling or value
sentences: Her grandmother worked hard to imbue the children with a respect for education, reading to them each night and praising every small achievement.
The sculptor imbued the marble figure with such emotion that visitors often felt the statue was about to speak or begin moving.

pervasive.definition: spreading widely and present throughout every part of something
sentences: Smartphones have become so pervasive that it is now unusual to see a commuter on a train who is not staring at a screen.
The pervasive smell of smoke filled every room of the house, and no amount of open windows could remove it entirely.
pervasive.mnemonic: Per-vasive ≈ « envahir » : ça se répand partout.

bolster.definition: to support, strengthen or boost something
sentences: The new data helped bolster the researchers' hypothesis, giving skeptical colleagues a strong reason to take their controversial theory more seriously.
The central bank cut interest rates to bolster the struggling economy, hoping that cheaper loans would encourage businesses to hire and invest.
bolster.mnemonic: Bolster = traversin (coussin) : il soutient la tête.

buttress.definition: to support or strengthen an argument or structure
sentences: The lawyer cited three recent studies to buttress her claim, hoping the statistics would convince the skeptical jury of her client's innocence.
Workers added stone supports to buttress the crumbling wall of the cathedral, which had begun leaning dangerously toward the street.
buttress.mnemonic: Buttress : arc-boutant, le contrefort des cathédrales.

underscore.definition: to emphasize or highlight the importance of something
sentences: The recent earthquake serves to underscore the importance of strict building codes, which saved many lives in the better constructed districts.
In her closing remarks, the speaker underscored the urgency of the climate crisis, repeating that further delay would make the damage irreversible.
underscore.mnemonic: Under + score : on souligne (le tiret bas, c'est l'underscore).

substantiate.definition: to provide evidence that proves a claim to be true
sentences: The journalist could not substantiate the rumor, since no witness would speak openly and no document supported the shocking allegation.
Scientists must substantiate their claims with repeatable experiments before the wider community will accept a surprising new theory as fact.
substantiate.mnemonic: Substance : on donne de la substance (des preuves) à l'affirmation.

uphold.definition: to confirm or maintain, especially a decision, law or principle
sentences: The appeals court voted to uphold the original verdict, rejecting the defense argument that the trial had been conducted unfairly.
A good judge must uphold the law even when it conflicts with personal opinion or the shifting demands of popular sentiment.

mainstay.definition: a person or thing that is the chief support of something
sentences: Agriculture has long been the mainstay of the local economy, employing most residents and supplying nearly all of the region's exports.
The veteran goalkeeper was the mainstay of the team for a decade, and the club struggled badly after he retired.
mainstay.mnemonic: Main + stay : l'étai principal d'un navire, le pilier.

credence.definition: acceptance of something as true or believable
sentences: The discovery of the ancient letter lends credence to the legend, which most historians had previously dismissed as pure invention.
Few scientists give credence to the claim, since no laboratory has ever managed to reproduce the supposed result.

undermine.definition: to weaken gradually, especially by secretly damaging the foundations of something
sentences: Constant rumors and gossip began to undermine the manager's authority, until even her closest allies doubted that she could lead the team.
Critics argued that the new law would undermine public trust in the courts by allowing wealthy defendants to buy favorable treatment.
undermine.mnemonic: Under + mine : on creuse sous les fondations.

undercut.definition: to weaken the effect of; or to sell at a lower price than a competitor
sentences: The small airline managed to undercut its larger rivals by charging far lower fares, and within a year it had captured much of the market.
Her sarcastic comment undercut the seriousness of the speech, and the audience, which had been listening attentively, began to laugh.
undercut.mnemonic: Under + cut : couper en dessous (le prix ou l'effet).

vitiate.definition: to spoil or impair the quality or validity of something
sentences: The lawyer argued that the discovery of bribery would vitiate the entire contract, making it legally void despite the signatures of both parties.
A single contaminated sample can vitiate weeks of careful laboratory work, forcing the researchers to repeat every experiment from the very beginning.
vitiate.mnemonic: Vitiate ressemble à « vice » : un vice de forme annule l'acte.

impair.definition: to weaken or damage something, especially an ability or quality
sentences: Prolonged exposure to loud machinery can impair a worker's hearing, so the factory now requires protective earplugs on every production floor.
Lack of sleep can seriously impair judgment and memory, which is why surgeons are limited in how many consecutive hours they may work.

mar.definition: to spoil the appearance or perfection of something; to damage
sentences: A few careless typographical errors marred an otherwise brilliant report, leaving readers with a poor impression of the author's attention to detail.
Allegations of corruption threatened to mar the mayor's reputation just weeks before the election, despite his long record of honest public service.
mar.mnemonic: Mar ≈ « marque » : une marque qui gâche la surface.

vindicate.definition: to clear of blame or suspicion; to prove someone right
vindicate.definitionFr: donner raison, laver de tout soupçon
sentences: The newly discovered video footage vindicated the accused man, proving beyond doubt that he had been miles away when the robbery occurred.
Years later, the economist felt vindicated when the financial crisis unfolded exactly as she had warned, after colleagues had mocked her predictions.
vindicate.mnemonic: Vindicate ≈ « vindicte » : on rend justice, on blanchit.

exculpate.definition: to show or declare that someone is not guilty of wrongdoing
sentences: DNA evidence from the crime scene helped exculpate the prisoner, who had spent two decades in jail for an offense he did not commit.
The committee's report did not exculpate the director, though it did show that several of his subordinates shared responsibility for the accounting failures.

evince.definition: to show or reveal a quality or feeling clearly
sentences: Although she tried to remain calm, the nervous candidate could not help but evince anxiety, fidgeting constantly throughout the entire interview.
The young pianist's performance evinced a maturity far beyond her years, convincing the skeptical judges that she deserved the first prize.

contend.definition: to assert or maintain something as a position in an argument
sentences: Critics contend that the new tax policy will hurt small businesses, though supporters insist that it will ultimately stimulate economic growth for everyone.
The historian contends that the empire collapsed not because of foreign invasion but because of internal political decay, and she cites extensive evidence.
contend.mnemonic: Contend ≈ « contention » : soutenir, se battre pour une thèse.

aver.definition: to state something confidently as a fact; to declare firmly
sentences: Despite hours of intense questioning by detectives, the suspect continued to aver that he had never met the victim in his entire life.
The witness averred under oath that she had seen the defendant leave the building at midnight, and she never wavered from her account.
aver.mnemonic: Aver : le ver- de « vérité » : affirmer que c'est vrai.

purport.definition: to claim or appear to be something, often falsely
sentences: The document purports to be a letter written by Napoleon, but historians who examined the handwriting believe it is a clever nineteenth-century forgery.
Many websites that purport to offer miracle cures turn out to be scams designed to take money from desperate and poorly informed patients.
purport.mnemonic: Purport : il se « porte » prétendant, souvent à tort.

surmise.definition: to guess or suppose something without firm evidence
sentences: Seeing the empty coffee cups and the unfinished papers, the detective could only surmise that the meeting had ended abruptly, though he had no proof.
Archaeologists surmise that the ancient settlement was abandoned because of drought, but without written records they cannot confirm this tentative explanation.
surmise.mnemonic: Sur-mise : on met une idée au-dessus des faits, une supposition.

deem.definition: to consider or judge something to be a certain way
sentences: The committee deemed the proposal too risky and rejected it, even though several members admired its originality and ambition.
If the judge deems the evidence inadmissible, the jury will never hear it, and the prosecution's case may well collapse entirely.
deem.mnemonic: Deem ≈ « doom », jugement : juger, tenir pour.

ascribe.definition: to attribute something to a particular cause, source, or author
sentences: Scholars long ascribed the anonymous poem to Chaucer, but recent analysis of its vocabulary suggests that a much later writer composed it.
The coach refused to ascribe the team's defeat to bad luck, insisting instead that poor preparation and weak defense had caused the loss.
ascribe.mnemonic: As-cribe ≈ « inscrire » : on inscrit la faute à quelqu'un, on attribue.

discount.definition: to dismiss as unimportant, unreliable, or unworthy of consideration
sentences: The board chose to discount the consultant's warnings as exaggerated, a decision they would later regret when the predicted problems materialized.
We should not discount the possibility of error simply because the equipment is new, since even the best instruments occasionally produce faulty readings.

gainsay.definition: to deny or contradict a statement or claim
sentences: No one could gainsay the surgeon's remarkable skill, for her patients recovered faster than those of any other doctor in the hospital.
The evidence was so overwhelming that even his bitterest rivals could not gainsay his achievements, and they grudgingly acknowledged his contribution.

belie.definition: to give a false impression of; to contradict
belie.definitionFr: démentir ; donner une fausse image de
sentences: His calm, cheerful manner belied the terror he felt, and none of the guests suspected that he was about to lose his business.
The company's glossy brochures belie the reality of its crowded, poorly ventilated factories, where employees work long hours for very low wages.
belie.mnemonic: Be-lie : trahir par le mensonge (lie), donner une fausse image.

conflate.definition: to combine two separate things into one, wrongly treating them as the same
sentences: Many readers conflate correlation with causation, wrongly assuming that because two events occur together, one must necessarily have produced the other.
It is a serious error to conflate patriotism with blind obedience, since a loyal citizen may criticize the government precisely out of love for the country.
conflate.mnemonic: Du latin conflare, souffler ensemble : on fond deux choses en une.

misconstrue.definition: to interpret something wrongly; to misunderstand
sentences: Her polite refusal was easily misconstrued as hostility, though she had merely wanted to decline the invitation without offending the host.
Critics misconstrued the senator's remarks, taking a casual joke as a serious policy proposal, and the resulting uproar forced her to issue a clarification.

misnomer.definition: a wrong or inaccurate name or designation
sentences: Calling the small, windowless room a conference hall is a misnomer, since it barely holds six people and has no space for presentations.
The term "fast food" is something of a misnomer when the line is so long that customers wait nearly half an hour for their order.

fathom.definition: to understand something difficult after thinking deeply about it
sentences: Even after hours of study, the students failed to fathom the complex theorem, which seemed to contradict everything they had learned earlier.
Few people could fathom why the successful executive abandoned a lucrative career to live alone in a remote cabin without electricity.
fathom.mnemonic: Une brasse (fathom) mesure la profondeur : sonder = comprendre en profondeur.

ascertain.definition: to find out or establish something with certainty
sentences: Investigators worked for months to ascertain the cause of the explosion, examining every fragment of debris before reaching a final conclusion.
Before signing the contract, the buyer hired an inspector to ascertain whether the house had any structural defects hidden behind its fresh paint.

elicit.definition: to draw out a response, reaction, or piece of information
sentences: The comedian's clever joke failed to elicit even a smile from the stern audience, who sat in complete and uncomfortable silence.
Skilled interviewers know how to elicit candid answers by asking open questions and listening patiently, rather than pressuring the witness for quick replies.
elicit.mnemonic: Elicit ≠ illicit : elicit tire une réponse, illicit est illégal.

discern.definition: to perceive or recognize something that is not obvious
sentences: In the dim light, the sailor could barely discern the outline of the coast, though he sensed that land was near.
A good editor can discern subtle flaws in an argument that most readers would overlook, and she helps writers repair them before publication.

blatant.definition: obvious in an offensive, shameless way
sentences: The senator's blatant disregard for the rules shocked even his allies, who could no longer defend his open and unapologetic misuse of public funds.
The advertisement made a blatant attempt to mislead consumers, claiming a product was free when customers actually had to pay hidden fees.
blatant.mnemonic: Blatant ≈ « bêlant » : on l'entend à des lieues, flagrant.

glaring.definition: strikingly obvious, especially as a mistake or fault
sentences: The report contained a glaring error on its very first page, which suggested that no one had bothered to proofread it before publication.
One glaring omission from the history textbook was any mention of women, whose contributions the authors had simply left out of the account.
glaring.mnemonic: Glare = éblouissement : une erreur qui saute aux yeux.

conspicuous.definition: easily seen or noticed; standing out clearly
sentences: In a room full of black suits, her bright red dress made her conspicuous, and every guest turned to look as she entered.
The new tower is a conspicuous landmark that can be seen from almost anywhere in the city, rising far above the surrounding low buildings.
conspicuous.mnemonic: Con-spic ≈ « spectacle » : on le voit, il se détache.

overt.definition: done or shown openly, not concealed
sentences: Unlike the covert operations of the past, the government's new campaign was an overt effort to influence public opinion, announced in newspapers and on television.
The two rivals made no overt display of hostility during the meeting, though the tension between them was obvious to everyone watching.

stark.definition: sharply clear or plain, with no softening; harsh and severe
sentences: The photograph showed a stark contrast between the gleaming skyscrapers and the crumbling slums directly beneath them, with nothing to soften the difference.
The doctor gave a stark warning that continued smoking would almost certainly shorten the patient's life, leaving no room for comforting ambiguity.
stark.mnemonic: Stark : nu, brut (stark naked), sans nuance.

egregious.definition: outstandingly bad; shockingly and obviously wrong
sentences: The judge condemned the company's egregious violation of safety regulations, which had put thousands of workers at risk for the sake of higher profits.
Leaving the most important witness out of the investigation was an egregious mistake that undermined the credibility of the entire inquiry.
egregious.mnemonic: E-gregious : hors du troupeau (grex), tellement mauvais qu'on le remarque.

uncanny.definition: strange and unsettling in a way that seems almost supernatural
sentences: The robot's face bore an uncanny resemblance to a real human being, and visitors felt a strange unease as its eyes followed them.
She had an uncanny ability to predict what others were thinking, which left her friends wondering whether she possessed some kind of supernatural gift.

quirky.definition: charmingly odd or unconventional in character or behavior
sentences: The village is known for its quirky shopkeeper, who greets customers in rhyme and keeps a tame parrot perched on the cash register.
Critics praised the film's quirky humor and eccentric characters, though some viewers found its odd storytelling too unconventional to follow comfortably.

offbeat.definition: unconventional and unusual; different from what is typical
sentences: The director is famous for her offbeat comedies, which avoid the predictable plots of mainstream Hollywood and often feature strange, unlikely heroes.
Tired of crowded tourist attractions, the couple chose an offbeat vacation, spending a week at a remote farm learning traditional cheese making.
offbeat.mnemonic: Off-beat : à côté du rythme, décalé.

whimsical.definition: playfully fanciful or capricious; driven by sudden odd impulses
sentences: The illustrator's whimsical drawings of dancing teapots and flying fish delighted children and adults alike, who enjoyed their playful and fanciful humor.
The king's whimsical decisions, changing laws on a sudden impulse, left his ministers unable to plan or predict what he would demand next.

idiosyncrasy.definition: a peculiar habit or characteristic belonging to one particular person
sentences: One of the professor's many idiosyncrasies was that he insisted on grading every exam while standing on one leg beside the window.
Each writer has stylistic idiosyncrasies, such as unusual punctuation or favorite words, that allow attentive readers to identify the author without seeing a name.
idiosyncrasy.mnemonic: Idio- = propre, particulier (idiome) : une manie bien à soi.

fanciful.definition: imaginative and unrealistic; based on fancy rather than fact
sentences: The explorer's fanciful tales of cities made of gold impressed the crowds but convinced few serious scholars, who demanded actual evidence.
Her plan to build a house on a floating cloud was too fanciful to be taken seriously by the practical engineers on the committee.

quixotic.definition: extremely idealistic and impractical, pursuing noble but unrealistic goals
sentences: His quixotic campaign to end all poverty in a single year touched many hearts but was far too impractical to succeed.
Many dismissed the activist's quixotic attempt to stop the huge corporation single-handedly, though others admired her noble determination despite the hopeless odds.
quixotic.mnemonic: Don Quichotte se bat contre des moulins à vent.

protean.definition: readily taking on different forms or changing shape and character
sentences: The actor's protean talent allowed him to play a villain, a clown, and a saint within a single year, each role completely different.
Language is a protean thing, constantly shifting its shape as new slang, technologies, and cultural influences transform the way people speak and write.
protean.mnemonic: Protée, dieu grec marin qui changeait de forme à volonté.

sentences: The boutique sells modish clothing for young shoppers eager to wear whatever is currently popular on social media and fashion runways.
Critics accused the architect of designing a modish building that would look dated within a decade, once the current trend had passed.
modish.mnemonic: Proche de « mode » : ce qui suit la mode.

trifling.definition: of very little importance or value; trivial
sentences: The two companies had been arguing for months over a trifling sum that was less than the cost of the lawyers' fees.
Compared with the enormous losses of the previous quarter, the trifling profits from the new product line barely deserved a mention in the annual report.

extraneous.definition: irrelevant or unrelated to the subject at hand; not essential
sentences: The editor removed several extraneous details from the essay, because they distracted readers from the author's central argument about economic reform.
To get accurate results, scientists must eliminate extraneous variables, such as room temperature or noise, that might interfere with the experiment.

slight.definition: an insulting act of disrespect or deliberate neglect
sentences: Not being invited to the ceremony felt like a deliberate slight to the retired director, who had founded the organization decades earlier.
The ambassador regarded the delayed reply as a diplomatic slight, and he warned that such disrespectful treatment could damage relations between the two nations.
slight.mnemonic: Slight : léger… et un affront léger mais blessant (a slight).

shrewd.definition: clever and sharp in judgment, especially in practical or business matters
shrewd.definitionFr: fin, qui flaire le bon coup
sentences: The shrewd investor sold her shares just before the market collapsed, having sensed trouble that more naive traders failed to notice.
A shrewd negotiator, he never revealed his true budget, and he waited patiently until the seller lowered the price on his own.
shrewd.mnemonic: Shrewd : fin et vif comme une musaraigne (shrew).

canny.definition: careful and clever, especially in business or practical dealings
sentences: The canny shopkeeper stocked umbrellas near the entrance whenever the forecast predicted rain, earning extra profit with almost no effort.
Although she appeared easygoing, the canny politician had carefully calculated every move, and she outmaneuvered her rivals without ever seeming to compete.
canny.mnemonic: Canny : celui qui sait y faire, malin.

acumen.definition: keen insight and quick judgment, especially in practical matters
sentences: Her business acumen turned a small family bakery into a national chain within ten years, as she consistently anticipated changes in customer taste.
The general's political acumen was as impressive as his military skill, for he always sensed which alliances would prove profitable and which dangerous.

keen.definition: sharp, quick, and sensitive in mind or senses
sentences: The detective's keen eye for detail allowed him to notice a tiny stain that every other investigator had completely overlooked.
Owls have an extraordinarily keen sense of hearing, which enables them to locate mice scurrying beneath the snow in total darkness.

sound.definition: based on good reasoning or evidence; valid and reliable
sentences: The lawyer built a sound argument supported by clear evidence, and the judges could find no logical flaw in her reasoning.
Financial advisers recommend sound investments that grow steadily over time rather than risky schemes that promise enormous profits but often collapse.
sound.mnemonic: Sound : solide (a sound argument, sound sleep).

polymath.definition: a person with wide knowledge and expertise in many different fields
sentences: Leonardo da Vinci was a true polymath, equally celebrated as a painter, an engineer, an anatomist, and an inventor of flying machines.
The university seeks a polymath who can lecture on physics, philosophy, and music, since the department values broad knowledge over narrow specialization.
polymath.mnemonic: Poly (nombreux) + math (apprendre) : qui sait beaucoup de choses.

shortsighted.definition: lacking foresight; ignoring the long-term consequences of one's actions
sentences: Cutting the research budget to save money this year was a shortsighted decision that would cost the company far more in the future.
Critics called the mayor's plan shortsighted because it solved the immediate traffic problem while ignoring the pollution it would cause for generations.
shortsighted.mnemonic: Short-sighted : myope, ne voit pas loin dans l'avenir.

oblivious.definition: unaware of or not paying attention to what is happening around one
sentences: Absorbed in her novel, the commuter was completely oblivious to the commotion around her, and she missed her stop by several stations.
The young prince, oblivious to the growing anger of his subjects, continued to hold lavish banquets while the harvest failed and prices soared.
oblivious.mnemonic: Oblivious ≠ obvious ; lié à « oubli » (oblivion) : qui oublie son entourage.

sentences: After winning the first round, the smug champion strutted around the room, convinced that none of his opponents could possibly defeat him.
A smug smile spread across her face when the rival's prediction proved wrong, and her colleagues found her self-satisfaction rather hard to bear.
smug.mnemonic: Smug : un sourire suffisant qui agace.

sanctimonious.definition: making a hypocritical show of moral superiority; self-righteous
sentences: The sanctimonious neighbor lectured everyone about honesty, yet he was secretly cheating on his taxes, which made his preaching hard to tolerate.
Readers grew tired of the columnist's sanctimonious tone, as she constantly implied that her own moral standards were far above those of ordinary people.
sanctimonious.mnemonic: Sanctimonious ≈ « saint » : il fait le saint, donneur de leçons.

haughty.definition: arrogantly proud and scornful toward others
sentences: The haughty duchess looked down on the servants, rarely speaking to them and treating them with cold, scornful contempt whenever she passed.
Her haughty manner, with its raised chin and dismissive tone, offended the other guests, who had expected a more gracious host.
haughty.mnemonic: Haughty ≈ « haut » : il vous regarde de haut.

wield.definition: to hold and use power, influence, or a tool effectively
sentences: The media tycoon wielded enormous influence over public opinion, and politicians of every party feared offending the newspapers he controlled.
The knight wielded his heavy sword with surprising ease, striking down his opponents one by one before the astonished crowd.

domineering.definition: arrogantly controlling and forcing one's will on others
sentences: The domineering manager insisted on approving every minor decision, and his employees grew resentful of his constant need to control everyone.
Her domineering father chose her university, her career, and even her friends, leaving her little freedom to make any choices of her own.

yoke.definition: something that oppresses or burdens people, especially a harsh rule or servitude
sentences: The colonies finally rose up to throw off the yoke of foreign rule, which had taxed them heavily and denied them any political voice.
