Farmers once fastened a wooden yoke across the necks of two oxen so that the animals could pull the heavy plow together.

oust.definition: to force someone out of a position of power or a place
sentences: After the scandal, the board voted to oust the chief executive, replacing him with a respected outsider who promised to restore public trust.
Rebel forces attempted to oust the dictator from power, but his loyal army defended the capital and quickly crushed the uprising.

fickle.definition: changing often and unpredictably in loyalties, interests, or affections
sentences: Fashion designers know that the public is fickle, for a style adored this season may be mocked and forgotten by the next.
The fickle voters abandoned the popular governor as quickly as they had embraced him, switching their loyalty to whichever candidate promised the most.
fickle.mnemonic: Fickle : girouette, il change tout le temps.

waver.definition: to hesitate or become unsteady in opinion, resolve, or position
sentences: The senator began to waver in his support for the bill after receiving thousands of angry letters from voters in his home district.
Her voice wavered slightly as she began the speech, but she soon regained her composure and delivered the rest with confident calm.
waver.mnemonic: Waver ≈ « wave » : ça ondule, il hésite.

quandary.definition: a state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
sentences: The young doctor faced a quandary: reporting her mentor's mistake would protect patients but might destroy the career of the man she admired.
Unable to choose between two excellent job offers, the graduate found herself in a quandary that kept her awake for several nights.

supersede.definition: to replace or take the place of something regarded as outdated
sentences: The new regulations will supersede the old ones, so companies must update their procedures before the law takes effect next January.
Digital cameras gradually superseded film cameras, which are now used mostly by hobbyists and artists who prefer the look of traditional photography.
supersede.mnemonic: Super + sedere (s'asseoir) : s'asseoir à la place de l'ancien.

overshadow.definition: to make something seem less important by comparison; to outshine
sentences: The younger brother's modest achievements were often overshadowed by the spectacular success of his famous sister, the Olympic champion.
Concerns about the cost of the project threatened to overshadow its many benefits, and the public debate ignored the genuine advantages of the plan.

outstrip.definition: to surpass or go beyond in speed, amount, or achievement
sentences: Demand for the new phone soon outstripped supply, leaving customers waiting weeks for deliveries from a factory that could not keep up.
The talented runner easily outstripped her rivals in the final lap, crossing the finish line several seconds before the second-place competitor.

outpace.definition: to move or progress faster than someone or something else
sentences: Technological innovation continues to outpace regulation, leaving lawmakers struggling to write rules for products that did not exist a few years ago.
The cheetah can easily outpace any other land animal over short distances, reaching extraordinary speeds within just a few seconds of starting.
outpace.mnemonic: Out-pace : aller plus vite en rythme.

shun.definition: to deliberately avoid or keep away from someone or something
sentences: After the betrayal, his former friends began to shun him, crossing the street whenever they saw him and refusing to answer his calls.
The reclusive author has shunned publicity for decades, refusing all interviews and declining every invitation to appear at literary festivals or award ceremonies.
shun.mnemonic: Shun ≈ « chut / shoo » : on fuit, on évite.

eschew.definition: to deliberately avoid or abstain from, often on principle
sentences: The monks eschew all worldly luxuries, living in bare cells and eating only simple food in accordance with their vows of poverty.
A careful scientist should eschew sensational claims and rely instead on cautious, well-tested conclusions supported by repeated and independent experiments.

scorn.definition: to reject or dismiss with open disdain
sentences: The veteran critic scorned the new film as shallow entertainment, refusing even to review it because she considered it unworthy of serious attention.
Proud of their independence, the villagers scorned every offer of foreign aid, insisting that accepting charity would dishonor their community and its long traditions.

skirt.definition: to avoid dealing directly with a difficult issue or question
sentences: Asked about the budget deficit, the senator skirted the question by praising her opponent's record on education and then abruptly changing the subject.
Rather than confront his sister about the unpaid loan, Marcus skirted the issue throughout dinner, chatting about the weather and their parents' vacation plans.
skirt.mnemonic: Skirt : la jupe qui contourne ; contourner (un sujet).

circumvent.definition: to find a clever way around a rule or obstacle
sentences: Several large corporations circumvented the new environmental regulations by relocating their factories to countries where such strict laws did not yet exist.
Unable to enter through the locked front gate, the hikers circumvented the barrier by following a narrow trail that wound around the edge of the property.

amity.definition: friendly relations, especially between nations or groups
sentences: After decades of hostility, the two neighboring countries signed a treaty of amity, pledging to settle future disputes through dialogue rather than armed conflict.
The committee members, who had once quarreled bitterly, worked together in such amity that the final report was approved without a single dissenting voice.
amity.mnemonic: Amity ressemble à « amitié » : relations amicales.

comity.definition: courteous and considerate behavior among peers or nations
sentences: Despite their sharp ideological differences, the judges maintained a spirit of comity, listening respectfully to each other's arguments and never resorting to personal insults.
International law relies partly on comity, the habit of nations recognizing one another's legal decisions out of mutual courtesy rather than strict obligation.

congenial.definition: pleasant and agreeable because suited to one's tastes or temperament
sentences: Elena found the small, quiet seminar far more congenial than the huge lecture hall, since she preferred thoughtful discussion to passive note-taking.
The innkeeper's warm manner and the crackling fireplace created such a congenial atmosphere that the weary travelers happily lingered long after their meal ended.
congenial.mnemonic: Con-genial : du même génie, de même nature, sympathique.

estrange.definition: to cause someone to become unfriendly or distant from another
sentences: The bitter dispute over their father's inheritance estranged the two brothers, who did not speak to each other for nearly twenty years afterward.
Critics warned that the president's harsh rhetoric would estrange longtime allies, leaving the country increasingly isolated and without friends in the international community.
estrange.mnemonic: Estrange ≈ « étranger » : rendre quelqu'un étranger à soi.

interloper.definition: an unwelcome person who intrudes into a place or group
sentences: The longtime members of the club regarded the newcomer as an interloper and pointedly ignored him whenever he tried to join their conversation.
Biologists worry that the aggressive species, an interloper in the fragile ecosystem, will drive out the native birds that have lived there for centuries.

dalliance.definition: a brief, casual romantic involvement; also, idle or frivolous toying
sentences: Her brief dalliance with a charming musician ended as quickly as it had begun, leaving neither of them with any lasting regrets or serious commitments.
The young painter's dalliance with sculpture lasted only one summer before he returned to canvas, the medium to which he devoted the rest of his career.

abet.definition: to encourage or assist someone in wrongdoing
sentences: The accountant was charged with abetting the fraud, since his falsified records had helped his employer hide the stolen funds from investigators for years.
By supplying the thieves with the building's security codes, the night guard abetted the burglary and later faced the same penalty as the burglars themselves.
abet.mnemonic: Abet : pousser à la faute (à l'origine, exciter un chien).

adulterate.definition: to make impure by adding inferior or unwanted substances
sentences: Dishonest merchants sometimes adulterate expensive spices with cheap powders, so that customers unknowingly pay premium prices for a diluted and inferior product.
Health inspectors discovered that the dairy had adulterated its milk with water and chemicals, and the company was promptly fined and ordered to close.
adulterate.mnemonic: Adultérer (le produit) en français = le frelater, pas tromper un conjoint.

akin.definition: similar in nature or character; related
sentences: Her fascination with the stars was akin to a religious devotion, shaping every decision she made about her education, friendships, and eventual career.
The two languages are so closely akin that speakers of one can usually follow a simple conversation in the other without any formal study.

apt.definition: suitable for the occasion; also, likely or inclined to do something
sentences: The poet's comparison of memory to a river was so apt that the audience nodded in recognition, instantly grasping the fleeting nature of the past.
Students who skip the preparatory exercises are apt to struggle with the final exam, since the more difficult problems build directly upon the earlier lessons.

artless.definition: natural and innocent, without deceit; also, lacking skill
sentences: The child's artless honesty charmed the guests, who were accustomed to polished politicians and who rarely heard anyone speak without calculation or hidden motives.
Though the amateur sketch was artless and clumsy in its proportions, the gallery displayed it because of the raw emotion that seemed to radiate from the page.
artless.mnemonic: Art-less : sans art, donc sans artifice (ou sans talent).

behemoth.definition: an enormous, powerful creature, organization, or thing
sentences: The retail behemoth drove dozens of small neighborhood shops out of business within a few years, simply because it could offer lower prices than anyone else.
Standing beside the enormous ship, a behemoth of steel and rivets, the dockworkers looked like tiny figures dwarfed by its towering hull.

bemoan.definition: to express sorrow or discontent about something
sentences: Older residents often bemoan the loss of the town's traditional markets, complaining that the new shopping malls have destroyed the friendly spirit of the community.
The coach bemoaned his team's careless errors after the defeat, lamenting that months of careful training had been wasted in a single disappointing afternoon.
The strange symbols carved into the stone bemused the archaeologists, who could find no similar markings in any known ancient language or cultural record.
Her sudden decision to quit a lucrative job and raise goats bemused her friends, none of whom could understand what had prompted such a dramatic change.
bemuse.mnemonic: Be-muse : l'esprit dans la lune (muse = rêver).

bequeath.definition: to leave property or a legacy to someone in a will
sentences: The elderly professor bequeathed his entire collection of rare manuscripts to the university library, hoping that future scholars would benefit from his lifetime of careful collecting.
Ancient Greece bequeathed to later civilizations a rich legacy of philosophy and democratic ideas that continue to shape political thought across the modern world.
bequeath.mnemonic: Bequeath : « je lègue » dans un testament.

betray.definition: to reveal unintentionally; also, to be disloyal to
sentences: Although the diplomat smiled calmly, the slight trembling of his hands betrayed his deep anxiety about the outcome of the delicate negotiations.
His trembling voice betrayed the nervousness that he was desperately trying to conceal from the interviewers, who noticed it despite his confident words.
betray.mnemonic: Betray ≈ « trahir » : trahir, ou laisser paraître malgré soi.

sentences: The general's blunder of sending his troops across the flooded valley cost the army hundreds of lives and ultimately decided the outcome of the war.
Forgetting to attach the contract was an embarrassing blunder, and the young lawyer spent the rest of the afternoon apologizing to the furious client.
The boisterous crowd cheered, sang, and stamped their feet throughout the match, making it nearly impossible for the commentators to be heard.
After a quiet morning, the nursery filled with boisterous toddlers who shouted, laughed, and chased one another around the room until the teacher called for calm.
boisterous.mnemonic: Boisterous : une bande turbulente qui fait du boucan.

sentences: The discovery of fresh water beneath the desert village was a tremendous boon, allowing farmers to grow crops in soil that had long been barren.
For the struggling author, the unexpected scholarship proved a boon, freeing her from financial worry so that she could finally finish her long-delayed novel.

broach.definition: to bring up a subject for discussion, often a delicate one
sentences: Nervous about the reaction, Daniel waited until after dinner to broach the subject of moving abroad with his aging and rather conservative parents.
The chairman carefully broached the topic of layoffs at the end of the meeting, aware that the announcement would alarm employees who feared for their jobs.
broach.mnemonic: Broach ≈ « broche » : on perce un tonneau, on aborde un sujet.

buffer.definition: something that cushions against shock or acts as a protective barrier
sentences: The small neutral nation served as a buffer between the two rival empires, absorbing tensions that might otherwise have erupted into open warfare along their shared border.
Her savings acted as a buffer against financial disaster, so the sudden loss of her job did not immediately threaten her ability to pay rent.
buffer.mnemonic: Buffer : le tampon qui amortit le choc.

bumbling.definition: clumsy and inept in a foolish way
sentences: The bumbling detective in the comedy tripped over furniture, lost his notes, and accidentally arrested his own partner before finally stumbling upon the real culprit.
Critics blamed the bumbling officials for the chaotic rollout of the program, citing lost paperwork, missed deadlines, and a series of embarrassing public mistakes.

cipher.definition: a secret code or system of writing
sentences: During the war, the spy transmitted his reports in a complicated cipher that enemy analysts struggled for months to decode without success.
Historians finally cracked the medieval cipher in the monk's diary, revealing that the seemingly meaningless symbols concealed a detailed account of a forbidden alchemical experiment.

coin.definition: to invent a new word or phrase
sentences: The economist coined the term "stagflation" to describe the unusual combination of stagnant growth and rising prices that baffled policymakers during the decade.
Shakespeare is credited with coining hundreds of words that are still in daily use, from "lonely" to "bedroom," enriching the English language enormously.
coin.mnemonic: Coin : on « frappe » un mot nouveau comme une monnaie.

colloquial.definition: informal and conversational, typical of everyday speech rather than formal writing
sentences: The novelist's colloquial prose, full of slang and contractions, made her characters sound like real neighbors rather than figures in a formal literary work.
Although expressions like "gonna" and "kinda" are acceptable in colloquial conversation, the professor warned that they had no place in a scholarly dissertation.
colloquial.mnemonic: Colloquial ≈ « colloque » : la langue de la conversation.

commensurate.definition: corresponding in size, degree, or amount; proportionate
sentences: The firm promised to offer a salary commensurate with each candidate's experience, so that senior engineers would earn considerably more than recent graduates.
Critics argued that the punishment was not commensurate with the offense, since a minor clerical error had resulted in the employee's immediate dismissal.

compendium.definition: a concise but comprehensive collection of information on a subject
sentences: The botanist's latest book is a compendium of garden lore, gathering in a single volume everything known about the cultivation of rare alpine flowers.
Students relied on the thick compendium of grammar rules, which summarized centuries of linguistic scholarship in a form that was easy to consult before examinations.

compromise.definition: to weaken or endanger something, such as one's principles or reputation
sentences: The scandal threatened to compromise the senator's reputation, and several of his allies quietly distanced themselves to avoid being damaged by association.
Engineers refused to compromise safety standards in order to meet the deadline, insisting that a flawed bridge would endanger lives far more than a delayed opening.

conducive.definition: making a certain result or outcome likely or possible; favorable
sentences: A quiet room with good lighting is conducive to concentrated study, whereas a noisy cafe tends to scatter the attention of even the most diligent students.
The country's stable laws and educated workforce were conducive to economic growth, attracting foreign investors who had previously hesitated to enter the market.
conducive.mnemonic: Con-ducive ≈ « conduire » : mène à un résultat, propice.

consummate.definition: perfect or supremely skilled; complete in every respect
sentences: The pianist's consummate technique and emotional depth left the audience breathless, and critics hailed the recital as the finest performance of the entire season.
As a consummate diplomat, she calmed the angry delegates with such skill that even her harshest opponents admitted they could not fault her tact.

contempt.definition: a feeling that someone or something is worthless and deserves scorn
sentences: The dictator's open contempt for ordinary citizens, whom he described as ignorant sheep, gradually turned even his early supporters against his government.
She regarded the plagiarist with contempt, unable to forgive someone who had stolen years of her colleague's research and then claimed the credit.

conundrum.definition: a confusing or difficult problem that is hard to solve
sentences: The council faced a genuine conundrum: building the new highway would ease traffic, but it would also destroy the neighborhood that residents had fought to preserve.
How the ancient builders moved such enormous stones across the desert remains a conundrum that has puzzled engineers and historians for several generations.
conundrum.mnemonic: Conundrum : mot d'origine incertaine ; retenir : casse-tête.

cunning.definition: clever at getting what one wants, often through deceit
sentences: The cunning merchant pretended to lose interest in the carpet, knowing that the eager buyer would soon offer a much higher price to secure it.
Fables often portray the fox as a cunning creature that uses trickery rather than strength to outwit larger and more powerful animals in the forest.
cunning.mnemonic: Cunning ≈ can (savoir) : il sait comment s'y prendre, rusé.

daunting.definition: seeming difficult enough to cause fear or loss of confidence
sentences: For the novice climber, the sheer ice wall looked like a daunting obstacle, and several members of the group quietly wondered whether they should turn back.
Rebuilding the war-torn city seemed a daunting task, requiring billions of dollars, thousands of skilled workers, and many years of patient political cooperation.

debunk.definition: to expose the falseness of a claim, belief, or myth
sentences: The physicist devoted his career to debunking pseudoscientific claims, patiently demonstrating with careful experiments that the supposed miracle device could not possibly work.
A team of journalists debunked the viral story by tracing it to a satirical website, proving that the alleged scandal had never actually taken place.

deft.definition: skillful and quick in movement or handling
sentences: With a few deft strokes of her brush, the artist transformed the blank canvas into a lively portrait that captured the subject's mischievous smile.
The mayor's deft handling of the budget crisis impressed even her critics, who admitted that she had resolved the conflict quickly and without offending anyone.
deft.mnemonic: Deft ≈ « doigté » : habile de ses mains.

demise.definition: the end or downfall of something; also, death
sentences: Analysts attributed the company's demise to its refusal to adapt to digital technology, since competitors had steadily taken away its customers over the past decade.
The sudden demise of the old king plunged the kingdom into a bitter struggle for succession among his ambitious sons and their scheming supporters.
demise.mnemonic: De-mise : mise à bas, la fin ; ou le décès.

despicable.definition: deserving hatred and contempt because of vileness
sentences: Stealing donations meant for earthquake survivors was a despicable act, and the public reacted with outrage when the treasurer's crime was finally exposed.
The villain of the novel is truly despicable, betraying his closest friends and mocking the poor while he enjoys a life of luxury.

dilatory.definition: tending to delay or waste time; slow to act
sentences: The dilatory contractor missed every deadline, making endless excuses while the homeowners waited months for repairs that should have taken only a few weeks.
Lawyers for the defense used dilatory tactics, filing unnecessary motions again and again in the hope that the trial would be postponed indefinitely.
dilatory.mnemonic: Dilatory ≈ « différer » : il traîne, il retarde.

din.definition: a loud, confusing, and unpleasant noise that continues
sentences: The din of the factory machinery was so overwhelming that workers had to shout directly into one another's ears to be understood.
Over the din of honking horns and shouting vendors, the tourist could barely hear her guide describing the history of the crowded marketplace.

discrepancy.definition: a lack of agreement between facts or figures that should match
sentences: The auditor noticed a troubling discrepancy between the reported revenue and the bank statements, which suggested that someone had been altering the company's records.
Investigators were puzzled by the discrepancy in the two witnesses' accounts, since one swore the car was blue while the other insisted it was red.

discriminating.definition: having or showing refined taste and good judgment
sentences: A discriminating collector, she examined every painting with great care and purchased only those works that truly demonstrated originality and technical mastery.
The restaurant caters to a discriminating clientele that can easily distinguish an excellent vintage from a merely ordinary bottle of wine.
discriminating.mnemonic: Faux ami : ici « avisé, de goût sûr », pas « discriminant » (injuste).

dispassionate.definition: not influenced by strong emotion; impartial and objective
sentences: A good judge must remain dispassionate, weighing the evidence calmly rather than allowing personal sympathy or anger to influence the verdict.
The scientist gave a dispassionate account of the disaster, listing the facts and figures without any of the emotion that the tragedy might have provoked.

dispel.definition: to drive away or make disappear, especially doubts or fears
sentences: The company's clear financial report dispelled rumors of bankruptcy, and investors who had been planning to sell their shares quickly regained their confidence.
A strong wind rose in the afternoon and dispelled the thick morning fog, revealing the mountain peaks that had been hidden for days.

elate.definition: to fill with great joy and pride
sentences: News of the unexpected victory elated the whole town, and thousands of residents poured into the streets to sing, dance, and embrace complete strangers.
The young scientist was elated by the results of her experiment, which finally confirmed the theory she had defended for nearly ten difficult years.

epitome.definition: a perfect or typical example of a quality or type
sentences: With her generosity, patience, and quiet humility, the nurse was the epitome of compassion, and patients remembered her kindness long after they had recovered.
The sleek glass tower, with its minimalist design, is often considered the epitome of modern architecture, and students travel across the globe to study it.
epitome.mnemonic: Épitomé se prononce « é-pi-to-mi » (4 syllabes), pas « épitome ».

exonerate.definition: to officially clear someone of blame or wrongdoing
sentences: New DNA evidence exonerated the prisoner after fifteen years behind bars, proving that he could not possibly have committed the crime for which he was convicted.
The official investigation exonerated the pilot of any responsibility for the crash, concluding instead that a mechanical failure in the engine had caused the accident.

extemporaneous.definition: spoken or done without preparation; improvised
sentences: Although the senator seemed to deliver an extemporaneous speech, aides later revealed that he had rehearsed every pause and gesture for several days beforehand.
When the microphone failed, the lecturer gave an extemporaneous talk without notes, drawing on decades of experience to hold the audience's attention until the end.
extemporaneous.mnemonic: Ex tempore : hors du temps de préparation, improvisé.

fester.definition: to grow worse through neglect; also, to rot or become infected
sentences: Resentment over the unfair promotion festered for months, poisoning the atmosphere in the office until two of the best employees finally resigned.
The untreated wound began to fester, and by the second day the soldier's arm was swollen, painful, and dangerously infected.
fester.mnemonic: Fester : une plaie qui pourrit, une situation qui s'envenime.

fodder.definition: raw material for creative work or discussion; also, food for livestock
sentences: The senator's embarrassing remark became fodder for late-night comedians, who joked about it for weeks and kept the story alive long after it should have faded.
During the harsh winter, the farmers stored enough fodder in the barn to feed their cattle until the spring grass finally began to grow.
fodder.mnemonic: Fodder ≈ « fourrage » : même mot, même racine.

sentences: The two senators, once close friends, became bitter foes after the election, refusing to share a stage or even to acknowledge each other in public.
Facing a formidable foe on the battlefield, the commander ordered his weary troops to retreat to the hills and wait for reinforcements to arrive.

garner.definition: to gather, collect, or earn, often with effort
sentences: The independent film garnered several prestigious awards at the festival, earning its young director a level of attention that she had never expected.
Through months of tireless campaigning, the candidate garnered enough support among rural voters to overcome her opponent's early lead in the polls.
garner.mnemonic: Garner ≈ « grenier » : on engrange, on récolte.

germane.definition: relevant and closely connected to the subject under discussion
sentences: The moderator interrupted the speaker, reminding him that his long story about childhood vacations was not germane to the question of municipal zoning laws.
Only evidence that is germane to the case may be presented to the jury, so the judge excluded testimony about the defendant's unrelated hobbies.
germane.mnemonic: Germane ≈ « cousin germain » : étroitement lié au sujet.

grapple.definition: to struggle to deal with or overcome a difficult problem
sentences: Governments around the world are still grappling with the ethical questions raised by artificial intelligence, and no clear consensus has yet emerged among experts.
For years the young poet grappled with self-doubt, wondering whether her work had any real value before she finally published her first collection.
grapple.mnemonic: Grapple ≈ « grappin » : on s'accroche, on se colleter.

sentences: After the brilliant presentation, even the skeptical director offered a grudging nod of approval, though he clearly disliked admitting that his rival had been right.
The landlord gave his grudging consent to the renovation, muttering complaints about the cost and the noise throughout the entire conversation.

hallmark.definition: a distinctive feature or characteristic that identifies something
sentences: Careful attention to detail is the hallmark of a great surgeon, whose steady hands and patient discipline can mean the difference between life and death.
Dense, flowing sentences are a hallmark of the author's style, so that readers can often recognize a page of her prose within seconds.
hallmark.mnemonic: Hallmark : le poinçon d'orfèvre, le signe distinctif.

sentences: The two scientists met by sheer happenstance, when a delayed train forced them to share a table at a station cafe and discover their common research.
Rather than planning, the explorer attributed his famous discovery to happenstance, saying that a wrong turn in the fog had led him to the hidden valley.

haven.definition: a place of safety or refuge
sentences: The quiet mountain monastery served as a haven for refugees fleeing the war, providing food, shelter, and protection to hundreds of frightened families.
For the overworked executive, the small cabin by the lake was a peaceful haven, a place where no telephone could reach her and no deadline mattered.

heartening.definition: giving courage, hope, or cheer; encouraging
sentences: After months of discouraging reports, the sharp decline in unemployment was a heartening sign that the struggling economy might finally be starting to recover.
It was heartening to see so many volunteers arrive after the flood, and their generosity restored the survivors' hope that their town could be rebuilt.
heartening.mnemonic: Heart = cœur : ça redonne du cœur.

heed.definition: to pay careful attention to advice or a warning
sentences: Had the captain heeded the warnings about the approaching storm, he would have kept his ship in harbor and spared the crew a terrible ordeal.
Investors who heed the advice of cautious economists tend to avoid risky speculation, preferring slow and steady returns to the lure of sudden wealth.
heed.mnemonic: Heed : prête l'oreille, tiens compte du conseil.

hodgepodge.definition: a confused mixture of unrelated things
sentences: The apartment was a hodgepodge of mismatched furniture, faded posters, and boxes of books, with no evident plan connecting any one object to another.
Critics dismissed the museum's new exhibit as a hodgepodge of random artifacts that lacked any coherent theme to guide visitors through the collection.
hodgepodge.mnemonic: Hodgepodge ≈ « hochepot » : un ragoût de mélanges.

impervious.definition: not allowing penetration; unaffected by or unable to be influenced by something
sentences: The fabric was impervious to water, so the hikers stayed dry even through the long afternoon downpour on the mountain trail.
The senator remained impervious to criticism, ignoring every editorial and protest that urged her to reconsider her unpopular stance on the budget.
impervious.mnemonic: Im-pervious : pas de voie (via) à travers, imperméable.

indiscriminate.definition: done at random or without careful judgment or selection
sentences: The critic condemned the indiscriminate use of pesticides, which killed beneficial insects along with the harmful pests that farmers were actually trying to eliminate.
Her indiscriminate reading habits meant she devoured cheap romances, technical manuals, and philosophical treatises with equal enthusiasm, never pausing to judge their quality.

infatuate.definition: to inspire with an intense but short-lived passion or foolish love
sentences: The charismatic young actor managed to infatuate half the audience, though most of them forgot his name within a few weeks of the premiere.
Investors were so infatuated with the flashy start-up that they ignored its mounting debts, a passion that faded quickly once the losses became public.
infatuate.mnemonic: In-fatu : fatuus = fou en latin ; on devient fou d'amour.

ingrained.definition: firmly fixed or deeply rooted and therefore difficult to change
sentences: Her ingrained habit of rising at dawn persisted even after she retired, since decades of early shifts had made it almost impossible to break.
Sociologists argue that prejudice is so deeply ingrained in some communities that it is passed from generation to generation without anyone questioning it.
ingrained.mnemonic: In-grained : dans le grain, profondément ancré.

innocuous.definition: not harmful or offensive; unlikely to provoke a reaction
sentences: Although the remark seemed innocuous to the speaker, several guests were deeply offended by its hidden implications about their families.
The doctor assured the patient that the small mole was innocuous and posed no threat, so no surgery or further treatment was necessary.

insular.definition: narrow-minded and uninterested in ideas or people outside one's own group; isolated
sentences: The villagers were so insular that they distrusted every outsider and refused to adopt any custom that had not originated in their own valley.
Critics described the committee as insular, since its members rarely consulted experts from other fields and dismissed any viewpoint that differed from their own.
insular.mnemonic: Insula = île en latin : vivre comme sur une île, coupé du monde.

interplay.definition: the way two or more things affect each other; reciprocal action
sentences: The novel explores the interplay between ambition and guilt, showing how each feeling intensifies the other as the protagonist climbs the corporate ladder.
Biologists study the interplay of genes and environment, since neither factor alone can fully explain why identical twins sometimes develop different personalities.
interplay.mnemonic: Inter-play : le jeu entre deux choses.

intricate.definition: having many small, interconnected parts or details; very complicated
sentences: The watchmaker spent months assembling the intricate mechanism, whose hundreds of tiny gears had to fit together with flawless precision.
Historians struggle to untangle the intricate web of alliances that drew so many nations into the war within only a few weeks.

ironclad.definition: so firmly established that it cannot be broken, challenged, or changed
sentences: The lawyers drafted an ironclad contract with no loopholes, so the company could not escape its obligations even when the market collapsed.
Prosecutors presented an ironclad alibi for the defendant, supported by video footage and several witnesses, and the jury acquitted him within an hour.
ironclad.mnemonic: Iron + clad : revêtu de fer, donc impossible à briser.

jingoistic.definition: aggressively and excessively patriotic, favoring a belligerent foreign policy
sentences: The tabloid's jingoistic headlines demanded war against the neighboring country and portrayed anyone urging negotiation as a traitor to the nation.
Moderate voters grew uneasy with the candidate's jingoistic speeches, which glorified military power and mocked foreigners while offering no practical plan for the economy.
jingoistic.mnemonic: Jingo (« by jingo ! ») : chauvin et belliqueux.

layman.definition: a person without professional or specialized knowledge in a particular field
sentences: The physicist explained black holes in terms a layman could follow, avoiding equations and technical jargon so the whole audience understood.
Insurance contracts are often written in language so dense that the average layman cannot tell what is actually covered without consulting a lawyer.

levity.definition: lack of seriousness; humor or frivolity, especially when out of place
sentences: The judge rebuked the lawyer for his levity, insisting that jokes were inappropriate in a courtroom where a man's freedom was at stake.
A moment of levity relieved the tension at the tense negotiations when the mediator cracked a joke, and even the rival delegates laughed.
levity.mnemonic: Levity = lever : léger comme ce qui s'envole ; le contraire de gravity.

loathe.definition: to feel intense dislike or disgust for
sentences: Although she loved the theater, she loathed the long intermissions, which she found tedious and an irritating waste of an otherwise pleasant evening.
Many commuters loathe the morning traffic so intensely that they would gladly accept lower salaries in exchange for jobs within walking distance of home.
loathe.mnemonic: Loathe : abhorrer ; à ne pas confondre avec loath (réticent).

lukewarm.definition: only slightly warm; showing little enthusiasm or interest
sentences: The audience gave the film a lukewarm reception, offering polite applause but none of the excited praise the director had hoped for.
He left the tea sitting so long that it turned lukewarm, neither hot enough to comfort him nor cold enough to refresh him.
lukewarm.mnemonic: Luke + warm : tiède (luke = tiède en vieil anglais).

lurid.definition: presented in a shocking, sensational way, often with disturbing detail
sentences: The tabloid printed lurid details of the scandal, hoping that the shocking descriptions would attract more readers than a sober report ever could.
The paperback's lurid cover, with its garish colors and violent imagery, promised a sensational story that the plain, quiet plot never actually delivered.

lush.definition: growing thickly and abundantly; rich and luxurious
sentences: After weeks of heavy rain, the valley turned lush and green, with thick vegetation covering every hillside and riverbank.
The restaurant's lush decor, with velvet curtains, gilded mirrors, and deep carpets, signaled to diners that the evening would be an expensive indulgence.

mellifluous.definition: sweet and smooth in sound, pleasant to hear
sentences: The radio host's mellifluous voice soothed listeners so effectively that many admitted they would listen to him read the phone book.
The soprano's mellifluous tones filled the cathedral, and the hushed audience sat spellbound by a sound as smooth and sweet as honey.
mellifluous.mnemonic: Melli- = miel (mel en latin) : une voix qui coule comme du miel.

mores.definition: the customs and accepted behaviors of a particular society or group
sentences: Anthropologists must learn the social mores of a community before studying it, lest they unknowingly violate its traditions and offend the people they hope to understand.
The novel scandalized Victorian readers because it openly challenged the sexual mores of its day, which demanded strict silence on such subjects.

mount.definition: to organize and launch (an effort); to increase gradually in amount or intensity
sentences: The opposition party plans to mount a vigorous campaign against the new tax, beginning with rallies in every major city this spring.
As the deadline approached, the pressure on the engineers continued to mount, and tempers frayed with every day that passed without a working prototype.
mount.mnemonic: Mount : monter ; on lance une offensive, la tension monte.

multifarious.definition: having many varied parts, kinds, or forms
sentences: The museum's multifarious collection includes ancient pottery, modern sculpture, rare manuscripts, and even a stuffed dinosaur, so every visitor finds something unexpected.
The mayor faced multifarious problems, from crumbling bridges and unpaid bills to rising crime, and no single policy could address all of them.

nexus.definition: a connection or link between things; a central point where things meet
sentences: Researchers have identified a nexus between poor sleep and weakened immunity, showing that the two problems are closely linked and reinforce one another.
The city, sitting where three major rivers meet, became the nexus of regional trade, drawing merchants from every direction to its crowded markets.
nexus.mnemonic: Nexus : un nœud, un lien (≈ « connexion »).

noxious.definition: harmful or poisonous to health; unpleasant and damaging
sentences: Workers at the chemical plant were required to wear masks because the noxious fumes could damage their lungs after only a few minutes of exposure.
The editorialist argued that the noxious rhetoric of hatred poisoned public debate, harming the whole community even more than the most dangerous pollutants.
noxious.mnemonic: Noxious ressemble à « nocif » : même racine nocere, nuire.

sentences: The small startup had an outsize influence on the industry, shaping standards that much larger rivals felt obliged to follow.
He arrived at the party carrying an outsize bouquet so enormous that he could barely see over it as he squeezed through the door.

overlook.definition: to ignore or excuse (a fault); to fail to notice
sentences: The teacher agreed to overlook the student's late homework this once, because the boy had been ill and had always handed in his work on time before.
Careless investors often overlook hidden fees, which quietly reduce their returns by thousands of dollars over decades because they never read the fine print.
overlook.mnemonic: Over-look : regarder par-dessus : ne pas voir, ou fermer les yeux.

overrun.definition: to invade and spread over in great numbers; to infest
sentences: Within a week, enemy troops had overrun the border towns, forcing thousands of terrified residents to flee toward the capital with whatever they could carry.
After the family abandoned the garden, weeds quickly overran it, choking the flowers and covering the paths until the whole yard looked like a jungle.

overstate.definition: to describe something as greater or more important than it really is
sentences: It would be hard to overstate the importance of the discovery, which transformed medicine and saved millions of lives within a single generation.
The spokesman was accused of trying to overstate the company's profits, inflating the figures to reassure nervous shareholders before the quarterly meeting.

overwhelm.definition: to overpower or defeat completely; to affect so strongly that one cannot cope
sentences: The sheer volume of emails threatened to overwhelm the small staff, who could not possibly answer every message before the end of the week.
Grief can overwhelm even the strongest person, leaving her unable to eat, work, or think clearly for many days after the loss.

parochial.definition: limited in outlook to narrow local concerns; narrow-minded
sentences: The council's parochial attitude led it to reject the national highway plan, since members cared only about their own village and ignored wider benefits.
Traveling abroad helped cure the student of his parochial view of the world, showing him that his small hometown's customs were not universal.
parochial.mnemonic: Paroisse en français : l'esprit de clocher, qui ne voit pas plus loin.

partial-to.definition: having a particular liking or fondness for
sentences: My grandmother is partial to sweet pastries, and she never lets a visit to the bakery pass without buying at least two of them.
The director was openly partial to older actors, often casting them in leading roles even when younger performers auditioned with more polished technique.
partial-to.mnemonic: Partial ≠ partiel ici : on penche d'un côté, on a un faible.

ploy.definition: a clever maneuver or trick used to gain an advantage
sentences: The salesman's offer of a free gift was merely a ploy to get customers into the store, where they would then be pressured to buy.
Critics dismissed the senator's sudden concern for the poor as a political ploy designed to win votes before the election rather than a genuine conviction.
ploy.mnemonic: Ploy : une manœuvre pour s'en sortir.

plummet.definition: to fall or drop straight down rapidly
sentences: When news of the scandal broke, the company's share price began to plummet, losing half its value before the markets closed that afternoon.
The injured hawk seemed to plummet from the sky, dropping so swiftly that the watching children gasped before it finally spread its wings near the ground.
plummet.mnemonic: Plomb en français : tomber comme un plomb.

precipitous.definition: dangerously steep; sudden and rapid, especially of a decline
sentences: The climbers edged along a precipitous cliff, where one wrong step would have sent them tumbling hundreds of feet onto the jagged rocks below.
Economists were alarmed by the precipitous decline in consumer spending, which fell by almost a third within a single month and caught everyone by surprise.
precipitous.mnemonic: Precipitous ≈ « précipice » : à pic, très rapide.

prevailing.definition: most common or widespread at a particular time; currently in force
sentences: Contrary to the prevailing opinion of the time, which held that the earth was flat, the young astronomer insisted that the world was round.
Sailors rely on the prevailing winds, which blow from the west across the ocean for most of the year, to plan their long voyages.

pristine.definition: in its original, unspoiled condition; perfectly clean and untouched
sentences: The explorers were astonished to find a pristine lake, untouched by tourists or pollution, whose water was so clear they could see the bottom.
Although the vintage car was fifty years old, its pristine paint and spotless leather seats made it look as though it had just left the factory.

proclivity.definition: a natural tendency or inclination, especially toward something undesirable
sentences: His proclivity for gambling worried his friends, who had watched him lose his savings several times and yet return eagerly to the casino.
Psychologists have long debated whether a proclivity for violence is inherited or learned, since both family and environment seem to shape such behavior.
proclivity.mnemonic: Pro-clivity : une pente (clivus) vers : un penchant.

prone.definition: likely to suffer from or do something; having a tendency toward
sentences: Because the coastal region is prone to flooding, residents build their houses on stilts and keep emergency supplies ready throughout the stormy season.
She was prone to exaggeration, so her friends usually divided any story she told by half before deciding what had actually happened.
prone.mnemonic: Prone : couché face contre terre, donc enclin à.

proponent.definition: a person who argues in favor of a theory or policy
sentences: As a leading proponent of renewable energy, the senator introduced a bill to fund solar farms and urged colleagues to abandon fossil fuels.
The professor was a staunch proponent of free public education, defending the idea in lectures, newspaper columns, and even in conversations at dinner parties.
proponent.mnemonic: Proponent = qui « propose » et défend une idée ; l'opposé d'opponent.

puzzle.definition: to confuse or perplex by being hard to understand or explain
sentences: The sudden disappearance of the bees continues to puzzle scientists, who have tested dozens of theories without finding a convincing explanation.
His strange refusal to attend the ceremony puzzled his relatives, who knew how long he had worked for the award and could not understand his decision.
puzzle.mnemonic: Puzzle : un casse-tête qui rend perplexe.

remedial.definition: intended to correct a deficiency or help those who are struggling to learn
sentences: Students who failed the placement test were enrolled in a remedial math course designed to fill gaps in the basic skills they had missed.
The government introduced remedial measures to repair the damage caused by the earlier policy, hoping to correct its worst unintended consequences for rural families.
remedial.mnemonic: Remedial vient de remède : un cours qui soigne les lacunes.

reminisce.definition: to recall and talk about past experiences with pleasure
sentences: The old friends gathered on the porch to reminisce about their college days, laughing at pranks they had not mentioned in decades.
Retired soldiers often reminisce about the camaraderie of the army, remembering the friendships fondly while forgetting many of the hardships they endured.
reminisce.mnemonic: Reminisce ≈ « réminiscence » : on évoque ses souvenirs.

rendition.definition: a particular performance or interpretation of a song, play, or piece of music
sentences: The pianist's moving rendition of the sonata brought tears to the audience, many of whom said they had never heard the piece played so tenderly.
Critics praised the film as a faithful rendition of the classic novel, preserving its tone and characters while updating the setting for modern viewers.
rendition.mnemonic: Rendition ≈ « rendre » : rendre une chanson, une interprétation.

rescind.definition: to officially cancel or revoke a law, order, or decision
sentences: After widespread protests, the council voted to rescind the controversial parking ordinance, restoring the old rules that residents had preferred.
The university threatened to rescind the scholarship if the student's grades continued to fall, which would make it impossible for her to finish her degree.

revamp.definition: to renovate or improve by making major changes to structure or appearance
sentences: The restaurant plans to revamp its menu and dining room, replacing the tired old decor in a bid to attract a younger crowd.
The editor decided to revamp the struggling magazine completely, redesigning its layout and hiring new writers in hopes of reviving its declining readership.

rote.definition: done by mechanical repetition without understanding or thought
sentences: Critics of the school system argue that rote memorization of dates and formulas teaches children to repeat facts without ever understanding the underlying ideas.
The clerk answered every question in a rote manner, reciting the same script without listening, so customers left feeling that nobody had actually heard them.

ruffle.definition: to disturb the smoothness or calm of; to upset or irritate
sentences: The unexpected criticism did not ruffle the calm diplomat, who answered each hostile question in the same measured and polite tone as before.
A sudden gust of wind began to ruffle the surface of the pond, breaking the perfect reflection of the trees into countless trembling pieces.
ruffle.mnemonic: Ruffle : on froisse les plumes, on perturbe.

ruthless.definition: having or showing no pity or compassion; cruel
sentences: The ruthless dictator crushed every protest without mercy, jailing thousands of innocent citizens and showing no compassion even toward the families of his victims.
Known for his ruthless tactics, the executive fired hundreds of loyal employees overnight, caring only about quarterly profits and not at all about their futures.

salable.definition: fit to be sold; likely to find buyers
sentences: After the flood, only a few pieces of furniture remained salable, and the dealer had to throw away the rest as ruined and worthless.
The publisher rejected the manuscript, not because it lacked merit, but because she doubted that such an obscure poetry collection would be salable to the general public.

salvage.definition: to save or recover something from loss, damage, or destruction
sentences: Divers worked for weeks to salvage valuable cargo from the sunken ship, hoping to recover gold coins before storms covered the wreck with sand.
The coach tried to salvage the team's season by changing tactics, but too many games had been lost for the playoffs to remain realistic.
salvage.mnemonic: Salvage vient de sauver : même racine latine que « salut ».

sentences: The famously shy author seldom gave interviews, so the rare appearance on television drew a much larger audience than the network had expected.
In the desert, rain falls so seldom that when a storm finally arrives, flowers burst into bloom within days and the whole landscape changes color.

serendipity.definition: the happy discovery of something valuable by chance rather than by design
sentences: Pure serendipity led to the discovery of penicillin, when a stray mold happened to contaminate a dish and killed the surrounding bacteria.
It was serendipity that she sat next to the publisher on the train, a chance encounter that eventually led to her first book contract.
serendipity.mnemonic: Les princes de Serendip trouvaient toujours des trésors sans les chercher.

stern.definition: serious and strict, especially in demanding obedience; severe
sentences: The stern headmaster allowed no talking in the corridors and punished even minor offenses, so students feared his stare more than any detention.
Her father gave her a stern warning never to drive without a license, and his grave expression made clear that he was not joking.
stern.mnemonic: Stern : sévère (et aussi la poupe d'un bateau).

stopgap.definition: a temporary solution used until a permanent one can be found
sentences: The city built a wooden footbridge as a stopgap while engineers designed a permanent structure to replace the bridge that the flood had destroyed.
Critics said the subsidy was merely a stopgap that would postpone the crisis without resolving the deeper problems that had caused the industry's decline.
stopgap.mnemonic: Stop + gap : on bouche un trou en attendant mieux.

suit.definition: to be appropriate or becoming for; to befit
sentences: The somber tone of the music did not suit the cheerful wedding, and several guests exchanged puzzled glances as the band began to play.
Her calm and patient temperament suits her well for a career in nursing, where steady empathy is needed more than quick wit.
suit.mnemonic: Suit : un costume… ou convenir : ça te va.

sweeping.definition: wide-ranging and extensive in effect; radical, often too broad or general
sentences: The new president announced sweeping reforms that would transform the tax code, the healthcare system, and the education budget within only two years.
The historian cautioned against sweeping generalizations about the era, noting that the lives of peasants, merchants, and nobles differed far too much for one description.
sweeping.mnemonic: Sweeping : un coup de balai, radical et de grande ampleur.

tawdry.definition: showy but cheap and of poor quality; sordid
sentences: The carnival's tawdry decorations, made of cheap plastic and flaking gold paint, looked glamorous at night but shabby in the harsh light of morning.
Critics dismissed the reality show as a tawdry spectacle that exploited its contestants' private misery to entertain viewers with gossip and cheap drama.
tawdry.mnemonic: De la dentelle de Sainte Audrey (St Audrey's lace) bon marché : clinquant.

sentences: After the long hike, the tepid water from the old canteen was far from refreshing, but the thirsty travelers drank it gratefully.
The proposal received only tepid support from the board, whose members offered polite nods but declined to commit any money to the project.

trappings.definition: the outward signs or symbols associated with a role, status, or office
sentences: Although he enjoyed the trappings of success, such as the luxury car and the corner office, he privately felt his work had little meaning.
The prime minister's residence, with its uniformed guards and gilded rooms, displayed all the trappings of power that the voters had once criticized.
trappings.mnemonic: Trappings : les harnais d'apparat, les attributs du rang.

typify.definition: to be a characteristic example of; to embody
sentences: The small stone cottage with its thatched roof and flower garden seems to typify the rural English countryside that tourists love to photograph.
Critics say the senator's refusal to compromise typifies the stubborn partisanship that has paralyzed the legislature and prevented even modest agreements for years.
typify.mnemonic: Typify : être le type même de.

understated.definition: presented in a subtle, restrained way rather than being showy
sentences: Her understated elegance, a plain black dress and a single pearl necklace, drew more admiration than the flashy outfits of the other guests.
The novelist's understated prose never raises its voice, yet the quiet restraint makes the tragic events of the story feel all the more powerful.

uptick.definition: a small or modest increase, especially in a statistic or business figure
sentences: Analysts noted a slight uptick in consumer confidence last month, though it was too small to suggest that the long recession had truly ended.
The hospital reported an uptick in flu cases after the holidays, a modest rise that officials expected to subside by the end of winter.
uptick.mnemonic: Up-tick : un petit cran vers le haut.

verisimilitude.definition: the appearance of being true or real; believability in fiction
sentences: The author gave her fantasy novel a surprising verisimilitude by including realistic details about food, weather, and money, so readers believed in its invented kingdom.
Film historians admire the director's commitment to verisimilitude, noting that he insisted on authentic costumes and dialect so that the period drama would appear genuine.
verisimilitude.mnemonic: Veri- (vrai) + similis (semblable) : semblable au vrai, donc vraisemblance.

vicarious.definition: experienced in the imagination through the actions or feelings of another person
sentences: Never having traveled herself, she took vicarious pleasure in her sister's adventures, reading every letter as though she were walking through those distant cities.
Many parents live vicariously through their children, hoping the young athletes will achieve the glory that they themselves were never able to win.
vicarious.mnemonic: Vicarius = remplaçant : vivre à la place d'un autre (le vicaire).

vivid.definition: producing strong, clear images in the mind; bright and intense in color
sentences: The veteran gave such a vivid account of the battle that listeners could almost hear the cannons and smell the smoke drifting across the field.
The artist favored vivid reds and yellows, and her canvases glowed so brightly that they seemed to light up even the darkest corners of the gallery.
vivid.mnemonic: Vivid ≈ « vif » : couleurs et images éclatantes.

abhorrent.definition: inspiring disgust and loathing; utterly repugnant
sentences: The human rights committee condemned the violent acts as abhorrent, urging international courts to prosecute those responsible for such horrific cruelty.
To anyone who values honesty and integrity, the politician's shameless deceit was utterly abhorrent and provoked widespread public outrage.
abhorrent.mnemonic: Pensez à « abhorrer » en français : ce qui est abhorrent provoque l'horreur.

abridge.definition: to shorten a text without losing the core meaning
sentences: The publisher decided to abridge the massive historical biography so that high school students could finish reading it in one semester.
Constitutional scholars warned that the newly proposed law would severely abridge the freedom of assembly guaranteed to all citizens.
abridge.mnemonic: Abridge crée un « bridge » (pont) pour raccourcir le chemin à travers le texte.

abstain.definition: to restrain oneself from doing or enjoying something
sentences: Because of his intense training schedule, the athlete chose to abstain from sugary snacks and alcohol until the championship concluded.
Several neutral countries decided to abstain during the tense council vote rather than aligning themselves with either rival faction.
abstain.mnemonic: Comme le français « s'abstenir », souvent suivi de « from » en anglais.

abstract.definition: existing as an idea or concept rather than concrete reality
sentences: The philosophy professor explained that justice is an abstract concept that requires practical laws to be realized in everyday life.
Rather than discussing abstract economic theories, the speaker presented concrete data about how inflation directly affected family grocery bills.
abstract.mnemonic: Identique au français : s'oppose à ce qui est concret.

abundant.definition: existing or available in large quantities; plentiful
sentences: Thanks to the heavy spring rains, the fertile valley yielded an abundant harvest that easily fed the entire regional population.
The coral reef provided an abundant supply of nutrients, allowing thousands of distinct marine species to flourish in close proximity.
abundant.mnemonic: Même racine qu'« abondant » en français.

accentuate.definition: to make something more noticeable or prominent
sentences: The bright overhead stage lights served to accentuate the dramatic contrast between the colorful costumes and the dark background.
Rising economic inequality only served to accentuate the deep political divisions that had been brewing across the country for decades.
accentuate.mnemonic: « Accentuer » : mettre un accent, faire ressortir.

acclaim.definition: enthusiastic and public praise or approval
sentences: The director's innovative debut film earned widespread international acclaim from both seasoned critics and enthusiastic moviegoers around the globe.
Despite receiving critical acclaim for her groundbreaking architectural design, the firm struggled to secure enough financing to begin construction.
acclaim.mnemonic: Pensez aux acclamations d'une foule enthousiaste.

accommodating.definition: willing to please others; obliging and adaptable
sentences: The hotel staff was remarkably accommodating, readily adjusting dinner reservations and preparing special meals for our dietary restrictions without complaint.
Although the manager was usually quite accommodating to flexible work schedules, she refused to grant extensions during the busy audit week.
accommodating.mnemonic: Quelqu'un qui sait s'accommoder de vos demandes pour vous aider.

accord.definition: an official agreement, harmony, or state of mutual conformity
sentences: After weeks of intense bilateral negotiations, the two rival nations finally signed a peace accord ending decades of border conflict.
Her personal values were in complete accord with the charitable mission of the nonprofit organization where she chose to volunteer.
accord.mnemonic: Même mot qu'en français : un accord officiel ou être d'accord.

acute.definition: sharp, severe, or intense; possessing perceptive insight
sentences: The patient experienced an acute pain in his lower abdomen that required immediate emergency surgery to prevent further medical complications.
Known for her acute intellect, the detective noticed subtle inconsistencies in the witness testimony that everyone else had completely overlooked.
acute.mnemonic: Un angle aigu est pointu : une douleur ou un esprit aigu(ë).

adequate.definition: sufficient for a specific requirement; acceptable but not exceptional
sentences: Although the salary was adequate to cover basic living expenses, it left little extra money for emergency savings or luxury items.
The old generator provided an adequate amount of emergency power during the severe blizzard, keeping the hospital heaters running safely.
adequate.mnemonic: Adéquat : juste ce qu'il faut, ni trop peu ni extraordinaire.

adverse.definition: preventing success or development; harmful, unfavorable
sentences: The clinical trial was abruptly halted after several patients reported adverse side effects that threatened their overall long-term health.
Despite facing adverse weather conditions that included gale-force winds and torrential rain, the mountaineers managed to reach the summit safely.
adverse.mnemonic: Adverse comme un vent adverse ou des adversaires : opposé et nuisible.

affable.definition: friendly, good-natured, and exceptionally easy to talk to
sentences: Because of his warm demeanor and affable personality, the new department chair quickly gained the trust of all faculty members.
Even when dealing with irritable and demanding customers, the customer service representative remained unfailingly affable and thoroughly polite throughout the call.
affable.mnemonic: Affable en français : quelqu'un d'agréable et facile d'accès.

agile.definition: able to move or think quickly and easily
sentences: The mountain goat proved remarkably agile as it bounded effortlessly across steep, rocky cliffs that would terrify human climbers.
In modern technology sectors, companies must remain intellectually agile enough to adapt their business strategies to sudden consumer trends.
agile.mnemonic: Agile, aussi bien physiquement que mentalement.

alarming.definition: worrying, disturbing, or causing great fear and apprehension
sentences: Scientists reported an alarming decline in bee populations, warning that agricultural food production could collapse without essential insect pollination.
The sudden and alarming rise in regional inflation forced the central bank to sharply increase interest rates within three months.
alarming.mnemonic: Ce qui sonne l'alarme : inquiétant au plus haut point.

alienate.definition: to cause someone to feel isolated, estranged, or hostile
alienate.definitionFr: aliéner, éloigner, se mettre à dos
sentences: The senator's harsh and uncompromising rhetoric threatened to alienate moderate voters who were crucial to winning the upcoming election.
By constantly criticizing his coworkers in public meetings, the arrogant manager managed to alienate everyone on his development team.
alienate.mnemonic: Rendre étranger (alien) à soi : s'aliéner quelqu'un.

alleviate.definition: to make pain, distress, or a problem less severe
sentences: The doctor prescribed physical therapy and mild painkillers to alleviate the chronic discomfort caused by the patient's spinal injury.
Constructing a new bypass highway helped to alleviate traffic congestion that had plagued the downtown business district for years.
alleviate.mnemonic: Alléger un fardeau : alleviate soulage la douleur ou le problème.

altruistic.definition: showing a selfless concern for the well-being of others
sentences: Driven by purely altruistic motives, the wealthy philanthropist spent his retirement building free medical clinics in impoverished rural regions.
Skeptics questioned whether the billionaire's generous charitable foundation was genuinely altruistic or merely an elaborate strategy to reduce corporate taxes.
altruistic.mnemonic: Altruiste : tourné vers l'autre (alter) plutôt que vers soi.

amateur.definition: one engaging in an activity for pleasure rather than profession
sentences: Although he was only an amateur astronomer using a backyard telescope, he managed to discover a previously undocumented distant comet.
The difference in technical quality between a seasoned professional photographer and a careless amateur was immediately evident in the portraits.
amateur.mnemonic: Fait par amour de l'art plutôt que pour l'argent (pro).

ambivalent.definition: having simultaneous conflicting feelings or contradictory attitudes
sentences: She remained deeply ambivalent about accepting the lucrative job offer, torn between career advancement and having to relocate abroad.
Voters held ambivalent attitudes toward the controversial economic policy, appreciating the tax cuts while worrying about the growing public debt.
ambivalent.mnemonic: Ambi- (deux) + valence : tiré par deux forces opposées.

ameliorate.definition: to make something bad or unsatisfactory significantly better
sentences: The new community food bank did much to ameliorate poverty and hunger among struggling families throughout the harsh winter months.
Diplomats worked tirelessly to ameliorate hostile tensions between the neighboring states before minor skirmishes escalated into an all-out war.

amend.definition: to modify, revise, or make improvements to a formal document
sentences: Lawmakers agreed to amend the outdated legislation after consumer advocacy groups demonstrated that the statute failed to regulate digital privacy.
The treaty was subsequently amended to include stringent environmental protections that had been neglected during the original round of talks.
amend.mnemonic: Déposer un amendement pour amender une loi.

amiable.definition: displaying a friendly, pleasant, and good-natured manner
sentences: Our host was an amiable gentleman who went out of his way to make every visiting guest feel comfortable and welcome.
Despite the grueling schedule, the tour guide maintained an amiable attitude that kept the spirits of tired tourists surprisingly high.

amicable.definition: characterized by friendliness and absence of discord
sentences: After months of negotiations, the business partners reached an amicable settlement that allowed both to pursue separate ventures without resentment.
The couple decided that an amicable divorce was the healthiest choice for their young children, avoiding bitter courtroom battles entirely.
amicable.mnemonic: Un accord « à l'amiable » : qualifie souvent un accord ou une relation pacifique.

ample.definition: enough or more than enough; plentiful and spacious
sentences: There was ample time before the flight departed, so we leisurely enjoyed lunch at an airport café without feeling rushed.
The defense attorney presented ample evidence proving that her client was in another city when the crime was committed.
ample.mnemonic: Ample : largement suffisant en quantité ou espace.

amplify.definition: to increase the volume, strength, or scope of something
sentences: Social media algorithms often amplify extreme viewpoints by promoting controversial content that generates intense emotional engagement from users.
The acoustic design of the ancient stone theater was engineered to amplify the actors' voices without modern electronic equipment.
amplify.mnemonic: Comme un amplificateur audio qui augmente le volume.

anecdotal.definition: based on personal narrative rather than systematic scientific evidence
sentences: Although there was abundant anecdotal evidence praising the herbal remedy, clinical researchers found no rigorous scientific data supporting its effectiveness.
Relying on mere anecdotal claims from a few satisfied users is never sufficient to justify launching an expensive public health initiative.
anecdotal.mnemonic: Fondé sur des anecdotes plutôt que sur des preuves statistiques.

animosity.definition: strong hostility, ill will, or active opposition between entities
sentences: The lingering animosity between the two corporate executives made it nearly impossible for their respective departments to collaborate effectively.
Despite decades of mutual suspicion and political animosity, the rival nations agreed to sign a temporary ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid.

antagonistic.definition: showing or feeling active opposition or hostility toward someone
sentences: The attorney adopted an antagonistic tone toward the hostile witness, challenging every assertion made during the contentious cross-examination.
Constantly adopting an antagonistic attitude toward constructive feedback will only alienate your colleagues and impede your professional growth.
antagonistic.mnemonic: L'antagoniste est le rival hostile dans une histoire.

antiquated.definition: old-fashioned, outdated, or no longer suitable for modern times
sentences: The hospital desperately needed modern computing systems, as its antiquated paper filing method frequently caused dangerous administrative delays.
Many younger employees criticized the company's dress code as antiquated, arguing that formal business attire had no bearing on productivity.

apathetic.definition: showing or feeling lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
sentences: Voters had grown so apathetic after years of empty political promises that turnout dropped to an all-time low in the municipal election.
The teacher tried various interactive games to engage her students, but the exhausted teenagers remained largely apathetic throughout the morning lecture.

appease.definition: to pacify or placate someone by making concessions
appease.definitionFr: apaiser en cédant, calmer par des concessions
sentences: In an attempt to appease angry demonstrators, the mayor announced immediate reforms to address police oversight and community safety.
Offering minor tax exemptions did little to appease the frustrated union leaders, who insisted on substantial wage increases for all workers.
appease.mnemonic: Appease = apaiser (souvent historiquement par des concessions).

apprehensive.definition: anxious or fearful that something bad will happen
sentences: First-time homeowners felt deeply apprehensive about rising mortgage rates, fearing they might be unable to manage their monthly mortgage payments.
She was visibly apprehensive before stepping onto the stage, but her nervousness vanished the moment the audience applauded warmly.
apprehensive.mnemonic: Avoir de l'appréhension face à l'avenir.

appropriate.definition: to take for one's own use; allocate
sentences: The corrupt official attempted to appropriate state funds for his lavish private estate before auditors uncovered the illicit transfers.
Congress voted overwhelmingly to appropriate fifty million dollars in emergency funds for urgent disaster relief following the devastating coastal hurricane.
appropriate.mnemonic: En tant que verbe, prononcé /-eɪt/ : s'approprier ou allouer des crédits.

archaic.definition: very old, belonging to an earlier period, no longer current
sentences: The legal document was filled with archaic terms like 'heretofore' and 'whereupon' that modern readers found completely incomprehensible.
Relying on archaic banking software exposed the financial institution to security vulnerabilities that modern cybersecurity systems easily prevent.
archaic.mnemonic: Archaïque : qui appartient à un âge ancien.

arduous.definition: involving or requiring strenuous effort; difficult and tiring
sentences: The explorers embarked on an arduous journey across the frozen Arctic tundra, enduring frostbite and fierce blizzards for six weeks.
Drafting a comprehensive constitutional reform proved to be an arduous task that required endless compromises among rival political factions.

assertive.definition: having or showing a confident, forceful, and self-assured personality
sentences: To succeed in high-stakes corporate negotiations, one must be assertive without crossing the delicate line into rude aggressiveness.
The therapist encouraged the timid client to adopt more assertive communication strategies when expressing his personal boundaries at work.
assertive.mnemonic: To assert (affirmer) -> assertive (qui s'affirme avec assurance).

astronomical.definition: relating to astronomy; extraordinarily or exceedingly large
sentences: The cost of building the new underground transit line escalated to astronomical figures that far exceeded initial municipal projections.
Purchasing a penthouse in central Manhattan requires an astronomical amount of wealth that only a few billionaires possess.
astronomical.mnemonic: Aussi grand que les distances en astronomie.

astute.definition: having or showing an ability to accurately assess situations
sentences: Thanks to her astute financial investments during the market downturn, the entrepreneur doubled her venture capital within two years.
An astute political observer noticed that the minister's subtle choice of words signaled an imminent change in foreign policy.
astute.mnemonic: Astucieux au sens de très fin d'esprit et perspicace.

augment.definition: to make something greater by adding to it; increase
sentences: Many freelance workers take on evening tutoring jobs to augment their regular income and cope with rising living expenses.
The museum decided to augment its permanent art collection by acquiring several valuable masterpieces from prominent twentieth-century sculptors.
augment.mnemonic: Augmenter : ajouter pour rendre plus grand.

auspicious.definition: conducive to success; favorable, promising good fortune
sentences: Winning the first three matches of the season was an auspicious beginning for the newly appointed head soccer coach.
A bright and sunny morning provided an auspicious start to the outdoor wedding, delighting the nervous bride and groom.
auspicious.mnemonic: Sous de bons auspices : de bon augure.

austere.definition: severe, strict in manner; plain and unadorned in appearance
sentences: The monastery rooms were remarkably austere, containing nothing more than a simple wooden cot, a desk, and plain whitewashed walls.
Faced with soaring inflation and ballooning deficits, the finance minister introduced austere budget measures that sharply curtailed government spending.
austere.mnemonic: Austère : sans fard ni luxe, très sobre ou sévère.

avarice.definition: extreme greed for wealth or material gain
sentences: Driven by insatiable avarice, the corporate tycoon hoarded billions while paying his factory workers wages far below subsistence levels.
In classic moral literature, excessive avarice is consistently portrayed as a fatal flaw that inevitably destroys wealthy dynasties from within.
avarice.mnemonic: L'avarice : le vice de l'avare de Molière, soif d'argent.

averse.definition: having a strong dislike of or opposition to something
sentences: Because he was risk-averse by nature, the cautious investor avoided volatile tech stocks in favor of safe treasury bonds.
Although many traditional chefs are averse to using molecular gastronomy techniques, innovative culinary pioneers enthusiastically embrace scientific kitchen experimentation.
averse.mnemonic: Averse to = avoir de l'aversion pour.

avid.definition: having or showing a keen interest in or enthusiasm for
sentences: An avid reader since early childhood, Maria finished at least three dense literary novels each week throughout her summer vacation.
The young collector was an avid fan of antique postage stamps, constantly scouring flea markets for rare nineteenth-century editions.
avid.mnemonic: Avide de connaissances ou de lecture : passionné.

banal.definition: so lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring
sentences: Film critics panned the romantic comedy for its banal plot, noting that every twist was entirely predictable from the opening scene.
Instead of offering groundbreaking solutions to the housing crisis, the politician repeated banal slogans that voters had heard for years.

benevolent.definition: well meaning, kindly, and dedicated to charitable acts
sentences: The benevolent ruler established free schools and hospitals throughout his kingdom, earning the enduring love of his grateful subjects.
Behind her stern demeanor lay a benevolent heart that frequently motivated her to anonymously fund scholarships for disadvantaged college students.
benevolent.mnemonic: Bene (bien) + volent (vouloir) : qui veut le bien d'autrui.

benign.definition: gentle, harmless, kindly, or not malignant in medical terms
sentences: The patient breathed a huge sigh of relief when the biopsy revealed that the small tumor was entirely benign and harmless.
The island's benign climate, with mild temperatures and gentle sea breezes year-round, made it a popular haven for retired couples.
benign.mnemonic: Bénin : qui n'est pas grave ou dangereux.

bias.definition: prejudice in favor of or against one thing or group
sentences: The study was rejected by scientific peers because the researchers had exhibited an obvious confirmation bias while interpreting experimental data.
To ensure a fair trial, the judge dismissed potential jurors who displayed any personal bias toward the high-profile defendant.
