sentences: The tech billionaire announced grandiose plans to build an underwater metropolis, but investors remained skeptical about its actual engineering feasibility.
The ruined palace featured grandiose marble staircases and towering gilded columns that reflected the former royal family's extravagant imperial vanity.
grandiose.mnemonic: Grandiose : qui veut paraître grand et grandiose, souvent avec excès.

gratifying.definitionFr: gratifiant, source de satisfaction et de fierté
sentences: Seeing her students graduate and launch successful scientific careers was the most gratifying achievement of her thirty-year teaching journey.
It was immensely gratifying for the rescue volunteers to see the lost hikers reunited safely with their worried families yesterday.
gratifying.mnemonic: Gratifiant : qui apporte une récompense morale, gratifie le cœur.

grave.definition: giving cause for serious concern; solemn and somber in manner
sentences: The physician delivered the grave diagnosis with quiet empathy, warning the family that the patient faced severe complications without immediate surgery.
Mounting fiscal deficits posed a grave threat to the nation's financial stability, forcing lawmakers to convene an emergency legislative session.
grave.mnemonic: Grave signifie à la fois grave au sens de sérieux, et la tombe (the grave).

heterogeneous.definition: composed of diverse and dissimilar elements or parts
sentences: The university boasted a heterogeneous student population composed of individuals from dozens of distinct cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds.
Because the research sample was heterogeneous, scientists had to account for wide variations in age, diet, and lifestyle habits.
heterogeneous.mnemonic: Hétéro- (différent) + genre : formé d'éléments de natures variées.

homogeneous.definition: of the same kind; uniform throughout in composition or character
sentences: The small rural enclave remained remarkably homogeneous, sharing the same cultural traditions, religious beliefs, and architectural styles for generations.
Before conducting the chemical assay, the laboratory technician stirred the solution thoroughly until it became a completely homogeneous mixture.
homogeneous.mnemonic: Homo- (identique) : tout est semblable d'un bout à l'autre.

hypocrisy.definition: the practice of claiming to have moral standards one does not possess
hypocrisy.definitionFr: hypocrisie, décalage entre les principes affichés et les actes
sentences: Voters grew disgusted by the mayor's hypocrisy when journalists revealed that the politician routinely evaded the very taxes he championed.
Accusing others of extreme greed while hoarding millions in secret overseas accounts was widely condemned as the height of corporate hypocrisy.
hypocrisy.mnemonic: L'hypocrite joue un rôle comme au théâtre antique (hypokrites = acteur).

illicit.definition: forbidden by law, rules, or prevailing custom
sentences: Customs agents intercepted a cargo container packed with illicit drugs that smugglers had hidden beneath layers of fresh agricultural produce.
The executive was sentenced to prison after investigators uncovered his illicit scheme to embezzle millions of dollars from public pensions.
illicit.mnemonic: Il- (privatif) + licit (licite, légal) : contraire à la loi.

immutable.definition: unchanging over time or unable to be changed
sentences: Fundamental physical constants like the speed of light are considered immutable principles that govern the behavior of the entire universe.
Although technology transforms society rapidly, certain basic human emotions and moral impulses remain largely immutable across different eras.
immutable.mnemonic: Im- (sans) + mutation : qui ne mute ni ne change jamais.

impassive.definition: not showing or feeling any emotion; expressionless
sentences: Throughout the tense trial, the defendant remained completely impassive, showing neither remorse nor fear as the guilty verdict was read.
A professional bodyguard must cultivate an impassive exterior, observing hostile crowds calmly without ever displaying personal anxiety or anger.
impassive.mnemonic: Pas de passion visible : reste calme et stoïque quoi qu'il arrive.

imperceptible.definition: so slight, gradual, or subtle as not to be perceived
imperceptible.definitionFr: imperceptible, trop infime pour être remarqué
sentences: The movement of the glaciers down the mountain valley was so imperceptible that observers could only detect changes over decades.
An imperceptible tremor in the pianist's fingers revealed the stage fright she fought desperately to hide from the captivated audience.
imperceptible.mnemonic: Im- (impossible) + perceive : qu'on ne peut pas percevoir à l'œil nu.

imperious.definition: assuming power or authority without justification; arrogant and domineering
sentences: With an imperious wave of her hand, the aristocrat dismissed the nervous servants and demanded to see the estate manager immediately.
Subordinates resented the manager's imperious management style, which allowed no dissenting opinions and treated skilled employees like obedient servants.
imperious.mnemonic: Agit comme un empire ou un empereur : donne des ordres sans appel.

impertinent.definition: not showing proper respect; rude or insolent
sentences: The professor reprimanded the student for asking an impertinent question that mocked the guest speaker rather than engaging with the topic.
Victorian etiquette strictly prohibited young children from making impertinent remarks or interrupting their elders during formal dinner conversations.
impertinent.mnemonic: Impertinent = qui manque de respect aux convenances ou aux aînés.

implicit.definition: implied though not plainly expressed; understood without statement
sentences: Although neither side mentioned money directly, there was an implicit understanding that the lucrative contract would follow successful negotiations.
The poem carried an implicit criticism of wartime propaganda, allowing readers to decipher the author's subtle antiwar message between the lines.
implicit.mnemonic: Implicit = dans les plis (sous-entendu), à l'inverse d'explicit (explicité).

improvident.definition: not having or showing foresight; failing to save for future needs
improvident.definitionFr: imprévoyant, dépensier sans penser au lendemain
sentences: Because of his improvident spending habits, the heir squandered an enormous family fortune on frivolous luxuries within a single decade.
The improvident administration failed to accumulate financial reserves during economic booms, leaving the municipality bankrupt when the unexpected crisis arrived.
improvident.mnemonic: Im- (non) + provident (prévoyant comme la Providence) : sans prévoyance.

imprudent.definition: not showing care for the consequences of an action; rash
sentences: Embarking on the treacherous mountain hike during a sudden winter blizzard proved to be an imprudent decision that endangered the entire group.
Financial analysts warned that it was highly imprudent to invest one's life savings in volatile, unproven cryptocurrency ventures without diversification.
imprudent.mnemonic: Im- (non) + prudent : qui prend des risques évitables.

impudent.definition: not showing due respect for another person; insolently bold
impudent.definitionFr: impudent, effronté, insolent et sans gêne
sentences: The impudent young clerk dared to scoff aloud at the chairman during the shareholders meeting, shocking everyone present with his audacity.
Tired of the child's impudent behavior and sarcastic retorts, the nanny sent him straight to his bedroom without any dessert.
impudent.mnemonic: Pudeur = retenue. Impudent = sans pudeur, effronté, culotté.

inadvertent.definition: not resulting from or achieved through deliberate planning; unintentional
sentences: An inadvertent slip of the tongue by the spokesperson prematurely revealed the secret merger before legal documents were signed.
The software engineer apologized for the inadvertent deletion of user files, explaining that a tiny syntax error triggered the automated wipe.
inadvertent.mnemonic: Par inadvertance = sans faire exprès, sans attention délibérée.

incendiary.definition: tending to stir up conflict or designed to cause fires
incendiary.definitionFr: incendiaire, séditieux, propre à attiser les tensions
sentences: The demagogue delivered an incendiary speech that inflamed racial tensions and provoked violent clashes between rival protest groups in the streets.
Security forces seized caches of incendiary bombs intended to destroy critical infrastructure and ignite mass panic throughout the besieged capital city.
incendiary.mnemonic: Met le feu au sens propre (bombe incendiaire) ou figuré (discours incendiaire).

incessant.definition: continuing without pause or interruption, often to an annoying degree
incessant.definitionFr: incessant, continu, qui ne s'arrête jamais
sentences: Residents near the busy international airport lodged complaints about the incessant roar of jet engines disrupting their sleep night after night.
The teacher struggled to conduct the morning lecture over the incessant chatter and rustling papers of thirty unruly high school students.
incessant.mnemonic: In- (sans) + cesser : qui ne cesse jamais.

incongruous.definition: not in harmony or keeping with the surroundings or other aspects
incongruous.definitionFr: incongru, décalé, en désaccord avec son contexte
sentences: The ultra-modern glass skyscraper looked strikingly incongruous among the quaint cobblestone streets and centuries-old brick cottages of the historic village.
Wearing flip-flops and bright Bermuda shorts to a solemn state funeral struck everyone as bizarrely incongruous with the dignified occasion.
incongruous.mnemonic: Incongru = bizarrement déplacé par rapport au décor environnant.

incredulous.definition: unwilling or unable to believe something; skeptical
sentences: When the lottery officials announced that he had won the grand jackpot, he gave an incredulous gasp and checked the ticket repeatedly.
Jurors remained incredulous after hearing the suspect's far-fetched alibi, which contradicted video surveillance footage captured outside the jewelry store.
incredulous.mnemonic: In- (non) + crédule : qui refuse d'avaler une histoire sans preuves.

indefatigable.definition: persisting tirelessly; incapable of being fatigued
sentences: The indefatigable volunteer spent fourteen hours each day rebuilding homes destroyed by the hurricane, refusing to rest until everyone had shelter.
Thanks to her indefatigable campaigning across dozens of rural counties, the underdog candidate steadily gained ground and won the election.
indefatigable.mnemonic: In- (ne peut pas) + fatigue : ne connaît jamais l'épuisement.

indelible.definition: making marks that cannot be removed; impossible to forget
indelible.definitionFr: indélébile, ineffaçable, qui laisse une trace permanente
sentences: The horrific disaster left an indelible impression on the young nurse, shaping her humanitarian career for the next fifty years.
Voters dipped their fingers into indelible ink at polling stations to prevent anyone from casting a fraudulent second ballot.
indelible.mnemonic: Encre indélébile = impossible à effacer, au propre comme au figuré.

indigenous.definition: originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native
sentences: The botanist documented dozens of indigenous plant species that had evolved exclusively within this isolated mountain valley for millennia.
Advocates fought to preserve the indigenous languages of the archipelago, which were threatened with extinction by rapid cultural assimilation.
indigenous.mnemonic: Indigène / autochtone : né et ancré sur place depuis toujours.

indolent.definition: wanting to avoid activity or exertion; habitually lazy
sentences: Instead of searching for employment, the indolent youth spent his entire summer lounging on the sofa playing video games all day.
During the sultry heat wave, even the most industrious farmhands became indolent, seeking shade beneath spreading oaks until dusk arrived.
indolent.mnemonic: Indolent au sens médical ne sent pas la douleur, au sens GRE = trop paresseux pour bouger.

inert.definition: lacking the ability or strength to move; chemically unreactive
sentences: After swallowing the tranquilizer dart, the rampaging bear collapsed onto the grass and lay completely inert for nearly two hours.
Noble gases like helium and neon are chemically inert under normal conditions, rarely forming covalent bonds with other elements.
inert.mnemonic: Inertie : sans élan propre, incapable de bouger ou de réagir.

ingenious.definition: clever, original, and inventive in character or design
ingenious.definitionFr: ingénieux, plein de ressource et d'inventivité
sentences: The engineer devised an ingenious filtration system using discarded plastic bottles and river sand to supply clean water to refugees.
Detectives praised the detective's ingenious deduction, which cracked the baffling murder mystery when all conventional clues had failed.
ingenious.mnemonic: Ingénieux ≠ ingenuous (ingénu, naïf) ! Ingenious vient du génie inventif.

insidious.definition: proceeding in a gradual, subtle way, but with harmful effects
sentences: High blood pressure is often described as an insidious killer because it damages internal organs without producing any noticeable early symptoms.
The dictator used insidious censorship tactics, gradually rewriting historical textbooks until citizens forgot the democratic freedoms they once possessed.
insidious.mnemonic: S'insinue sans bruit avant de frapper mortellement.

insipid.definition: lacking flavor, vigor, or interest; dull and flat
insipid.definitionFr: insipide, fade, sans saveur ni originalité
sentences: The restaurant served an insipid soup that tasted like watered-down broth, prompting diners to ask for salt and hot sauce immediately.
Critics panned the director's latest romantic comedy as an insipid rehash of predictable Hollywood tropes that failed to entertain audiences.
insipid.mnemonic: Insipide : manque de piquant et de saveur, au propre comme au figuré.

insoluble.definition: impossible to solve or dissolve in a liquid
insoluble.definitionFr: insoluble, sans solution ou impossible à dissoudre
sentences: Diplomats feared that the territorial dispute had become completely insoluble after both nations refused to compromise on border demarcation.
Certain synthetic polymers are insoluble in water, making them ideal materials for waterproofing electronic devices and outdoor clothing.
insoluble.mnemonic: Ne peut être résolu (problème insoluble) ni dissous (substance insoluble).

intransigent.definition: unwilling or refusing to change one's views or reach an agreement
sentences: The union leader remained intransigent during wage negotiations, declaring that workers would strike rather than accept even minor benefit cuts.
Because both political parties adopted intransigent stances on immigration reform, the legislative proposal stalled in Congress for months.
intransigent.mnemonic: Refuse toute transaction : in-transigent = ne transige pas.

intrepid.definition: fearless and adventurous, especially in dangerous situations
intrepid.definitionFr: intrépide, sans peur, téméraire face au danger
sentences: The intrepid explorer ventured deep into the unexplored arctic tundra, braving ferocious subzero blizzards and hungry polar bears along the way.
War correspondents must be intrepid journalists, documenting intense fighting from the front lines despite constant bombardment and extreme personal danger.
intrepid.mnemonic: Trépider = trembler de peur. In-trépide = qui ne tremble jamais.

intriguing.definition: arousing great curiosity or interest; fascinating
intriguing.definitionFr: intrigant, captivant, qui éveille la curiosité
sentences: The archeologist made an intriguing discovery when excavating the cave, uncovering strange symbols carved into stone thousands of years ago.
The novel featured an intriguing plot that kept readers guessing the killer's identity until the very final chapter of the book.
intriguing.mnemonic: Qui monte une intrigue ou éveille un mystère fascinant.

irresolute.definition: showing or feeling hesitancy; uncertain and indecisive
sentences: Confronted by angry shareholders demanding quick action, the irresolute CEO wavered between cutting costs and launching new marketing initiatives.
His irresolute demeanor during the crisis undermined public confidence, as citizens expected a decisive leader rather than a hesitant bureaucrat.
irresolute.mnemonic: In- (non) + résolu : qui n'a pas la volonté de trancher.

irreverent.definition: showing a lack of respect for people or things generally taken seriously
irreverent.definitionFr: irrévérencieux, irrespectueux, insolent envers ce qui est sacré
sentences: The satirical magazine was famous for its irreverent cartoons mocking powerful politicians, religious dogmas, and stuffy cultural traditions.
Conservative critics denounced the comedian's irreverent jokes about historical icons, arguing that venerated national traditions deserved utmost solemnity.
irreverent.mnemonic: Manque de révérence : se moque de ce qu'on vénère habituellement.

itinerant.definition: traveling from place to place, especially to work
itinerant.definitionFr: itinérant, nomade, qui se déplace pour travailler
sentences: The itinerant preacher journeyed between remote frontier settlements, holding revival meetings inside makeshift tents before moving on each Monday.
During harvest season, hundreds of itinerant farmworkers travel throughout the fertile valley to pick ripe fruit from orchard to orchard.
itinerant.mnemonic: Suit un itinéraire permanent : ne reste jamais au même endroit.

judicious.definition: having, showing, or done with good sense or judgment
judicious.definitionFr: judicieux, avisé, plein de bon sens
sentences: Thanks to a judicious allocation of resources, the cash-strapped nonprofit organization funded all its primary charitable programs without incurring debt.
The seasoned diplomat used judicious language during delicate peace talks, choosing each word carefully to avoid offending either belligerent party.
judicious.mnemonic: Fait preuve de jugement (judicious) : mesure et sagesse.

languish.definition: to grow weak or deteriorate; to be neglected in an unpleasant place
languish.definitionFr: languir, dépérir, croupir dans l'oubli ou l'abandon
sentences: Political dissidents were left to languish in damp prison cells for decades while authoritarian leaders ignored international pleas for clemency.
Without regular maintenance and municipal funding, the historic downtown district began to languish as shops closed and buildings decayed.
languish.mnemonic: Languir = perdre ses forces ou être oublié dans un coin morne.

largesse.definition: generosity in bestowing money or gifts upon others
sentences: The wealthy philanthropist was celebrated for her largesse, donating millions to construct free hospitals and libraries throughout impoverished neighborhoods.
Local charities depended heavily upon the annual largesse of corporate sponsors to provide warm coats and hot meals during winter.
largesse.mnemonic: Faire des largesses = ouvrir largement son portefeuille.

laud.definition: to praise a person or their achievements highly
laud.definitionFr: louer, célébrer, faire le panégyrique de
sentences: Critics and audiences united to laud the young director's debut film, hailing it as an artistic masterpiece of modern cinema.
Environmental groups laud the government's decision to ban single-use plastics, calling the progressive policy a crucial victory for ocean conservation.
laud.mnemonic: Louer (lauder / applaud) : tresser des lauriers à quelqu'un.

lucid.definition: expressed clearly and easy to understand; bright or luminous
sentences: The mathematics professor gave a lucid explanation of quantum mechanics that enabled even first-year humanities students to grasp key concepts.
Despite suffering from advanced dementia, the elderly statesman experienced occasional lucid moments where he recognized relatives and recalled wartime events.
lucid.mnemonic: Lux (lumière) : l'esprit est éclairé, tout devient limpide.

magnanimous.definition: very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or less powerful person
magnanimous.definitionFr: magnanime, généreux et clément, grand seigneur
sentences: In a magnanimous victory speech, the elected governor praised his defeated opponent's dedication and invited him to join the bipartisan cabinet.
Showing that she was truly magnanimous, the team captain forgave the rookie whose careless fumble had cost them the championship match.
magnanimous.mnemonic: Magna- (grand) + animus (âme) : avoir une grande âme, pardonner avec panache.

maladroit.definition: inept, clumsy, or lacking skill and tact
sentences: The foreign minister's maladroit comments at the international summit offended overseas dignitaries and sparked an unintended diplomatic row between allies.
A maladroit attempt to repair the delicate antique clock resulted in bent gears and fractured hands, ruining the valuable family heirloom.
maladroit.mnemonic: Emprunt direct au français maladroit (manque d'adresse physique ou verbale).

meander.definition: to follow a winding course; to wander aimlessly
sentences: Tourists love to meander through the narrow medieval alleys of the old town, discovering quaint pastry shops and hidden stone courtyards.
The gentle brook meanders across grassy meadows before cascading into a deep mountain lake nestled beneath the snow-capped alpine peaks.
meander.mnemonic: Faire des méandres comme une rivière qui serpente tranquillement.

nominal.definition: existing in name only; far below the real value or cost
nominal.definitionFr: nominal, symbolique, très minime par rapport au coût réel
sentences: The monarch served as the nominal head of state, while actual governing authority was exercised exclusively by the elected parliament.
Museum entry was free for students, although visitors were invited to make a nominal donation to support daily building maintenance.
nominal.mnemonic: N'a que le nom (nominal head), ou une somme purement symbolique (nominal fee).

nonchalant.definition: feeling or appearing calm and relaxed; not showing anxiety or interest
nonchalant.definitionFr: nonchalant, désinvolte, détaché sans laisser paraître d'émotion
sentences: Despite facing harsh questioning from aggressive reporters, the seasoned diplomat maintained a nonchalant demeanor and answered every query with a smile.
He shrugged in a nonchalant manner when told he had failed the examination, pretending that academic honors did not matter at all.
nonchalant.mnemonic: Emprunt direct au français nonchalant : attitude tranquille, flegmatique.

omnipresent.definition: widely or constantly encountered; present everywhere at the same time
omnipresent.definitionFr: omniprésent, présent en tout lieu et en tout temps
sentences: In modern metropolitan centers, digital billboards and smartphone screens have become omnipresent features that shape every aspect of urban commercial life.
During the sweltering tropical summer, humidity was an omnipresent nuisance that seeped into clothing and made outdoor physical exertion nearly unbearable.

omniscient.definition: knowing everything; having infinite knowledge and insight
omniscient.definitionFr: omniscient, qui sait tout, doué d'un savoir infini
sentences: Classic nineteenth-century novels often employ an omniscient narrator who reveals the secret thoughts and hidden motivations of every fictional character.
No human advisor is truly omniscient, so wise rulers consult diverse experts before enacting sweeping economic or foreign policy directives.

orthodox.definition: conforming to established doctrine, conventional beliefs, or accepted customs
orthodox.definitionFr: orthodoxe, conforme à la doctrine reçue et aux conventions
sentences: The maverick economist rejected orthodox fiscal models, arguing that traditional formulas failed to account for sudden behavioral shifts in digital markets.
Raised in an orthodox religious household, she found it liberating to explore secular philosophy and progressive art during her college years.
orthodox.mnemonic: Ortho- (droit) + doxa (opinion) : pensée conforme à la norme.

outmoded.definition: old-fashioned or no longer usable; out of date
outmoded.definitionFr: démodé, obsolète, dépassé par le temps
sentences: Relying on outmoded paper filing cabinets slowed hospital administration, prompting administrators to transition toward fully secure cloud-based medical records.
The general criticized the military's outmoded tactical doctrines, insisting that modern warfare required rapid drone surveillance rather than trench warfare.
outmoded.mnemonic: Hors de la mode (out of mode) : obsolète, dépassé.

palpable.definition: so intense as to seem almost tangible; plain to see
palpable.definitionFr: palpable, tangible, évident et presque matériel
sentences: When the jury returned to the packed courtroom, the tension in the air was palpable, making spectators hold their breath in anticipation.
There was a palpable sense of relief across the coastal village once the hurricane changed course and headed harmlessly out to sea.
palpable.mnemonic: On peut presque le toucher du doigt (palper) tellement c'est évident.

pantheon.definition: a group of particularly respected, famous, or important people
pantheon.definitionFr: panthéon, groupe des personnalités les plus illustres
sentences: With his historic Olympic triumphs, the young sprinter earned a permanent place within the pantheon of the greatest international athletic legends.
Scholars consider Shakespeare and Milton indisputable pillars of the English literary pantheon, whose poetic masterpieces continue to inspire global playwrights.
pantheon.mnemonic: Panthéon : le temple de tous les dieux, où l'on place les illustres.

paradox.definition: a seemingly contradictory statement that may nonetheless prove to be true
paradox.definitionFr: paradoxe, contradiction apparente renfermant une vérité
sentences: Economists study the paradox of thrift, which posits that individual efforts to save more money can inadvertently cause collective economic contraction.
It remains a frustrating paradox that despite having countless communication devices, modern citizens report feeling more isolated than previous generations.
paradox.mnemonic: Para- (contre) + doxa (opinion reçue) : vérité contraire au sens commun.

pariah.definition: an outcast rejected and despised by society or a group
pariah.definitionFr: paria, exclu rejeté et méprisé par tous
sentences: After exposing corporate embezzlement to federal regulators, the whistleblower became an outcast pariah whom former colleagues refused to speak to or acknowledge.
The rogue nation became an international pariah after violating multilateral nonproliferation treaties and test-firing ballistic missiles into neighboring waters.
pariah.mnemonic: Paria = intouchable rejeté au ban de la société.

pastoral.definition: portraying or evoking country life, typically in a romanticized form
sentences: The English landscape painter depicted an idyllic pastoral scene with grazing sheep, winding streams, and rolling emerald hills under sunny skies.
Seeking refuge from stressful urban noise, the novelist rented a secluded pastoral retreat where songbirds and rustling leaves provided peaceful company.
pastoral.mnemonic: Pasteur = berger : qui évoque la vie paisible des bergers et des champs.

pedantic.definition: excessively concerned with minor details, formal rules, or displaying knowledge
pedantic.definitionFr: pédant, pointilleux à l'excès, étalant son savoir
sentences: Students groaned whenever the pedantic professor interrupted interesting classroom debates to nitpick minor grammatical errors in their casual speaking.
Her pedantic insistence on verifying every trivial footnote slowed the editing process and annoyed authors working under strict publication deadlines.
pedantic.mnemonic: Pédant = qui fait la leçon et s'accroche aux virgules.

pejorative.definition: expressing contempt, disapproval, or a negative value judgment
sentences: Although the label was originally intended as a pejorative insult, the rebellious artists proudly adopted the moniker for their avant-garde movement.
The politician avoided using pejorative language when debating her rivals, preferring to criticize their specific policy proposals rather than launching personal attacks.
pejorative.mnemonic: Péjoratif : qui tire vers le pire (peior en latin).

pious.definition: devoutly religious; making a hypocritical show of righteousness
sentences: The pious monk devoted every morning to silent prayer and charitable work, seeking spiritual enlightenment away from worldly vanities.
Cynics dismissed the senator's pious declarations about family values, recalling numerous scandalous headlines published in the local press over the years.
pious.mnemonic: Pieux : très dévot, mais au GRE souvent teinté d'hypocrisie moralisatrice.

sentences: The lonely cello player produced a plaintive melody that echoed mournfully through the empty cathedral, moving several listeners to tears.
Across the frozen lake, the plaintive howl of a solitary wolf pierced the quiet night, signaling distress to its distant pack.
plaintive.mnemonic: Plaintif : qui ressemble à une plainte triste et touchante.

platitude.definition: a remark or statement that is flat, dull, or trite
sentences: Grieving mourners gained little comfort from the politician's empty platitude that everything happens for a reason during times of tragic loss.
Instead of offering concrete strategies to increase sales, the CEO merely repeated the tired corporate platitude that teamwork makes the dream work.
platitude.mnemonic: D'une grande platitude : une phrase plate et banale sans substance.

plethora.definition: a large or excessive amount of something
sentences: Shoppers faced a bewildering plethora of options in the cereal aisle, browsing dozens of colorful boxes boasting different nutritional claims.
Because the job opening attracted a plethora of highly qualified applicants, human resources had to conduct multiple rounds of intensive interviews.

poignant.definition: evoking a keen sense of sadness, regret, or emotion
poignant.definitionFr: poignant, émouvant, qui touche profondément le cœur
sentences: The documentary concluded with poignant footage of war refugees reuniting with their children after years of dangerous separation across closed borders.
Reading her late grandmother's wartime diaries proved to be a poignant experience that stirred both deep sorrow and immense family pride.
poignant.mnemonic: Poignant : qui poignarde le cœur d'émotion ou de nostalgie.

polarize.definition: to divide into two sharply contrasting groups or sets of opinions
polarize.definitionFr: polariser, diviser en deux camps opposés et irréconciliables
sentences: The controversial tax legislation threatened to polarize the legislature, driving moderate lawmakers into antagonistic ideological camps that refused to negotiate.
Social media algorithms often polarize public discourse by amplifying inflammatory rhetoric while burying nuanced, thoughtful perspectives beneath sensational headlines.
polarize.mnemonic: Créer deux pôles opposés (nord/sud) : diviser en deux extrêmes.

pragmatic.definition: dealing with things sensibly and realistically based on practical considerations
pragmatic.definitionFr: pragmatique, axé sur les résultats concrets et l'efficacité
sentences: Rather than pursuing idealistic theories that looked nice on paper, the pragmatic engineer selected affordable, readily available parts to finish construction.
The mayor adopted a pragmatic approach to homelessness, prioritizing immediate shelter construction over protracted debates about long-term urban sociology.
pragmatic.mnemonic: Pragmatique = ancré dans la pratique et le bon sens terre-à-terre.

precipitate.definition: to cause an event or situation to happen suddenly or prematurely
sentences: The sudden assassination of the archduke served to precipitate a devastating global conflict that engulfed world powers within a few weeks.
Reckless borrowing and excessive speculation can easily precipitate a nationwide banking collapse when real estate prices suddenly plummet downward.
precipitate.mnemonic: Précipiter les choses = faire tomber ou déclencher brusquement.

precocious.definition: having developed certain abilities or proclivities at an unusually early age
precocious.definitionFr: précoce, en avance sur son âge
sentences: The precocious child was solving advanced calculus problems and reading university-level literature before she had even celebrated her eighth birthday.
Mozart was widely celebrated as a precocious musical talent who composed complex symphonies and performed before European royalty while very young.
precocious.mnemonic: Précoce : mûr avant l'heure (prae + coquere = cuit en avance).

prodigal.definition: spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant
sentences: The prodigal prince spent thousands on lavish banquets each evening, draining state coffers until angry citizens revolted against the monarchy.
After years of prodigal living in cosmopolitan resorts, the bankrupt gambler returned home to seek assistance from his estranged family.
prodigal.mnemonic: L'enfant prodigue dans la Bible a dilapidé toute sa fortune.

prodigious.definition: remarkably or impressively great in extent, size, or degree
sentences: The legendary athlete consumed a prodigious quantity of calories each day to fuel grueling ten-hour training sessions before the Olympics.
Building the transcontinental railway across towering mountain ranges required a prodigious engineering effort that cost thousands of lives and fortunes.
prodigious.mnemonic: Prodigieux : qui tient du prodige par son immensité ou son éclat.

prodigy.definition: a person, especially a child, with exceptional abilities or qualities
prodigy.definitionFr: prodige, personne douée d'un talent extraordinaire
sentences: Hailed as a chess prodigy, the ten-year-old girl defeated experienced grandmasters and became the youngest champion in national history.
The young math prodigy was admitted into the prestigious university research lab before completing traditional secondary school education.
prodigy.mnemonic: Un enfant prodige (child prodigy) montre un talent hors norme dès l'enfance.

profuse.definition: plentiful; abundant; given or flowing in great amounts
profuse.definitionFr: profus, abondant, versé ou offert avec générosité
sentences: The runner collapsed across the finish line dripping with profuse sweat after completing the grueling marathon under the sweltering desert sun.
The embarrassed host offered profuse apologies to the dinner guests when the oven malfunctioned and burned the main course black.
profuse.mnemonic: Profusion : versé à grands flots, très abondant.

provincial.definition: narrow-minded or limited in perspective; unsophisticated
provincial.definitionFr: provincial, borné, d'esprit étroit et peu cosmopolite
sentences: Having never traveled outside his small agricultural hamlet, the merchant held provincial views regarding foreign cultures, cuisines, and languages.
Metropolitan critics mocked the local exhibition as provincial, but residents defended its honest celebration of regional traditions and folklore.
provincial.mnemonic: Provincial au sens péjoratif : qui manque d'ouverture sur le vaste monde.

quintessential.definition: representing the most perfect or typical example of a quality
sentences: With its afternoon tea service and red double-decker buses, London provided the quintessential backdrop for the British detective film.
A crisp white button-down shirt paired with dark denim jeans is often described as the quintessential casual American wardrobe.
quintessential.mnemonic: La quintessence : la cinquième essence des alchimistes, le concentré parfait.

rectify.definition: to put right; to correct or remedy an error
sentences: The accounting department worked through the weekend to rectify the billing error before clients noticed incorrect charges on monthly invoices.
Automakers issued an urgent recall to rectify a faulty brake sensor that had caused several minor collisions during cold weather.
rectify.mnemonic: Rectus = droit : remettre d'équerre, redresser, rectifier.

redouble.definition: to make or become much greater, more intense, or numerous
sentences: Following the disappointing tournament loss, the coach urged his players to redouble their training efforts and focus on basic defensive drills.
When rescue workers heard faint tapping beneath the collapsed concrete building, they redoubled their efforts to dig through the rubble.
redouble.mnemonic: Redoubler d'efforts = multiplier par deux l'intensité.

reiterate.definition: to say something again or several times, typically for emphasis
reiterate.definitionFr: réitérer, répéter avec insistance pour souligner
sentences: The prime minister held a press briefing to reiterate that national borders would remain closed until health authorities confirmed safety.
Let me reiterate the importance of wearing safety goggles in the laboratory, as chemical splashes can cause permanent blindness instantly.
reiterate.mnemonic: Itérer = répéter. Réitérer = redire une nouvelle fois pour bien insister.

reprisal.definition: an act of retaliation, especially in wartime or political conflict
sentences: Citizens feared violent reprisal from the ruthless military junta if they participated in the peaceful pro-democracy protests downtown.
The rebel militia launched targeted missile strikes as reprisal for government bombings that had destroyed civilian infrastructure earlier that morning.
reprisal.mnemonic: Représailles : riposte pour rendre coup pour coup.

reproach.definition: to express disapproval, disappointment, or criticism toward someone
sentences: The supervisor did not reproach the intern for making a mistake, but instead explained calmly how to solve the problem.
She could not reproach herself for the team's defeat, knowing that she had prepared thoroughly and performed at her best.
reproach.mnemonic: Faire des reproches : blâmer quelqu'un pour une faute.

respite.definition: a short period of rest or relief from something difficult
sentences: After weeks of grueling physical labor under scorching heat, the unexpected rain shower offered firefighters a welcome respite from the blaze.
The brief winter vacation provided college students with a much-needed respite from relentless exam preparation and difficult term papers.
respite.mnemonic: Un temps de répit : respirer un peu avant que l'épreuve ne reprenne.

revere.definition: to feel deep respect, veneration, or admiration for someone
sentences: Centuries after his peaceful civil rights marches, millions of citizens continue to revere the visionary leader for his moral courage.
In ancient Greece, citizens would revere the wisdom of philosophers and seek spiritual guidance from the famous oracle at Delphi.
revere.mnemonic: Révérer = traiter avec révérence, vénération et respect infini.

rhetoric.definition: the art of persuasive speaking; speech that sounds persuasive but lacks sincerity
rhetoric.definitionFr: rhétorique, art du discours persuasif ; paroles creuses
sentences: Voters dismissed the candidate's fiery rhetoric on social justice, noting that his voting record consistently contradicted his grandiose campaign speeches.
The defense attorney used masterful rhetoric to convince the hesitant jury that reasonable doubt existed regarding the defendant's guilt.
rhetoric.mnemonic: L'art de bien parler (rhétorique), souvent utilisé pour masquer le vide.

sentences: The executive summary outlined the salient points of the proposal, allowing the board to understand key financial projections without reading the lengthy report.
When assessing the candidate's qualifications, the committee considered her decade of international leadership experience to be her most salient asset.
salient.mnemonic: Pensez à « saillant » en français : ce qui saute aux yeux et dépasse du lot.

satire.definition: the use of humor, irony, or ridicule to expose flaws
sentences: The television show used biting political satire to ridicule government incompetence, prompting widespread debate among citizens and lawmakers alike.
Jonathan Swift employed dark satire in his essays to expose systemic poverty and mock the callous indifference of wealthy British aristocrats.
satire.mnemonic: Une satire utilise le rire pour critiquer et fustiger les travers humains.

satirical.definition: mocking human folly or vice through humor and irony
sentences: The satirical cartoons published in the weekly magazine mocked corporate greed, drawing furious complaints from several prominent industry executives.
Her satirical monologue highlighted the absurdity of modern beauty standards, entertaining the audience while delivering a profound social critique.
satirical.mnemonic: L'adjectif dérivé de satire : un ton piquant qui égratigne la bêtise.

schism.definition: a formal split or division between opposing factions
schism.definitionFr: schisme, rupture ou division au sein d'un groupe
sentences: A sharp ideological schism emerged within the political coalition, ultimately causing several disillusioned ministers to defect and form an independent party.
The bitter disagreement over doctrinal orthodoxy led to a permanent schism between the two branches of the ancient religious organization.
schism.mnemonic: Même mot en français : schisme, la déchirure irréversible d'une communauté.

scintillating.definition: brilliantly lively, witty, or exceptionally clever
sentences: The dinner guests were captivated by the author's scintillating wit, as she effortlessly recounted amusing anecdotes throughout the entire evening.
Critics praised the young pianist for delivering a scintillating performance that combined dazzling technical virtuosity with deep emotional resonance.
scintillating.mnemonic: Comme des étoiles qui scintillent : une conversation ou prestation étincelante.

secular.definition: not connected with religious or spiritual matters
sentences: The modern constitution established a strictly secular court system to guarantee that civil legal disputes remained independent of religious authority.
Although the ancient cathedral was built for worship, it frequently hosted secular events such as classical symphonies and community conferences.
secular.mnemonic: Séculier = du siècle (du monde profane), opposé au clergé et au religieux.

siphon.definition: to draw off or convey liquid, resources, or funds
siphon.definitionFr: siphonner, détourner des fonds ou des ressources
sentences: The corrupt accountant managed to siphon millions of dollars from charity accounts into offshore investments before auditors uncovered the discrepancy.
Desperate motorists used a flexible plastic hose to siphon fuel from an abandoned truck during the severe regional gasoline shortage.
siphon.mnemonic: Siphonner : vider un liquide ou subtiliser discrètement de l'argent.

stoic.definition: enduring pain or hardship without showing emotion
stoic.definitionFr: stoïque, impassible face à la douleur
sentences: Despite enduring intense physical discomfort throughout the grueling trek, the veteran mountaineer remained remarkably stoic and never voiced a complaint.
Her stoic composure during the tragic press conference impressed the reporters, who had expected her to break down in tears.
stoic.mnemonic: Comme les philosophes stoïciens de l'Antiquité : impassibles devant l'épreuve.

subvert.definition: to undermine the authority or principles of an established system
subvert.definitionFr: subvertir, saper l'autorité ou renverser l'ordre établi
sentences: Rebel factions attempted to subvert the democratic government by secretly financing extremist radio stations and inciting widespread civil unrest.
The experimental playwright sought to subvert theatrical conventions by removing the traditional stage and inviting the audience into the performance.
subvert.mnemonic: Sub (dessous) + vertere (tourner) : retourner par le dessous, saper les bases.

supplant.definition: to supersede and replace someone or something through force or strategy
sentences: Digital streaming platforms quickly managed to supplant traditional video rental stores, rendering physical media practically obsolete within a decade.
The ambitious young executive conspired with rival shareholders to supplant the aging chief executive and claim control of the firm.
supplant.mnemonic: Supplanter : faire un croc-en-jambe à quelqu'un sous ses pieds pour prendre sa place.

supple.definition: bending and moving easily and gracefully; flexible
sentences: Decades of daily stretching exercises helped the dancer maintain a remarkably supple body well past her fiftieth birthday.
The diplomat was admired for having a supple mind that adapted swiftly to unexpected shifts in delicate multilateral negotiations.
supple.mnemonic: Même sens et racine que « souple » : qui ploie sans se rompre.

surreal.definition: having a bizarre, dreamlike, or unreal quality
surreal.definitionFr: surréaliste, étrange et comme dans un rêve
sentences: Walking through the completely deserted downtown avenues at noon felt entirely surreal to the residents during the emergency lockdown.
The film created a surreal atmosphere by juxtaposing serene pastoral landscapes with monstrous clockwork figures floating across the sky.
surreal.mnemonic: Surréalisme : au-delà du réel, halluciné et onirique.

surreptitious.definition: done secretly, stealthily, or without open notice
sentences: The undercover detective cast surreptitious glances toward the back corner booth, hoping the suspects would not notice his surveillance.
She slipped a surreptitious note into his briefcase before the security officers escorted the dissident away from the building.
surreptitious.mnemonic: Subreptice en français : qui se glisse en douce comme un serpent.

synonymous.definition: closely associated with or having the same meaning
sentences: Over decades of excellence, the brand name became synonymous with impeccable luxury craftsmanship and uncompromising technological innovation across the globe.
In political commentary, the politician's name became synonymous with fiscal recklessness due to his disastrous economic mismanagement during his first term.
synonymous.mnemonic: Synonyme : deux mots ou idées qui expriment exactement la même chose.

taboo.definition: a social or religious custom forbidding a particular practice
sentences: In that conservative community, discussing mental illness remained a strict social taboo that prevented many troubled teenagers from seeking medical help.
Breaking an ancient tribal taboo by venturing into the sacred forest was believed to bring misfortune upon the entire village.
taboo.mnemonic: Un tabou : ce dont on ne doit pas parler ou ce qui est formellement interdit.

tacit.definition: understood or implied without being stated aloud
sentences: Although neither spouse mentioned the impending divorce during the dinner party, their awkward silence conveyed tacit acknowledgement of the problem.
By staying silent while his assistants altered the financial reports, the manager gave his tacit consent to the illegal scheme.
tacit.mnemonic: Tacite vient du latin tacere (se taire) : accord sans un mot dit.

tact.definition: skill and sensitivity in dealing with difficult people or issues
tact.definitionFr: tact, délicatesse et diplomatie dans les rapports humains
sentences: Handling the distraught customer complaints required immense tact, as any careless remark could easily provoke further outrage and viral backlash.
The ambassador was widely praised for his diplomacy and tact when resolving delicate border disputes between neighboring sovereign states.
tact.mnemonic: Avoir du tact : savoir manier les situations épineuses avec doigté.

tangential.definition: only slightly relevant or diverging from the main topic
tangential.definitionFr: tangentiel, secondaire ou marginal par rapport au sujet
sentences: The professor dismissed the student's tangential argument about ancient architecture because the seminar focused exclusively on twentieth-century urban sociology.
During the budgetary hearing, the senator made several tangential remarks that distracted the committee from voting on the crucial funding bill.
tangential.mnemonic: Comme une tangente : qui ne touche le sujet qu'en un seul point superficiel.

temperate.definition: moderate in behavior or climate; showing restraint
temperate.definitionFr: tempéré, modéré dans ses propos ou son climat
sentences: The diplomat maintained a temperate tone during the heated debate, avoiding inflammatory insults while firmly defending her country's vital security interests.
Retirees preferred moving to the coastal region because its temperate climate brought mild winters without the suffocating heat of tropical summers.
temperate.mnemonic: Tempéré : ni trop chaud ni trop froid, mesuré et calme.

tenable.definition: defensible against attack, criticism, or objection
sentences: Once new forensic evidence emerged, the defendant's alibi was no longer tenable, forcing his defense attorneys to rethink their courtroom strategy.
Holding the forward outpost became barely tenable after enemy artillery destroyed their primary supply bridges across the raging northern river.
tenable.mnemonic: Qui peut être « tenu » : une position qu'on peut défendre sans céder.

titillate.definition: to excite or stimulate pleasantly, often superficially
sentences: The tabloid relied on sensational headlines designed to titillate readers rather than inform the public about significant geopolitical developments.
A subtle blend of rare aromatic spices was used to titillate the diners' palates before the banquet's main course was served.
titillate.mnemonic: Titiller / émoustiller : piquer la curiosité ou le plaisir.

transgression.definition: an act that violates a law, rule, or moral code
transgression.definitionFr: transgression, infraction à une règle ou une loi
sentences: The company fired the junior trader after discovering his severe ethical transgression, which involved manipulating stock prices through falsified documents.
In puritanical societies, even the slightest social transgression could result in public shaming and severe ostracism by church leaders.
transgression.mnemonic: Transgresser : franchir la ligne interdite, enfreindre une loi.

transient.definition: lasting only for a short time; impermanent
transient.definitionFr: transitoire, éphémère, qui ne dure pas
sentences: Economists warned that the sudden surge in consumer spending was merely a transient trend driven by one-time government stimulus checks.
The tourist enjoyed the transient beauty of cherry blossoms in April, knowing the delicate petals would vanish within a week.
transient.mnemonic: En transit : qui passe rapidement sans s'installer.

transitory.definition: not permanent; lasting for only a brief period
sentences: Philosophers often remind us that human glory is entirely transitory, as even the mightiest ancient empires eventually collapsed into forgotten dust.
The medication offered only transitory relief from chronic pain, requiring patients to seek more comprehensive long-term physical therapy treatments.
transitory.mnemonic: Proche de transient : qui ne fait que passer, provisoire.

truncate.definition: to shorten by cutting off the top or end
truncate.definitionFr: tronquer, raccourcir en coupant une partie
sentences: Because the conference session ran dangerously behind schedule, the moderator had to truncate the question-and-answer period to only five minutes.
The editor decided to truncate the lengthy manuscript by removing several unnecessary background chapters before publishing the final edition.
truncate.mnemonic: Tronquer : couper le tronc ou l'extrémité d'un texte ou d'un objet.

tumultuous.definition: making a loud, confused noise; turbulent or disorderly
sentences: The rock star received a tumultuous ovation from fifty thousand cheering fans who stood on their chairs throughout the stadium.
Historians examined the tumultuous decades following the sudden collapse of the empire, when constant civil warfare ravaged the entire countryside.
tumultuous.mnemonic: Plein de tumulte : désordonné, fracassant et agité.

utilitarian.definition: designed to be useful or practical rather than attractive
sentences: The Soviet apartment blocks were built with a purely utilitarian design that maximized cheap living quarters while offering zero aesthetic charm.
He preferred simple utilitarian boots made of heavy waterproof rubber over expensive designer footwear when working on the family farm.
utilitarian.mnemonic: Utile avant tout : la fonction prime absolument sur l'apparence.

venerate.definition: to regard with great respect or profound reverence
venerate.definitionFr: vénérer, éprouver un profond respect pour
sentences: Many traditional cultures venerate their elders for their life wisdom, regularly seeking their council before deciding critical community matters.
Scholars continue to venerate the pioneering physicist whose revolutionary discoveries regarding quantum mechanics reshaped our modern view of reality.
venerate.mnemonic: Vénérer : porter aux nues, révérer comme un saint.

veracity.definition: conformity to facts; truthfulness and accuracy
veracity.definitionFr: véracité, sincérité et exactitude des faits
sentences: The investigative reporter doubted the veracity of the official government press release and launched an independent inquiry into the disaster.
Because the witness had previously lied under oath, defense attorneys questioned her veracity and credibility before the attentive jurors.
veracity.mnemonic: Véracité : vient du latin verus (vrai), la vérité scrupuleuse.

vociferous.definition: expressing feelings or opinions in a loud and forceful manner
sentences: Despite vociferous objections from environmental activists, the regional council approved the controversial pipeline project by a narrow majority vote.
The coach was a vociferous critic of the referee's decisions, repeatedly shouting protests from the sideline until he was ejected.
vociferous.mnemonic: Vociférer : crier très fort pour faire entendre ses griefs.

xenophobic.definition: having an unreasonable fear or hatred of foreigners
sentences: The populist politician used xenophobic rhetoric to inflame public resentment against immigrants during the hotly contested parliamentary election campaign.
Human rights organizations condemned the xenophobic attacks that broke out against migrant workers following the economic downturn in the capital.
xenophobic.mnemonic: Xéno (étranger) + phobe (peur/haine) : rejet hostile de l'étranger.

abstruse.definition: difficult to understand; obscure or esoteric
sentences: Most undergraduates struggled through the philosopher's abstruse treatise, finding its dense technical jargon nearly impossible to decipher without guidance.
The mathematician presented an abstruse proof that only a handful of international specialists in theoretical topology could fully comprehend.
abstruse.mnemonic: Abstrus = abscons : si abstrait et touffu qu'on s'y perd.

acolyte.definition: an assistant or devoted follower of a leader
sentences: The aging professor was always accompanied by an eager acolyte who carried his lecture notes and handled routine administrative chores.
As an enthusiastic acolyte of the tech guru, the young programmer adopted his mentor's strict habits and radical design philosophy.
acolyte.mnemonic: Un acolyte : à l'origine enfant de chœur, aujourd'hui bras droit fidèle.

acuity.definition: sharpness or keenness of thought, vision, or perception
acuity.definitionFr: acuité, finesse de perception ou vivacité d'esprit
sentences: Even in her nineties, the retired supreme court justice demonstrated remarkable intellectual acuity during complex legal panel discussions.
Predatory hawks rely on extraordinary visual acuity to spot tiny field mice scampering through dense prairie grass from soaring heights.
acuity.mnemonic: Acuité visuelle ou auditive : le tranchant aiguisé des sens.

agrarian.definition: relating to cultivated land or agricultural societies
agrarian.definitionFr: agraire, relatif à l'agriculture et aux terres cultivées
sentences: Before the industrial revolution transformed national economies, most European nations were predominantly agrarian societies dependent upon seasonal crop harvests.
The reform party advocated comprehensive agrarian policies designed to redistribute fallow farmland to impoverished peasant cooperatives across the province.
agrarian.mnemonic: Agraire, comme agriculture et agronome : qui touche aux champs.

amalgam.definition: a mixture or blend of diverse elements
sentences: The band's distinctive musical style was an eclectic amalgam of traditional Irish folk melodies and energetic contemporary punk rock rhythms.
The cosmopolitan metropolis became a vibrant amalgam of culinary traditions imported by immigrant communities arriving from every continent on Earth.
amalgam.mnemonic: Faire un amalgame : mélanger des éléments différents en un tout.

anachronism.definition: something out of its proper historical time period
anachronism.definitionFr: anachronisme, élément déplacé dans le temps
sentences: Eagle-eyed film critics immediately noticed an obvious anachronism when a Roman gladiator was filmed wearing a modern digital wristwatch.
Critics argued that the hereditary aristocratic title was a quaint anachronism that had no valid place in a modern democracy.
anachronism.mnemonic: Ana (en arrière) + chronos (temps) : erreur de repère temporel.

antedate.definition: to precede in time; to come before
sentences: Recent archaeological digs unearthed intricate stone tools that antedate the earliest known Egyptian monuments by more than two thousand years.
Her intense skepticism regarding corporate promises seemed to antedate her employment, having formed during her early university research days.
antedate.mnemonic: Ante (avant) + date : porter ou situer une date antérieure.

apostate.definition: a person who renounces a religious or political belief
apostate.definitionFr: apostat, renégat qui abandonne sa foi ou son parti
sentences: After renouncing his monastic vows and publishing a critique of dogma, the former monk was condemned as an apostate by church leaders.
The party faithful viewed the senator as a treacherous apostate when he voted against his own caucus on the vital tax measure.
apostate.mnemonic: Apostat : celui qui commet une apostasie, renonçant publiquement à sa foi.

approbation.definition: approval or praise, often formal or official
approbation.definitionFr: approbation, accord formel ou éloge officiel
sentences: The architect presented her ambitious museum designs to the municipal council, hoping to win their enthusiastic approbation and funding.
The young novelist craved the critical approbation of respected literary reviewers rather than the fleeting adoration of commercial best-seller lists.
approbation.mnemonic: Approbation : donner son blanc-seing ou approuver chaleureusement.

apropos.definition: very appropriate to a particular situation; relevant
sentences: Her humorous opening remark was remarkably apropos, breaking the tension in the boardroom before the tough financial review began.
The professor shared an apropos quotation from Shakespeare that perfectly illustrated the ethical dilemma being debated by the philosophy students.
apropos.mnemonic: Vient directement du français « à propos » : qui arrive au bon moment.

archetype.definition: a very typical example of a certain person or thing
archetype.definitionFr: archétype, modèle idéal ou exemple par excellence
sentences: In classical folklore, the brave knight setting forth to slay the dragon represents the enduring archetype of the heroic savior.
With his stoic demeanor and rugged leather jacket, the protagonist became the cinematic archetype of the brooding twentieth-century rebel.
archetype.mnemonic: Arché (origine) + type : le patron originel dont dérivent les autres.

ascetic.definition: characterized by severe self-discipline and abstention from indulgences
ascetic.definitionFr: ascétique, austère, rejetant les plaisirs matériels
sentences: The holy hermit led an austere ascetic life in the mountains, subsisting solely on wild roots and spring water for decades.
During his rigorous training camp, the marathon runner adopted an ascetic routine that eliminated all sugary foods and late-night entertainment.
ascetic.mnemonic: Ascète : personne qui s'impose de rudes privations pour s'élever.

assiduous.definition: showing great care, attention, and persistent effort
sentences: Through assiduous research in dusty cathedral archives, the historian uncovered previously lost manuscripts detailing medieval trade networks between merchant republics.
The medical student's assiduous study habits paid off when she received the highest score on the grueling licensing examination.
assiduous.mnemonic: Assidu : qui reste assis à sa table pour travailler sans relâche.

astringent.definition: harsh or severe in manner; sharp or bitter
astringent.definitionFr: astringent, piquant, acerbe dans le ton ou le goût
sentences: The drama critic was dreaded throughout the theatrical community for his astringent reviews, which often demolished actors' fragile reputations within sentences.
Unripe persimmons leave an unpleasantly astringent taste in the mouth that causes one's tongue to feel instantly dry and puckered.
astringent.mnemonic: Astringent : qui resserre les tissus ou blesse par sa verdeur mordante.

augur.definition: to portend a good or bad outcome
augur.definitionFr: augurer, présager une issue favorable ou défavorable
sentences: The sharp quarterly rise in manufacturing orders seemed to augur well for the country's economic recovery after two sluggish years.
Dark gathering storm clouds and sudden dropping temperatures did not augur well for the mountaineers stranded on the exposed ridge.
augur.mnemonic: Comme les augures romains observant le vol des oiseaux : présager.

bucolic.definition: relating to the pleasant aspects of the countryside
sentences: Tired of the frantic city noise, the family spent their summer vacation renting a cottage in a tranquil bucolic valley.
The poet composed verses celebrating bucolic scenes of grazing sheep and wildflower meadows bathed in the golden morning sunlight.
bucolic.mnemonic: Bucolique : le charme reposant de la campagne et des bergers.

byzantine.definition: excessively complicated and typically involving intricate bureaucracy
sentences: Foreign investors found it frustrating to navigate the byzantine bureaucracy required to obtain commercial building permits from the regional government.
The novel featured a byzantine plot involving double agents, secret pacts, and false identities that baffled even the most attentive readers.
byzantine.mnemonic: Querelle byzantine / complexité byzantine : le labyrinthe des cours d'Orient.

canonize.definition: to treat or regard as an authoritative classic
canonize.definitionFr: canoniser, consacrer comme un modèle ou un classique
sentences: Literary academics were quick to canonize the novelist's masterpiece, adding it to compulsory university reading lists across the English-speaking world.
Film festivals helped canonize the foreign director's experimental movies as monumental achievements in the history of twentieth-century world cinema.
canonize.mnemonic: Faire entrer dans le canon (la liste des œuvres saintes ou de référence).

capitulate.definition: to cease resisting an opponent or an unwelcome demand
capitulate.definitionFr: capituler, céder face à une pression ou un adversaire
sentences: After weeks of intense consumer boycotts and falling share values, the corporation had to capitulate to the union's fair wage demands.
The besieged fortress had to capitulate when its food supplies ran out completely after four grueling months under enemy bombardment.
capitulate.mnemonic: Capituler : signer les conditions de la reddition, s'avouer vaincu.

cathartic.definition: providing psychological relief through the open expression of strong emotions
cathartic.definitionFr: cathartique, libérateur sur le plan émotionnel
sentences: Weeping openly at the memorial service provided a cathartic release for the grieving family after months of keeping their sorrow bottled.
Writing the confessional memoir proved profoundly cathartic for the former soldier, helping him process painful memories from the battlefield.
cathartic.mnemonic: Catharsis aristotélicienne : purger ses émotions pour se sentir soulagé.

cavalier.definition: showing a lack of proper concern; dismissive or haughty
sentences: The factory manager displayed a cavalier attitude toward workplace safety regulations, dismissing workers' legitimate warnings until a serious accident occurred.
Investors were outraged by the executive's cavalier explanation for the multimillion-dollar budget deficit during the tense annual shareholders meeting.
cavalier.mnemonic: Traiter de façon cavalière : toiser de haut, avec dédain et désinvolture.

circumlocution.definition: the use of unnecessarily many words to express an idea
circumlocution.definitionFr: circonlocution, périphrase inutile pour éviter de parler franchement
sentences: Rather than admitting his mistake directly, the politician relied on evasive circumlocution to avoid taking responsibility during the televised debate.
The legal contract was filled with dense circumlocution that obscured the simple fact that tenants forfeited their initial security deposits.
circumlocution.mnemonic: Circum (autour) + locution (parler) : tourner autour du pot au lieu de trancher.

corollary.definition: a direct or natural consequence or result
sentences: A tragic corollary of the prolonged factory shutdown was the widespread economic devastation of local businesses that relied on worker patronage.
Increased personal liberty is an essential corollary of a healthy democratic system that respects the fundamental rights of all citizens.
corollary.mnemonic: En mathématiques et en logique, le corollaire découle immédiatement du théorème.

coterie.definition: a small, exclusive group of people with shared interests
coterie.definitionFr: coterie, cercle fermé ou clique de personnes aux mêmes intérêts
sentences: The avant-garde artist was surrounded by an intimate coterie of wealthy patrons and flattering intellectuals who praised his every painting.
Decision-making within the secretive agency was monopolized by a tight coterie of senior officials who deliberately excluded outside reformist experts.
coterie.mnemonic: Même mot en français : coterie, un cercle d'initiés qui se serrent les coudes.

dilettante.definition: a person who cultivates an area of interest without real commitment
sentences: The seasoned laboratory scientists regarded the aristocratic collector as a mere dilettante who treated complex botanical research as a casual weekend hobby.
Despite buying expensive brushes and rare pigments, he remained an artistic dilettante who never mastered the fundamental techniques of classical portraiture.
dilettante.mnemonic: Dilettante : qui s'intéresse à un art pour le plaisir sans approfondir.

sentences: The scandal sparked loud public disapprobation, forcing the disgraced mayor to resign from office before his term of service concluded.
Conservative parents voiced profound disapprobation regarding the explicit themes in the controversial play staged by the local high school drama club.
disapprobation.mnemonic: Dis + approbation : le contraire de l'approbation, un blâme appuyé.

dissolute.definition: lax in morals; debauched or licentious
dissolute.definitionFr: dissolu, débauché et livré aux excès
sentences: The heir squandered his vast family fortune through a dissolute lifestyle characterized by reckless gambling and nightly drunken revelry in luxury casinos.
Moralists criticized the dissolute behavior of the imperial court, warning that unchecked hedonism would soon lead to the ruin of the empire.
dissolute.mnemonic: Dissolu : dont les mœurs se sont dissoutes, débauché sans retenue.

droll.definition: curious or unusual in a way that provokes dry amusement
sentences: The playwright delivered a droll commentary on modern romance, eliciting quiet chuckles from theatregoers with his wry observations and deadpan timing.
Her droll wit kept her traveling companions entertained throughout the delayed flight, turning an annoying ordeal into an amusing shared adventure.
droll.mnemonic: Drôle au sens piquant et singulier, avec un humour subtil et pince-sans-rire.

echelon.definition: a level or rank in an organization, profession, or society
echelon.definitionFr: échelon, niveau ou grade dans une hiérarchie
sentences: After years of dedicated laboratory breakthroughs, the brilliant chemist finally reached the highest echelon of the prestigious international scientific academy.
Corruption within the upper echelon of the police department eroded public trust and sparked sweeping administrative reforms across the metropolitan force.
echelon.mnemonic: Gravir les échelons : monter dans les grades d'une institution.

edify.definition: to instruct or improve someone morally or intellectually
edify.definitionFr: édifier, élever l'esprit ou instruire moralement
sentences: The philosopher wrote inspiring parables designed to edify young citizens and encourage them to cultivate virtue over fleeting material wealth.
The public library hosted regular lectures meant to edify the local community about sustainable agricultural practices and local environmental conservation.
edify.mnemonic: Édifier : bâtir spirituellement et moralement la sagesse de quelqu'un.

elide.definition: to omit, suppress, or join together
elide.definitionFr: élider, omettre ou gommer une distinction
sentences: In attempting to simplify the complex historical narrative, the author chose to elide several crucial political rivalries that shaped the peace treaty.
The orator had a tendency to elide distinct syllables when speaking rapidly, making his impassioned arguments somewhat difficult for listeners to follow.
elide.mnemonic: Élision / élider : effacer une voyelle ou escamoter un détail.

ersatz.definition: used as a substitute, typically an inferior one
ersatz.definitionFr: ersatz, de substitution, imitation de moindre qualité
sentences: During the wartime blockade, citizens were forced to brew an ersatz coffee concocted from roasted acorns and bitter chicory roots.
The tourist trap offered cheap ersatz champagne made with carbonated cider, leaving patrons bitterly disappointed by the masquerade at midnight.
ersatz.mnemonic: Un ersatz : produit de remplacement inférieur au produit d'origine.

esoteric.definition: intended for or understood by only an initiated few
esoteric.definitionFr: ésotérique, réservé à un petit cercle d'initiés
sentences: The theoretical seminar focused on esoteric algebraic concepts that baffled everyone in attendance except the most senior doctoral students in physics.
Ancient alchemists encoded their laboratory recipes in esoteric symbols to ensure that uninitiated outsiders could never replicate their secret experiments.
esoteric.mnemonic: Ésotérique : opposé à exotérique (public) ; réservé à l'intérieur du temple.

euphony.definition: the quality of being pleasing to the ear
euphony.definitionFr: euphonie, harmonie sonore agréable à l'oreille
sentences: Poets carefully select each word not only for its literal meaning, but also for the pleasing euphony of its consonant sounds.
The classical composer favored the gentle euphony of wooden flutes and harps over the jarring dissonance of modern brass ensembles.
euphony.mnemonic: Eu (bon/beau) + phone (son) : belle sonorité douce à l'oreille.

evanescent.definition: soon passing out of sight, memory, or existence; fleeting
sentences: The rainbow cast a brilliant arc across the stormy lake, but its evanescent beauty faded completely within just a few brief minutes.
Morning mist clung to the damp riverbank, creating an evanescent shroud that vanished as soon as the warm sun rose over the hills.
evanescent.mnemonic: Évanescent : qui s'évanouit comme de la vapeur ou un souffle.

existential.definition: relating to existence, especially human survival or meaning
existential.definitionFr: existentiel, relatif à l'existence ou à la survie
sentences: Climate scientists warned that unmitigated global warming represents an existential threat to island nations threatened by catastrophic rising sea levels.
During his midlife crisis, the executive fell into deep existential anxiety regarding the true purpose and ultimate meaning of his career.
existential.mnemonic: Existentiel : qui touche à l'essence même de l'existence et de la survie.

explicate.definition: to analyze and develop an idea or principle in detail
explicate.definitionFr: expliciter, développer et analyser en détail
sentences: The literary scholar took great pains to explicate the subtle biblical allegories woven throughout the poet's celebrated nineteenth-century epic verse.
During the lecture, the economist attempted to explicate the mathematical model underpinning current interest rate decisions made by the central bank.
explicate.mnemonic: Expliciter : déplier les plis (pli-care) d'une pensée pour la rendre claire.

fecund.definition: producing or capable of producing an abundance of offspring or growth
fecund.definitionFr: fécond, très fertile ou intellectuellement productif
sentences: The river delta was renowned for its fecund soil, which yielded three abundant rice harvests every year without requiring artificial fertilizers.
Her remarkably fecund imagination produced dozens of bestselling fantasy novels, captivating generations of enthusiastic young readers across the globe.
fecund.mnemonic: Fécond : qui engendre en abondance (terre fertile, esprit inventif).

foment.definition: to instigate or stir up an undesirable or violent course of action
foment.definitionFr: fomenter, susciter ou attiser des troubles
sentences: Foreign agitators spread sensational propaganda on social media in a deliberate attempt to foment ethnic discord within the border province.
The corrupt general worked secretly behind the scenes to foment a military rebellion against the newly elected civilian government.
foment.mnemonic: Fomenter un complot : souffler sur les braises pour provoquer l'incendie.

frenetic.definition: fast and energetic in a rather wild and uncontrolled way
sentences: The trading floor descended into frenetic chaos as stockbrokers frantically shouted sell orders during the unexpected morning market crash.
After working at a frenetic pace for six consecutive weeks to meet the launch deadline, the exhausted developers finally took a vacation.
frenetic.mnemonic: Frénétique : emporté par une frénésie désordonnée et exténuante.

hedonism.definition: the pursuit of pleasure as the primary goal of life
hedonism.definitionFr: hédonisme, recherche du plaisir comme bien suprême
sentences: The wealthy socialite embraced unbridled hedonism, spending her inheritance entirely on lavish banquets, designer clothes, and exotic island cruises.
Critics argued that the philosophy promoted shallow hedonism rather than the civic duty and moral discipline essential to a stable society.
hedonism.mnemonic: Hédoné (plaisir en grec) : la philosophie de la quête exclusive du plaisir.

hermetic.definition: completely airtight or insulated from outside influence
hermetic.definitionFr: hermétique, étanche à l'air ou isolé du monde extérieur
sentences: The delicate pharmaceutical samples were stored inside an hermetic glass container to prevent any chemical degradation from ambient moisture or airborne microbes.
The reclusive sect lived in hermetic isolation from the surrounding society, refusing electricity, modern medicine, and contact with outside authorities.

heterodox.definition: not conforming with accepted or orthodox standards or beliefs
heterodox.definitionFr: hétérodoxe, non conforme à la doctrine officielle
sentences: The university economist was known for championing heterodox monetary theories that directly challenged traditional academic consensus on inflation control.
Because he dared to express heterodox religious opinions during the theological summit, the young scholar was accused of preaching dangerous heresy.
heterodox.mnemonic: Hétéro (autre) + doxa (opinion/dogme) : en rupture avec l'orthodoxie.

homage.definition: special honor or respect shown publicly
homage.definitionFr: hommage, marque publique de respect et d'admiration
sentences: The contemporary filmmaker created a stylish crime thriller as a loving homage to classic film noir cinema of the nineteen forties.
Thousands of grieving citizens gathered at the central monument to pay respectful homage to the firefighters who died rescuing civilians.
homage.mnemonic: Rendre hommage : témoigner publiquement son admiration et son respect.

iconoclast.definition: a person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditional institutions
iconoclast.definitionFr: iconoclaste, pourfendeur des traditions et des idées reçues
sentences: The young tech founder was an outspoken iconoclast who mocked established corporate hierarchies and advocated completely decentralized workplace structures.
In the conservative world of fine art, the painter was hailed as a brilliant iconoclast for rejecting classical figurative composition.
iconoclast.mnemonic: Icono (image sainte) + claste (briseur) : celui qui brise les idoles établies.

ignoble.definition: not honorable in character or purpose; base and dishonorable
sentences: The disgraced executive used ignoble tactics, such as leaking personal secrets to tabloids, to discredit the whistleblower who exposed his fraud.
Betraying his childhood friend to win a political promotion was regarded by everyone in town as a thoroughly ignoble deed.
ignoble.mnemonic: Ig-noble = non-noble : indigne de noblesse morale, vil.

impecunious.definition: having little or no money; penniless
sentences: During his early years in Paris, the impecunious painter often skipped meals so that he could afford expensive oil paints and canvases.
Coming from an impecunious immigrant family, the scholarship student worked three part-time campus jobs to pay his university tuition on time.

impetuous.definition: acting or done quickly and without thought or care; rash
sentences: His impetuous decision to quit his job without another offer surprised his colleagues, who knew how much he valued steady financial security.
The impetuous commander ordered a full charge into the canyon without scouting ahead, walking straight into the enemy's well-prepared ambush.
impetuous.mnemonic: Impétueux en français : qui agit sous l'impulsion du moment sans réfléchir.

implacable.definition: unable to be appeased, calmed, or placated; relentless
sentences: Despite the governor's repeated apologies, the implacable protesters refused to disperse until all criminal charges against the activists were dropped.
The detective pursued the elusive fugitive with implacable determination, working through freezing rain and sleepless nights across three remote provinces.
implacable.mnemonic: Im-placable : qu'on ne peut pas apaiser ou calmer (du latin placare).

incontrovertible.definition: not able to be denied or disputed; completely certain
sentences: The prosecutor presented incontrovertible video footage of the robbery, leaving the defense team with no plausible way to claim their client's innocence.
